text:
OpenAI has finally released its first open-weight large language models since 2019’s GPT-2. These new “gpt-oss” models are available in two different sizes and score similarly to the company’s o3-mini and o4-mini models on several benchmarks. Unlike the models available through OpenAI’s web interface, these new open models can be freely downloaded, run, and even modified on laptops and other local devices.

In the company’s many years without an open LLM release, some users have taken to referring to it with the pejorative “ClosedAI.” That sense of frustration had escalated in the past few months as these long-awaited models were delayed twice—first in June and then in July. With their release, however, OpenAI is reestablishing itself as a presence for users of open models.

That’s particularly notable at a time when Meta, which had previously dominated the American open-model landscape with its Llama models, may be reorienting toward closed releases—and when Chinese open models, such as DeepSeek’s offerings, Kimi K2, and Alibaba’s Qwen series, are becoming more popular than their American competitors.

“The vast majority of our [enterprise and startup] customers are already using a lot of open models,” said Casey Dvorak, a research program manager at OpenAI, in a media briefing about the model release. “Because there is no [competitive] open model from OpenAI, we wanted to plug that gap and actually allow them to use our technology across the board.”

The new models come in two different sizes, the smaller of which can theoretically run on 16 GB of RAM—the minimum amount that Apple currently offers on its computers. The larger model requires a high-end laptop or specialized hardware.

Open models have a few key use cases. Some organizations may want to customize models for their own purposes or save money by running models on their own equipment, though that equipment comes at a substantial upfront cost. Others—such hospitals, law firms, and governments—might need models that they can run locally for data security reasons. 

OpenAI has facilitated such activity by releasing its open models under a permissive Apache 2.0 license, which allows the models to be used for commercial purposes. Nathan Lambert, post-training lead at the Allen Institute for AI, says that this choice is commendable: Such licenses are typical for Chinese open-model releases, but Meta released its Llama models under a bespoke, more restrictive license. “It’s a very good thing for the open community,” he says.

Researchers who study how LLMs work also need open models, so that they can examine and manipulate those models in detail. “In part, this is about reasserting OpenAI’s dominance in the research ecosystem,” says Peter Henderson, an assistant professor at Princeton University who has worked extensively with open models. If researchers do adopt gpt-oss as new workhorses, OpenAI could see some concrete benefits, Henderson says—it might adopt innovations discovered by other researchers into its own model ecosystem.

More broadly, Lambert says, releasing an open model now could help OpenAI reestablish its status in an increasingly crowded AI environment. “It kind of goes back to years ago, where they were seen as the AI company,” he says. Users who want to use open models will now have the option to meet all their needs with OpenAI products, rather than turning to Meta’s Llama or Alibaba’s Qwen when they need to run something locally.

The rise of Chinese open models like Qwen over the past year may have been a particularly salient factor in OpenAI’s calculus. An employee from OpenAI emphasized at the media briefing that the company doesn’t see these open models as a response to actions taken by any other AI company, but OpenAI is clearly attuned to the geopolitical implications of China’s open-model dominance. “Broad access to these capable open-weights models created in the US helps expand democratic AI rails,” the company wrote in a blog post announcing the models’ release. 

Since DeepSeek exploded onto the AI scene at the start of 2025, observers have noted that Chinese models often refuse to speak about topics that the Chinese Communist Party has deemed verboten, such as Tiananmen Square. Such observations—as well as longer-term risks, like the possibility that agentic models could purposefully write vulnerable code—have made some AI experts concerned about the growing adoption of Chinese models. “Open models are a form of soft power,” Henderson says.

Lambert released a report on Monday documenting how Chinese models are overtaking American offerings like Llama and advocating for a renewed commitment to domestic open models. Several prominent AI researchers and entrepreneurs, such as HuggingFace CEO Clement Delangue, Stanford’s Percy Liang, and former OpenAI researcher Miles Brundage, have signed on.

The Trump administration, too, has emphasized development of open models in its AI Action Plan. With both this model release and previous statements, OpenAI is aligning itself with that stance. “In their filings about the action plan, [OpenAI] pretty clearly indicated that they see US–China as a key issue and want to position themselves as very important to the US system,” says Rishi Bommasani, a senior research scholar at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence. 

And OpenAI may see concrete political advantages from aligning with the administration’s AI priorities, Lambert says. As the company continues to build out its extensive computational infrastructure, it will need political support and approvals, and sympathetic leadership could go a long way.

text:
🗞️19 November 2026 | Daily Edition: Pre-Market

Anthropic Lit the Futures Board, Bitcoin Climbed Back From $62,000

Bitcoin tested $62,000 after the bell and spent the night climbing back toward $63,900 as Anthropic's record IPO lifted Nasdaq futures about 2%, while ETFs shed another $306 million, Hong Kong flagged Hyperliquid and court papers itemised the Binance theft.

Prepared around 5:55 AM EST on Thursday 19 November. This edition picks up from Wednesday's US Close, prepared at 4:05 PM EST, and only adds what happened since: the evening session, Anthropic's pricing, Wednesday's fund flows, Asia and the first hours of Europe. Crypto prices are live prints as of about 5:55 AM EST, and futures, oil, Treasury, dollar and gold figures are live overnight prints.

1⃣ Bitcoin defended $62,000 in the evening and climbed through the night

Bitcoin was near $62,538 at last night's edition. It kept sliding after the close and printed exactly $62,000 at 5:55 PM EST, about $50 above Saturday night's $61,950 low, before buyers stepped in. When stock futures reopened at 6:00 PM EST it jumped to about $63,200 inside the hour, then held about $62,320 to $62,350 twice, in the 8:00 PM and 10:00 PM EST hours. From there it climbed steadily: about $63,680 by 11:00 PM EST, about $63,800 in the Asia session at 2:00 AM EST and about $63,865 at 4:05 AM EST, with dips stopping at about $63,225 after midnight, $63,500 at 3:00 AM EST and $63,615 at 4:00 AM EST. It pushed to an overnight high of about $63,905 at 5:50 AM EST and trades near $63,780, about 2% above last night's edition but still about 0.7% lower over 24 hours.

🖊️ Market significance: The $61,950 to $62,000 zone held for a second time this week, and each pullback since 11:00 PM EST has stopped higher than the one before.

🗨️ My viewpoint: A clean defence of $62,000 followed by a staircase of higher lows after midnight is the best structure Bitcoin has shown since the weekend. But the whole night happened below $64,000, and that is the level that decides whether this is a recovery or just a bounce inside the range.

2⃣ Ether reclaimed $1,800, Solana and XRP lagged

Ether was near $1,754 at last night's edition. It dipped to about $1,748 at 5:50 PM EST, holding above Wednesday's $1,745 afternoon low and the $1,731 session low, then climbed through the night to about $1,812 at 5:05 AM EST, its best level since early Wednesday. It trades near $1,805, about 3% above last night's edition and slightly positive over 24 hours. Solana bottomed at about $72.20 at 5:50 PM EST, reached about $75.25 at 2:00 AM EST and is near $74.50, flat on the day. XRP fell to about $0.954 at 8:35 PM EST and is near $0.981, down about 1.4% over 24 hours. Zcash is near $950, up about 1.5%, and HYPE near $68.45, flat.

🖊️ Market significance: Ether outperformed Bitcoin overnight, while the two majors that led earlier this week, Solana and XRP, gave up the leadership.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Getting back above $1,800 matters, but $1,812 is still well below the $1,835 to $1,842 band that has capped Ether since Sunday. I treat this as repair, not a breakout, until that band goes.

3⃣ The rebound was short covering, and funding flipped negative

Bitcoin perpetual open interest fell about 6% since last night's edition to about 37,560 BTC on the largest on-chain perps venue and about 3% to about 32,890 BTC on a large offshore exchange, while price rose about 2%. Funding on Bitcoin perpetuals turned slightly negative on both venues, from positive at yesterday's close. In the evening dip, six large traders on the on-chain venue were liquidated 30 times for a total of about 618 BTC, roughly $38.7 million, at prices between $62,055 and $63,364. Ether positioning is split, with open interest down about 2% on the on-chain venue and up about 4% offshore. Looking further out, a Swiss digital asset bank forecast that the Bitcoin futures carry trade will beat three-month Treasury bills by more than 2% a year in 2027 as demand for leverage returns.

🖊️ Market significance: Rising price with falling open interest and negative funding means shorts closed into the rally. Nobody added fresh long leverage to drive it.

🗨️ My viewpoint: That cuts both ways. A move built on covering can run out once the shorts are gone, but negative funding near the lows also tells me the crowd is leaning bearish, which is usually where squeezes start. I want to see open interest rise with price above $64,000 before I trust the move.

4⃣ ETFs lost another $306 million, and Binance now sells 24/7 IBIT exposure

US spot Bitcoin ETFs had net outflows of about $306 million on Wednesday, the second outflow day in a row. BlackRock's IBIT led with about $149 million out, followed by Fidelity's FBTC at about $69 million, Bitwise's BITB at about $37 million, Grayscale's GBTC at about $20 million, ARK's ARKB at about $19 million and Grayscale's mini trust at about $11 million. No fund took in money. That takes November's net outflows to about $2.9 billion. Spot Ether ETFs lost about $40 million, led by BlackRock's ETHA at about $17 million and Grayscale's mini trust at about $15 million. Separately, Binance listed on Wednesday a perpetual contract tied to IBIT, settled in USDT, with up to 20 times leverage and trading around the clock, including when Nasdaq is closed.

🖊️ Market significance: All five of the largest issuers sold on Wednesday, so this was broad de-risking, not one large holder rotating.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The custody transfers we saw on Wednesday morning pointed to exactly this print. The IBIT perpetual is a useful reminder that the ETF wrapper is now being traded offshore with leverage. I still need two or three inflow days in a row, led by IBIT, before I read the flows as turning.

5⃣ Anthropic priced at $83, and on-chain markets already trade it above $105

Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share late Wednesday, above its $70 to $78 range, and upsized it to 980 million shares, about 956 million from the company and about 24 million from existing holders. That raises about $81.3 billion, the largest IPO on record, ahead of SpaceX's $75 billion in June, and values the company at about $1.5 trillion. It starts trading on Nasdaq today as ANT. The pre-IPO perpetual on the largest on-chain perps venue is near $105.50 and a similar contract offshore near $105.90, both up about 6.5% on the day and about 27% above the offer price. Kraken said Anthropic will be live on its platform from day one, and Solana's ecosystem account signalled day-one access on Solana, as tokenized equities on Solana passed $1.2 billion in circulating value, nearly double the October close. Polymarket opened a market on the size of the first-day pop.

🖊️ Market significance: Crypto rails are now pricing the biggest listing in history around the clock before it opens, and the deal is setting the tone for the whole risk complex this morning.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The on-chain contracts have called the direction of most big debuts this year, so a 27% implied premium is a real signal. The risk for crypto is the other way round: a weak opening would hit the same AI trade that is lifting futures, and Bitcoin would feel it.

6⃣ Hong Kong put Hyperliquid on its suspicious platforms list

Hong Kong's Securities and Futures Commission added "Hyperliquid / Hyperliquid Hong Kong" to its alert list of suspicious virtual asset trading platforms, naming the https://t.co/7mFtNrGwVp trading site. The regulator said the platform is not licensed in Hong Kong and is suspected of operating, or marketing, a virtual asset trading platform to the Hong Kong public. The entry is a warning, not an enforcement action, a block or a finding of misconduct, and it sits alongside other unlicensed venues on the same list.

🖊️ Market significance: A regulator in a licensed market has now formally flagged the biggest on-chain perps venue, just as its pre-IPO markets draw global attention.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The direct impact is small, since HYPE barely moved, but it sets a precedent. On-chain venues that market to retail in licensed jurisdictions will get the same treatment as offshore exchanges, and I expect other Asian regulators to follow.

7⃣ Six senators asked Treasury not to tilt the GENIUS Act toward federal charters

A bipartisan group of six senators, including Cynthia Lummis, Kirsten Gillibrand, Angela Alsobrooks, Kevin Cramer, Pete Ricketts and Mark Warner, wrote to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warning that Treasury's proposed GENIUS Act rules give a safe harbour to issuers with pending federal applications but no equivalent protection for state-supervised issuers. They said that could push firms toward a federal licence through the bank regulator, "the opposite of our intent", and asked Treasury to extend the safe harbour to issuers in states expected to have qualifying frameworks before 18 January 2028.

🖊️ Market significance: How the stablecoin law is implemented will decide whether the state path to issuance survives, which matters for every non-bank issuer.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is the authors of the law correcting the regulator in public. I read it as a sign the final rules will be softened for state issuers, which keeps competition in issuance alive.

8⃣ A ratings agency kept USDT at its weakest score, and Tether hit back

S&P Global Ratings kept USDT at 5, or weak, the lowest score on its stablecoin stability scale, unchanged from a year ago. It said higher-risk assets, including gold, Bitcoin, listed equities, secured loans and corporate bonds, covered 28% of USDT in circulation at 30 September, up from 24% a year earlier, and that a sharp fall in those assets could leave the token undercollateralized. Gold holdings were about $19 billion, about 10% of circulation, and Bitcoin holdings fell to about $8.4 billion from $9.9 billion. Tether's September report showed about $191.5 billion of assets against $183.5 billion of liabilities, and the company said "the problem is S&P's framework, not our reserves", comparing the agency to its record before 2008.

🖊️ Market significance: The largest stablecoin is moving further into volatile assets just as gold fell about 3% in a day and Bitcoin trades near cycle lows.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The $8 billion cushion is real, but a 30% drop across its roughly $27 billion of gold and Bitcoin would erase about that much on paper. I do not see a peg risk today, I see a reason why the regulated dollar tokens keep winning institutional share.

9⃣ Court papers listed 192 tokens taken from Binance, and the thief moved another $248 million of Ether

An asset schedule filed with the Abu Dhabi court order shows the October attack on Binance wallets took 192 different tokens across 11 networks. USDT was the largest item at about $2.50 billion, followed by about $1.42 billion of Bitcoin and about $826 million of USDC, about 76% of the total between them. Fiat-backed stablecoins made up at least $3.46 billion, or about 55%, including nine smaller dollar and euro tokens, alongside about $58 million of tokenized gold and about $38 million of memecoins. Overnight, the hacker's wallets moved another 137,602 ETH, about $248 million, with batches of 12,000 ETH leaving between about 1:50 and 1:55 AM EST.

🖊️ Market significance: More than half the stolen value sits in tokens that issuers can freeze, which is why the court's worldwide order matters so much for recovery.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The stablecoin share is the hopeful part of this story. The Ether is the part I watch, because every batch that moves is potential supply hitting markets through laundering routes, and this is the latest in a run of large batches this week.

1⃣0⃣ Washington opened a scam-disruption centre, and BTCPay pushed an emergency patch

The Homeland Security Task Force launched a Threat Disruption Center, co-led by Homeland Security Investigations and the FBI, to bring more than 30 federal agencies and over 440 state and local partners together to trace scam networks, warn victims sooner and stop payments, including crypto transfers, with a blockchain analytics firm as its main technology partner. Separately, BTCPay Server, the self-hosted Bitcoin payment software, issued an emergency update for five flaws in its Nginx web layer that the EU's cyber response team said could let attackers run code remotely without logging in. No attacks had been reported.

🖊️ Market significance: Federal enforcement is now formally wired into crypto rails for fraud, while merchant infrastructure had to patch a serious hole overnight.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Faster freezing is good for the industry's reputation and bad for the scam economy that still runs through stablecoins. Anyone running a BTCPay node should treat the patch as urgent.

1⃣1⃣ Singapore settled tokenized bills with central bank money, HSBC and PDAX brought tokens to savers

The Monetary Authority of Singapore said it issued S$100 million, about $77.5 million, of four-week tokenized bills on 6 November, paid for with wholesale central bank digital currency, and five banks bid more than twice the amount on offer. It will turn the test network into a live settlement system, renamed SG Digital Ledger, and plans more tokenized bills in 2027. In Hong Kong, HSBC opened a tokenized class of its Hong Kong dollar money market fund to retail customers from HK$100, subscribed and settled only with its RedCoin stablecoin. In the Philippines, the exchange PDAX now lets users turn PYUSD, USDG and USDPT on Solana into balances that can buy government retail dollar bonds, a first for the country.

🖊️ Market significance: Central bank settlement, a global bank's retail fund and a sovereign bond sale all moved onto tokens in Asia in one night.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is where the real adoption is happening while prices struggle. Singapore turning a pilot into infrastructure is the strongest signal, because it gives tokenized assets a settlement asset with no credit risk.

1⃣2⃣ Kraken's parent is buying its co-CEO's venture firm

Payward, Kraken's parent, agreed to acquire Tribe Capital, the venture firm co-founded by Kraken co-CEO Arjun Sethi, with about $2.7 billion under management and stakes in private companies including SpaceX. Terms were not disclosed, and the deal is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027.

🖊️ Market significance: An exchange owner is buying a private-markets manager on the day the biggest private company in AI goes public.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The strategy is clear: own the pipeline of private assets that can later be tokenized and listed. The related-party angle will draw questions, and I want to see how the deal is valued before calling it a win.

1⃣3⃣ Large holders shifted coins overnight, and USDC supply kept shrinking

Two large holders unstaked about 2.31 million SOL, roughly $169 million, and deposited it with Coinbase Prime, flagged around 5:00 AM EST, often a step before selling or hedging. Four wallets withdrew about 13,408 ETH, roughly $24 million, from institutional trading desks and a large exchange late Wednesday evening, a sign of accumulation. Total stablecoin supply is near $286 billion, and USDC supply fell by about $600 million to $700 million since yesterday's close to about $68.2 billion to $68.5 billion, while USDT held near $175.1 billion.

🖊️ Market significance: Solana faces a large potential supply overhang today, and dollar balances on-chain are still draining even as prices recover.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The SOL deposit may help explain why Solana lagged the overnight bounce. The USDC decline matters more to me, because a lasting bottom usually needs stablecoin supply to stop falling first.

1⃣4⃣ The global securities watchdog warned quantum upgrades will slow blockchains

The International Organization of Securities Commissions published a report warning that moving blockchains to quantum-resistant signatures could slow transactions, raise fees and increase storage, because the new signatures are much larger. It cited a test version of Solana that ran about 90% slower with quantum-resistant signatures, said wallets that keep older keys could stay exposed after an upgrade, and urged firms to start preparing now because the transition could take years, even though no known quantum computer can break today's cryptography.

🖊️ Market significance: The quantum question has moved from developer forums into the rulebook of securities regulators, which will shape what institutions ask of the chains they use.

🗨️ My viewpoint: No near-term risk, but the trade-off is real. Chains that plan the migration early, with minimal throughput loss, will have an edge with regulated money.

1⃣5⃣ Strategy faces its investors tonight, and a Korean Ether treasury turned to buybacks

Strategy's Michael Saylor and chief executive Phong Le hold an investor Q&A at 5:00 PM EST today, after STRC closed Wednesday near $96.11, about 4% below the $100 par it needs to keep selling new preferred stock. In Seoul, Parataxis Ethereum approved a KRW 1 billion share buyback of up to 632,911 shares over six months, while holding 11,729 ETH after its latest purchase of about 1,280 ETH.

🖊️ Market significance: Treasury companies are spending cash on their own paper rather than new coins, which removes a source of spot demand.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Tonight's call matters for the whole sector. I want to hear how Strategy plans to defend par without selling Bitcoin, because that answer sets the tone for every treasury firm trading below its coins.

1⃣6⃣ Anthropic lifted Nasdaq futures about 2% after a mixed Wednesday close

Nasdaq 100 futures are up about 2%, near 27,745 to 27,775, S&P 500 futures are up about 1.2%, near 7,425 to 7,430, and Dow futures are up about 0.6%, near 50,580 to 50,590, as Anthropic's pricing revived the beaten-down AI trade. On Wednesday the Dow lost about 1.1%, the S&P 500 slipped about 0.2% and the Nasdaq gained about 0.4%. Walmart reports before the open.

🖊️ Market significance: The bid is concentrated in tech and AI names, the same trade that sold off after Nvidia's leadership change and its post-earnings reversal.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Futures gave Bitcoin the lift overnight, so the cash open matters. If the Nasdaq holds most of this gap after 9:30 AM EST, Bitcoin has room to test $64,000; if the gap fades like Wednesday's Nvidia jump, I expect crypto to follow it down.

1⃣7⃣ Oil and gold steadied, yields edged up and the dollar eased off its high

Brent is near $92.20 to $92.50 and WTI near $83.60 to $83.90, both modestly higher after Wednesday's inventory-led drop. The 10-year Treasury yield is near 5.08% to 5.09%, up 1 to 2 basis points after Wednesday's rally, and markets price a December rate hike at above 90%. The dollar index is near 103.6 to 103.75, slightly softer but close to a 19-month high. Gold is near $3,734 to $3,740 after an overnight low of $3,694.50, steadying after Wednesday's drop of about 3.4%.

🖊️ Market significance: The macro backdrop has not changed overnight: a 10-year above 5% and a near-certain December hike keep pressure on anything that needs cheap money.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The equity bounce is about one IPO, not about rates. As long as the 10-year sits above 5%, I treat crypto rallies as tradeable, not as a regime change.

1⃣8⃣ Jobless claims and the Philly Fed open the US day, then Anthropic's first trade

Weekly jobless claims and the Philadelphia Fed manufacturing index are due at 8:30 AM EST, and the leading economic index at 10:00 AM EST. Anthropic should open on Nasdaq after the 9:30 AM EST bell, Strategy's investor Q&A follows at 5:00 PM EST, and Thursday's ETF flows publish tonight.

🖊️ Market significance: A low claims print would reinforce the case for a December hike, while Anthropic's first trade will set the tone for the AI and crypto risk trade into Friday.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The data matters less than the debut today. I watch the claims number for rate pressure, but the Anthropic opening price is the real event for crypto.

🗨️ My Overall Viewpoint:
The night gave me the best structure of the week, but on borrowed fuel. Bitcoin tested $62,000 for the second time in four days, held it to the dollar, held $62,320 to $62,350 twice in the evening and then built higher lows after midnight on the way to $63,905 as Anthropic's record pricing lifted Nasdaq futures. Ether did better, back above $1,800. Under the surface, though, the rebound was short covering with negative funding, not new demand. ETFs lost another $306 million with no fund taking in money, USDC supply kept shrinking, two whales moved $169 million of SOL to a prime broker and the Binance thief moved another $248 million of Ether. The build-out did not pause: Singapore made tokenized bills a settlement product, HSBC put a tokenized fund in a retail app, and Hong Kong put Hyperliquid on notice.

For the US session, my Bitcoin support is $63,500 to $63,615, the early-morning dips, then $63,225, the post-midnight low, then $62,320 to $62,350, the evening lows, and $61,950 to $62,000, the double bottom from Saturday night and Wednesday evening, with the long cluster between $59,500 and $62,200 and the bid near $60,000 below it. Resistance is $63,865 to $63,905, the overnight highs, then $64,000 to $64,050, the old ceiling and round number, $64,370, Wednesday morning's high, and $64,890, Wednesday's Asia high. A daily close above $64,050 would turn Wednesday's breakdown into a failed move, while losing $62,000 opens the long cluster. For Ether, support is $1,791, then $1,762, $1,748 and $1,731, Wednesday's low. Resistance is $1,812, the overnight high, then the $1,835 to $1,842 band that has capped every rally since Sunday. I stay defensive but less so than last night. I watch the 8:30 AM EST claims and Philly Fed data, Anthropic's opening trade, how open interest behaves if Bitcoin reaches $64,000, the 5:00 PM EST Strategy Q&A and Thursday's ETF flows tonight. These are my analytical levels, not forecasts, and nothing here is financial advice.

Putin makes major Arctic announcement at APEC Summit
The Russian leader addressed business executives ahead of historic talks with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping
Published 18 Nov, 2026 (FULL)
https://t.co/o9jye5ZsV7
Russian President Vladimir Putin has pitched the country’s Arctic and Far East to Asia-Pacific investors, unveiling new incentives set to take effect in January 2027 and special rules for testing advanced technologies.
The package would offer eligible investors tax breaks on profits, property, and land, as well as reduced payroll contributions and preferential leases. Russia also plans to simplify rules for testing drones, industrial robots, and AI in both regions.
“I am confident that the business community and investors from APEC economies will fully appreciate the opportunities emerging in the Russian market – and, naturally, will take advantage of them,” Putin said in a speech at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) CEO Summit in China on Wednesday.
Russia is modernizing its Trans-Siberian and Baikal-Amur railways, expanding the capacity of its Pacific ports, and developing infrastructure along its Northern Sea Route, he said.
Moscow has long promoted the Arctic as a region of international cooperation, including with Western countries.
Russia was a founding member of the Arctic Council in 1996, but joint work was largely suspended by the seven other member states following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022.
Despite deteriorating relations, Putin has repeatedly expressed a willingness to cooperate with Washington on Arctic development. In October, he confirmed that Russia and the US were exploring joint projects in the region, including in energy and advanced technologies.
Meanwhile, the EU has increasingly shifted its focus toward militarization under its new Arctic strategy, which it adopted last month. “To defend our interests, we plan to step up investments in surveillance, infrastructure, military mobility, and capabilities,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.
Britain has also moved to expand its naval presence in the Arctic and North Atlantic. Former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak recently urged London to prepare for strikes against Russian military installations on the Kola Peninsula.
Moscow has repeatedly warned that NATO’s growing military activity risks turning the Arctic into another theater of confrontation.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov accused NATO in August of “driving the region towards militarization,” while reaffirming Moscow’s commitment to “preserving the Arctic as an area of peace and cooperation.”
Russia’s economic initiatives have centered on developing the Northern Sea Route, an Arctic shipping corridor that has gained increased importance amid disruptions to Middle Eastern shipping routes caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Chinese and South Korean shipping companies have already sent container ships through the route in recent months. China’s Sea Legend launched a scheduled service in August, while South Korea’s PanStar completed its first trial voyage to Europe in September. India also plans to send its first pilot cargo vessel along the route in 2027.

text:
Trump, Xi Jinping & Putin: First Trilateral Meeting LIVE | APEC Summit 2026, Shenzhen

At APEC Summit 2026 in Shenzhen, the leaders of the world's three largest nuclear powers are meeting in the same room for the first time. We're covering it live — and we're covering the substance: what is being discussed, what each side is asking for, and what the words they use actually commit them to.

THE AGENDA

Nuclear arms control
The New START treaty between Washington and Moscow lapsed in February. Russia wants it extended. Trump wants something new, and wants Beijing inside it. Xi has shown little appetite for a treaty China had no hand in writing. This is the item with the most at stake and the least agreement behind it — so the language that comes out of it matters more than anything else said in the room.

Iran
The White House says Trump will raise the war directly. Putin will hear it out, but is unlikely to offer anything binding on Russian cooperation with Tehran.

Trade and supply chains
US tariffs peaked at 145% and China retaliated at 125% before the truce that now runs to January 2027. Chinese rare earth exports to Washington remain roughly 75% below normal levels. Xi is pushing open trade, supply chain cooperation and a "non-discriminatory" environment for the region.

AI and advanced chips
Formally on the APEC agenda and impossible to separate from everything else. Xi is calling for cooperation on AI and supply chains. Trump has said he opposes "any form of robust regulation or anything to control and stifle SI." US restrictions on advanced chips to China sit underneath the entire conversation.

Ukraine
Not on the formal agenda. Xi is reluctant to be drawn into what he regards as a European matter — which leaves the Trump–Putin bilateral carrying weight the trilateral will not.

WHAT EACH SIDE IS ACTUALLY THERE FOR

Trump wants a deal he can present as an accomplishment.
Putin wants out of sanctions isolation, and to stop the US sanctions bill now sitting paused.
Xi wants the meeting itself — and the signal that great-power questions get settled among three, not in Western capitals.

Analysts are close to unanimous that this is symbol before substance. Our job is to tell you the moment that stops being true — and to separate what is agreed from what is merely said.

text:
Podcast Summary | The Joe Rogan Experience: #2582 - Greg Anderson

Overview
A 46-year-old jiu-jitsu practitioner with a nearly bone-on-bone left knee rejected a full knee replacement, then rowed across the Pacific in 54 days. The throughline is resistance to outsourcing: surgery, comfort, and convenience all get questioned. The guest argues connective tissue responds to whole-body loading, that modern life strips people of agency and memory, and that voluntary hardship — jiu-jitsu, carrying heavy things, 12-hour rowing shifts — rebuilds capability. Bear encounters, elk math, lockdown defiance, and jiu-jitsu politics fill out a conversation about doing rather than consuming.

Key Themes
- Adventure has been outsourced: the guest was moved to row the Pacific by watching others do it, and argues most people consume sport rather than partake.
- Rejecting surgical fixes is framed as a bet on connective tissue, whole-body training, and biologics over replacement.
- Carrying heavy objects builds real-world strength — grip, back, whole-body connectivity — that gym isolation does not.
- Deliberate suffering is treated as preparation and identity: the ocean row was built around "no one's coming to save you."
- The physical challenge becomes mental: being soaked and freezing for weeks, sleep deprivation, and mutual watch for teammates' survival outweigh exertion.
- Modern tools farm out thinking: navigation apps degrade memory and spatial reasoning, while doers show humility and critics form purity-test echo chambers.
- Lockdowns are portrayed as a wealth transfer and a control exercise, with jiu-jitsu framed as the counter-model of earned hierarchy and community.
- Jiu-jitsu's structural weakness for MMA is takedowns and striking: elite grapplers enter the UFC late and past their prime.

Detailed Summary
The row began as inspiration, not a plan. Following an Instagram journey of men rowing from New York to London, Greg concluded that men outsource everything, including adventure and sport. He had zero rowing experience when he committed to crossing the Pacific.

His knee set the stakes. At 37, an orthopedic surgeon told him he needed a full knee replacement; a second surgeon later said a fake knee would prevent his jiu-jitsu style, the butterfly guard. Tests showed a nearly bone-on-bone left knee with no ACL tear and no surgery history; daily running after reading Can't Hurt Me had worsened it until he could barely walk.

The alternative is functional, whole-body training. Rogan argues conventional workouts overemphasize isolating muscle groups at the expense of connective tissue and fascia. His examples: slow isometric push-ups with pauses that leave him cooked after five or six reps, plus 100-push-up straight sets. Fascial work includes toe towel pulls and holding odd angles for 5–10 seconds until muscles shake.

Carrying is the centerpiece. Rogan has done farmers carries every other day for about six months, using barefoot-style Vivos, and praises loaded carries for back strength, connectivity, and grip — carried 70-pound kettlebells for roughly 20 minutes every other day, 150 yards uphill and back, with grip gains big enough to resize a wedding ring from 11.5 to 12. Tom Havlin, roughly 6'9" and 400 pounds, is cited as the model: heavy, rusty axle carries in flannel, face often unseen, and the claim that walking with weight builds strength. Rogan jokes Havlin triple-doses his TRT while he double-doses. Wrestlers raised on hay bales, with Matt Hughes as an example type, are called the scariest.

Rogan cites a study on eggshell membrane and cartilage growth, takes it himself, and claims biologics can reduce inflammation and regrow some cartilage without fully restoring it.

The hunting segments treat odds and terrain as a math problem. Elk hunting is framed as area covered times time spent: 10 days in the mountains of Idaho, 8,000–9,000 feet, bow hunting from a drop camp reached by horseback, tracks and scat every 50 feet, no elk seen by the speaker. Uphill taxes quads, downhill taxes knees; descending steep loose dirt in Utah cooked his knees.

Tree-stand hunting is defended as genuinely hard, and Wisconsin deer hunting is called a religion where people take off school. Grizzlies are framed as unlike black bears — more dominant, more dangerous, with coastal brown bears larger still. A grizzly encounter at 14 in Sitka, Alaska, ended with a run to the boat despite advice to stand still and look big.

Grizzly Man is treated as a cautionary tale, its subject staying past hibernation when bears are desperate enough to eat anything, even entering dens to eat cubs. Rogan's claim: black bear tastes good if brined and smoked, and bear meat can be safely eaten medium-rare if sous vide long enough to kill trichinosis. Elk is number one; axis deer is a close second and, he says, ruins everything else.

Axis deer in Hawaii are massively overpopulated: a Maui herd near 100,000, no season and no limit, and farmers who want them killed because they break irrigation pipes. Lanai is described as about 3,000 people and 30,000 deer, with a Four Seasons and abundant public land, where an audio podcast was filmed with professional hunters including John Dudley, Cam Haynes, Adam Greentree, and Remy Warren. Maui has little public land, so access depends on knowing people. Wild game can be bought from Maui Nui as USDA-inspected frozen venison sticks, roasts, steaks, and bone broth, with an origin story tracing the deer to a gift from India to King Kamehameha in the 1800s.

At sea, planning collided with weather. The 24-foot boat Ironic 45, built in London, self-rights when knocked past 90 degrees and did it repeatedly. They left La Push, Washington in May expecting mild spring weather and got low-40s temperatures, breaking waves, and constant wetness for roughly four to five weeks before switching abruptly to Hawaiian sun about three weeks out. They navigated with a Raymarine GPS, plotting and adjusting course by hand.

Early wildlife: whales, sea lions that played with the boat and bit oars, and two sunfish about 300 miles offshore, one roughly 8 feet fin to fin. A six-to-eight-foot shark, likely a blue shark, bit an oar. Fishing was constant and fruitless; one line was snapped by something large. Night rowing was so dark the sky and water merged — "like flying through the air," nicknamed the psychedelic express.

Work was 12 hours a day: three hours on, three off, around the clock, sleeping in bunks a third the size of the table they sat at. Sleep deprivation was the worst part; they shook each other awake and once feared a teammate had died.

The desalinator failed when life vests hit a pressure-release valve in a storm and flooded its waterproof compartment, frying the motor. Hand-pumping followed — an hour per person per day on top of rowing, for roughly two to two and a half weeks. They had carried a hand pump on the principle that two is one and one is none; the solar-powered system stripped minerals and electrolytes they replaced. Food ran long: 70 days of three meals planned, a sponsor sent four a day for 70 days, and the trip took 54, with many days of two meals. Peak Refuel supplied freeze-dried meals; Buffalo Goulash was a staple.

Wind and current decided everything. Favorable conditions meant about 100-mile days; headwinds and contrary current felt like rowing through molasses, and some days brought no ground or went backward. Nine days out off Oregon in a storm forecast to last nine days, they deployed a parachute anchor — about 12 feet across, 50 feet down, where water is relatively still — and made small circles going backward. When the system shifted, they pulled the anchor and surfed the boat for hundreds of miles, footage of which is said to exist on Instagram.

The team agreed they would not call for help no matter what; the brand was built around no one coming to save you. About 95% of people were supportive, and the roughly 5% who doubted became motivation. Nothing stayed waterproof, including merino base layers and Helly Hansen sailing gear. They estimated 50–70 days by studying boats in the Talisker Whiskey Challenge, now the World's Toughest Row, an annual Spain-to-Antigua race. Experienced ocean fishermen warned them off the trip, and the guest concedes a shorter trial run might have deterred him entirely, framing preparation as accepting a known period of hardship rather than rehearsing suffering.

That logic extends to modern convenience. He prefers paper maps to OnX, can recall a high-school phone number and his wife's but not his kids' numbers, and notes that after six years in Austin he knows routes to only a few places. His first cell phone, bought in 1988, paid for itself through last-minute comedy club work. Waze routing traffic through residential neighborhoods and police in New Jersey stopping drivers come up as symptoms.

Covid enforcement drew his defiance. As a cop, he argued law enforcement and government cannot violate constitutional rights because a mayor orders it, regardless of virus severity, citing sting operations on salons and jiu-jitsu gyms and gyms covering windows and using back doors. He kept his academy open prepared to face consequences, noting license offices counted as essential while his gym could not operate, that 70-plus percent of Los Angeles restaurants went under, and that The Comedy Store closed a year and a half while still paying Sunset Strip rent. He repeats a claim that outdoor dining was closed for optics and cites Chase Hughes on fear and control and a massive transfer of wealth. His structural argument: bigger government creates more jobs, more justifications for restrictions, and attracts people who enjoy controlling others, while real leaders avoid such roles.

Jiu-jitsu is the counter-model. His academy teaches 6:00 to 7:30 nightly with doors open until 8:30, a sauna and cold plunge, four acres, a field and picnic tables — a community center with a friend's CrossFit gym on site and mutual trash-talking. Better partners expose holes, so everyone improves; you can't do jiu-jitsu alone. Aggressive men become nicer, posturing disappears, and he rejects "sensei" and "professor," going by Greg. He calls pairing CrossFit with jiu-jitsu very detrimental — too much grinding, too little recovery — and criticizes competition-style strength training as dysfunctional fitness and an injury risk, echoing Steve Maxwell. Pavel Tsatsouline's method gets approval: strength as a skill, stop at five reps when you could do ten, rest three to five minutes, don't chase soreness. Mario Sperry built his triangle through repetition until it was muscle memory. A grappling dummy from Urijah Faber, nicknamed a robot, squeezes and has a light on its head.

Online criticism is dismissed as noise from people not doing anything, forming echo chambers with escalating purity tests that eventually turn on each other — crabs in a bucket, tearing down what took work to build. A critic objected to celebrating a white man rowing when Polynesian ancestors had rowed for millennia; the reply noted Icelandic heritage and two islanders on the crew. Kelsey Fendler, rowing solo from California to Hawaii at the same time, praised the team and offered advice, while hate mail from middle-aged women complained it took four men. Jealousy is called normal; what matters is whether you sit in it or ask what the other person sacrificed. Risk is probability versus possibility: enter the realm of possibility, avoid what likely gets you killed, especially as a parent. He didn't expect to survive Ramadi at 23, and that daily mortality made him free; at 46 with three kids he has more to live for but still resists fear. He won't wing suit because Andy Stump reportedly said all his wing suit friends have died.

Jiu-jitsu's hierarchy recurs. In Ramadi in 2004, a Navy SEAL teammate — a purple belt in jiu-jitsu and Muay Thai boxer — dominated him despite a 25-pound advantage and a wrestling and boxing background. He trained with him daily for the rest of the deployment, joined an MMA school and academy, took a few fights, earned a brown belt at Gracie Barra in the Pacific Northwest, then moved to Los Angeles and Checkmat. There, a 22-year-old unknown named Marcus Buchecha made him feel like he didn't know jiu-jitsu; he asked to restart as a white belt, and Buchecha refused, saying no one can take his belt and he should be the best brown belt he can be. Buchecha won the world title around 2012 and became a 13-time champion; he is defended against UFC critics as extremely difficult on top. He earned his black belt under João Assis within Checkmat. Hixon trained defense by starting rounds with black belts holding a fully locked rear naked choke, gi on. He began at Carlson Gracie's in 1996, choosing it over Hixon's first class only because it was closer.

Structure limits the sport's MMA pipeline. Jiu-jitsu isn't takedown- or wrestling-heavy, so many can't get fights to the ground, and elite striking generally starts in childhood. One academy rule starts every round on the feet. Untrained men are said to overestimate their fighting capacity by 4,000%. Defense matters: being very hard to submit is a legitimate skill. Jean Jacques Machado's missing fingers became an advantage in no-gi, since wrestling grips replaced gi grips that others lost with the gi. Rodolfo Vieira and Buchecha are cited as elite grapplers arriving past their prime, with Buchecha losing a couple UFC fights. Gordon Ryan shoulder-crunched and swept Buchecha like it was nothing and trains 365 days a year; he has serious stomach problems attributed to about a year of antibiotics and is not yet able to compete. John Danaher is the obsessive coach: a Columbia philosophy PhD who got hooked while bouncing, lives on the mats, owns one plate, one spoon, and one fork, and demands a strict schedule that drives many away. He coached Gary Tonin's striking, brought the guest in to help Georges St. Pierre with the spinning back kick, and has a new standout in Helina Carver. Ryan's instructionals are valuable but expensive; he reportedly says others won't do what he does and will need 20 years to catch up. At Who's Number One in Austin, he wrote down a picture of a triangle.

text:
So you call me politically illitarate for saying that you can't put a fag paper between them, Donna.  
To @Boo65864 (Definitely not a bot address) on claiming I was politicially ignorant for saying you couldn't put a fag paper between them.

So let's have a look. Both parties (as of late 2026) are now firmly on the right-of-centre ground: lower immigration, smaller government, tax cuts funded by spending cuts, energy security over Net Zero costs, and higher defence spending. The Conservatives under Kemi Badenoch have moved noticeably rightward since 2024 where Reform under Nigel Farage is still more radical, faster, and more absolute in both scale and rhetoric.

Political / Borders
Both want to leave the ECHR and repeal the Human Rights Act so they can control borders, speed up removals, and reduce judicial interference. Both prioritise sovereignty, tougher sentencing, more visible policing, higher defence spending, and less foreign aid. Both criticise “woke” institutional capture and favour stronger law-and-order measures.

The difference is mainly intensity. Conservatives talk about a Removals Force aiming for around 150,000 removals a year, a ban on asylum claims from illegal entrants, a binding annual migration cap, and extending the qualifying period for Indefinite Leave to Remain from 5 to 10 years. Reform goes further and faster: Operation Fortress (Royal Navy in the Channel within 100 days), mass identification/detention/deportation, abolishing and rescinding existing ILR in favour of short renewable high-skill visas, a freeze on non-essential immigration, and negative net migration. Reform also wants to disapply the 1951 Refugee Convention and make employers of illegal workers personally criminally liable. Conservatives still leave some exceptions; Reform is more absolute about prioritising British citizens. Reform also ties ministerial jobs more tightly to delivery (resign or be sacked if key pledges fail).

Economic
Both want tax cuts funded by public spending reductions (especially welfare and the size of the state), lower business burdens, planning deregulation to boost housing and infrastructure, and nuclear expansion. Both target stamp duty and inheritance tax relief on family homes, business rate relief or abolition in key sectors, and some form of employer National Insurance cut. Both stress fiscal responsibility and growth via lower taxes and regulation.

The gap is again scale and sequencing. Conservatives have a “Golden Economic Rule” (at least half of savings go to deficit reduction) and a more detailed Savings Plan (~£71bn, including ~£36bn from welfare) that funds specific measures such as abolishing inheritance tax on the family home, scrapping the Family Homes Tax, abolishing stamp duty on the family home, abolishing business rates for retail/hospitality/leisure, and halving employer NI for younger workers. Reform promises larger and faster personal tax relief (raising the personal allowance to £15,000 within 100 days, longer-term ambition £20,000), reversing the employer NI rise, and bigger immediate cuts to energy and food bills, plus broader measures. Conservatives are more focused on costed welfare savings and deficit prioritisation; Reform is more aggressive on speed and size.

Social / Welfare
Both want to shrink welfare dependency, prioritise British citizens for benefits and social housing, and make work pay more than benefits. Both support education reforms that emphasise standards over ideology. Both link high migration to pressures on housing, services, and social cohesion.

Differences are mainly depth and explicitness. Conservatives’ Welfare that Works plan targets specific savings (ending claims for mild mental health and routine back/joint pain with extra health support instead, ending access for many non-EUSS foreign nationals, housing benefit reform, reinstating the two-child limit). Reform restricts Universal Credit, housing benefit, free childcare and most non-contributory benefits to British citizens only and places heavier emphasis on social housing exclusively for British workers. On culture, Reform is more explicit about opposing “woke” capture and promoting British identity, although as we'll see later, this claim can be challenged through their actions as opposed to their words; Conservatives frame it more around responsibility, high standards, and parental pledges.

Technological / Energy
Both prioritise domestic energy production (especially nuclear), cut the cost of Net Zero policies on bills and building, and deregulate planning and environmental rules that delay infrastructure and housing. Both support accelerating nuclear (including small modular reactors).

Reform is more aggressive: larger and faster bill cuts (£250 within 100 days), fully scrapping Net Zero as a driver of deindustrialisation, restarting oil and gas licensing (including onshore/shale), and abolishing the Emissions Trading Scheme. Conservatives focus more on selective cost reduction (~£165 bill cut by scrapping specific Net Zero costs, repealing net-zero building rules, leaving the Aarhus Convention) while still referencing a revised climate approach.

There is substantial convergence. Both now occupy similar ground on borders, welfare restraint, tax cuts funded by a smaller state, and cheaper energy. The Conservatives present a more fiscally sequenced, institutionally cautious version with detailed costings and a deficit-first rule. Reform offers larger, faster, and more absolute versions of many of the same ideas — especially on immigration and immediate tax/energy relief — while accepting greater implementation risk.  None of this should be a suprise - this is what all 'right-wing' governments want.

Being British

Both the conservatives and Reform have another issue (as far as the British people are concerned) in that neither is willing (With the exception of Suella) to say that the British are a people, with their own history, culture (which is very different from even European cultures, let alone third world) and both are happy to stand non-native English as candidates. 

It's like neither the Conservatives or Reform, are willing to accept that foreigners bring foreing influence into our cities. Reform candidates proudly wear their ancestral costumes, what - as a sign of their integratedness?  

The Rape Gang Inquiry

Where the conservatives are actually preferable to Reform in that some Conservative MPs (including Esther McVey) supported or participated in it, and Lowe publicly thanked Badenoch for following and supporting the work. 

Reform has a well-documented rift with Lowe and has not backed his private inquiry in the same way; some Reform-aligned voices (and figures such as Maggie Oliver) have been critical of him proceeding independently.

Why any woman would support a party that refused to put bile aside for a greater cause - to expose the crimes of the Labour politicians - to a world-wide audience (Thank you Asmongold) is beyond me. 

As a father with two daughters, I cannot support Reform, because by refusing to participate in the Rape Gang Inquiry, they are showing they cannot see the greater good over their own egos, unlike the Tories.

And I say this all, as someone who has followed Farage for more than two decades. Who was a UKIP member, a Reform member, and now - Restore Britain.

text:
Sports Brand News

Under The Media Man Watercooler

Past, Present And Future

The world's top sports brands include Nike, Adidas, Lululemon, Puma, and Under Armour.

These brands dominate the market in terms of revenue, brand value, and global recognition. Nike consistently ranks as the most valuable sports brand, followed by Adidas, with a significant gap in brand value.

The List

Nike: A global leader in athletic footwear, apparel, and equipment, known for its iconic swoosh logo and strong brand recognition.

Adidas: A major competitor to Nike, offering a wide range of sports apparel, footwear, and accessories.

Lululemon: Specializing in athletic apparel, particularly yoga wear, but expanding into other areas like running shoes and personal care.

Puma: A well-known sportswear brand with a strong presence in football and other sports.

Under Armour: A prominent brand known for its performance apparel and innovative technologies.

Other notable brands: ASICS, Fila, New Balance, Skechers, Decathlon, and more, each with their own niche in the market.

News Flashback

Sports Brands: News

Nike: Nike has launched a new soccer campaign, “Scary Good,” focusing on talented players redefining the sport. This aligns with their “Sport Offense” strategy, emphasizing performance wear and storytelling in key sports like running and basketball, following a quarter of underwhelming financial results. CEO Elliott Hill aims to differentiate Nike, Jordan Brand, and Converse by sport for sharper brand distinction. Additionally, tennis player Carlos Alcaraz debuted Nike’s retro-inspired 2025 London Collection cardigan at Wimbledon, blending classic tennis tradition with modern flair.

New Balance: The 119-year-old brand is making waves by signing young superstars like Cooper Flagg, Shohei Ohtani, and Coco Gauff, aiming to redefine its position in the sports hierarchy. This move has shifted its image from “dad shoe” to a top contender, notably with Flagg as the No. 1 NBA Draft prospect.

Adidas: Adidas unveiled the new Team India T20 jersey, available since May 2024, ahead of the T20 World Cup, reinforcing its presence in cricket sponsorships.

JD Sports Fashion: As a global omnichannel retailer, JD Sports continues to expand its portfolio, including brands like Nike, Adidas, and The North Face, alongside private labels like Pink Soda. Its segments include DTLR, Shoe Palace, and Sizeer, focusing on athletic footwear and apparel with strong community ties.

Grassroots Sports Marketing: Brands are increasingly investing in grassroots sports for deeper emotional connections. In India, non-cricket sports sponsorships surpassed ₹2,000 crore in 2023, with platforms like SportVot boosting grassroots athletes’ visibility through digital identities and streaming lesser-known sports.

Other Developments: Athleta, a Gap-owned brand, has partnered with female athletes like Katie Ledecky and Simone Biles, pioneering sports marketing in women’s sports. Sephora’s sponsorship of the WNBA’s Golden State Valkyries signals growing brand interest in women’s sports. Meanwhile, brands like Red Lobster and Ram are leveraging CEOs in campaigns tied to smaller sports markets for affordable, intimate marketing.

News

Combat Sports Brands

Several well-known brands dominate the combat sports market, offering a wide range of equipment and apparel for various disciplines. Some of the most popular brands include Venum, Adidas, Everlast, Fairtex, Hayabusa, Rival, and Ringside. These brands are recognized for their quality, innovation, and unique designs, catering to both professional athletes and enthusiasts.

Media

Combat Sports Brands

These brands cater to various combat sports, offering specialized gear for different disciplines and skill levels. For beginners, brands like Everlast and RDX Sports are budget-friendly, while Hayabusa and Fairtex appeal to advanced practitioners seeking premium quality. Always consider your discipline, budget, and needs (e.g., durability, fit) when choosing gear. Here’s a concise overview of notable combat sports brands, focusing on those specializing in gear and apparel for disciplines like MMA, boxing, Muay Thai, BJJ, and more, based on available information:

Venum: A leading brand since 2006, known for durable, stylish gear for MMA, boxing, BJJ, and karate. Became the UFC’s exclusive outfitting partner in 2021, offering gloves, shorts, and rashguards. Popular for innovative designs and high-quality materials.

Hayabusa: A premium brand specializing in MMA, boxing, and BJJ gear. Known for advanced technology, ergonomic designs, and durable gloves, shin guards, and training equipment. Highly regarded for performance and comfort.

Fairtex: A renowned Thai brand focused on Muay Thai and MMA gear, particularly gloves and shin guards. Trusted for durability and quality, widely used by Muay Thai practitioners.

Combat Sports International: Offers affordable, high-quality MMA gear, including gloves, grappling dummies, and heavy bags. Based in Kansas City, known for innovation and catering to all skill levels.

Everlast: A household name in boxing, also offering MMA and fitness gear. Known for reliable, durable equipment like gloves and protective gear, suitable for beginners and pros.

Adidas Combat Sports: Brings the iconic athletic brand into martial arts, offering gear for judo, taekwondo, and MMA. Known for quality and versatility, with a focus on fitness enthusiasts.

RDX Sports: Provides affordable gear for MMA, boxing, and fitness. Popular for reliable gloves, shin guards, and training equipment, ideal for budget-conscious athletes.

Fuji Sports: A top choice for BJJ and judo, known for high-quality gis that prioritize comfort and fit. Favored by grapplers for durability and performance.

Twins Special: Another Thai brand excelling in Muay Thai and MMA gear, particularly gloves and shin guards. Renowned for durability and quality, a go-to for striking arts.

Leone 1947: An Italian brand specializing in boxing and kickboxing gear, offering affordable, high-quality gloves, shin guards, and accessories. Popular among professional fighters.

Elite Sports: Offers affordable, premium-quality fight wear for BJJ, MMA, boxing, and more. Known for stylish gis, rashguards, and gloves, catering to men, women, and kids.

Revgear: A California-based brand since 1996, recognized for innovative, durable equipment for boxing, MMA, Muay Thai, and BJJ. Trusted by athletes for high-performance gear. (Grok)

News

Sports Promoters: Brands

Sports promoters are critical in bridging brands like Nike, Adidas, Red Bull, and emerging players like YouTube with sports ecosystems. They craft partnerships that resonate with fans, leveraging events, athletes, and digital platforms to drive engagement and revenue. For brands seeking to enter or expand in sports, working with agencies like Octagon, SPORTFIVE, or rEvolution ensures strategic alignment and impactful campaigns.

Sports promoters are key players in connecting brands with sports events, athletes, and fans to create mutually beneficial partnerships. They facilitate sponsorships, endorsements, and marketing campaigns that amplify brand visibility while enhancing the sports experience. Below is an overview of notable brands involved in sports promotion, based on their prominence in the industry and partnerships, as well as the role of sports promoters in these collaborations.

Key Brands in Sports Promotion

Sports promoters often work with global brands across various industries, leveraging the emotional and cultural appeal of sports to drive engagement. Some prominent brands include:

Nike: A leader in sports marketing, Nike partners with athletes and teams worldwide, using campaigns like #BetterForIt to promote inclusivity and fitness through influencer and athlete endorsements.

Example: Nike’s campaigns often feature athletes as brand ambassadors, such as their work with social media influencers and everyday athletes to motivate active lifestyles. Adidas: Known for high-profile collaborations with teams, athletes, and designers, adidas merges sports and lifestyle through partnerships like those with Ivy Park, Bad Bunny, and Gucci.

Promoters facilitate these deals, ensuring alignment with events like soccer tournaments or fashion-driven campaigns. Red Bull: Specializes in extreme sports and high-energy branding, Red Bull works with promoters to create visually stunning campaigns, such as those featuring snowboarder Travis Rice, aligning with their adventurous brand image.

Promoters manage event sponsorships and athlete endorsements to maximize Red Bull’s reach. Gatorade: A staple in sports hydration, Gatorade signs college athletes like Cooper Flagg, Paige Bueckers, and JuJu Watkins for endorsement deals, expanding its influence in youth markets.

Promoters negotiate these contracts to ensure brand alignment with emerging talent. Reebok: Recently extended a multiyear endorsement with Chicago Sky’s Angel Reese, including a signature shoe release planned for 2026.

Promoters handle such deals to integrate Reebok’s branding into WNBA events and fan engagement. Under Armour, Puma, and New Balance: These brands compete in the athleisure and performance markets, often collaborating with promoters to secure sponsorships for events like marathons or partnerships with rising stars.

Example: New Balance’s revival through collaborations with designers and athletes highlights promoter-driven strategies. Non-Traditional Brands: Companies like YouTube (partnering with Mr. Beast for NBA jersey patches) and luxury brands like Hugo Boss and Gucci (F1 and tennis sponsorships) are increasingly entering sports through innovative partnerships.

Promoters bridge these brands with sports audiences, crafting campaigns that appeal to diverse demographics.

Role of Sports Promoters

Sports promoters act as intermediaries, orchestrating partnerships that benefit brands, athletes, and events.

Their roles include:

Event Promotion: Organizing and marketing events like tournaments, matches, or festivals, ensuring brands gain visibility through sponsorships (e.g., Sports Marketing Australia’s work with AusTriathlon).

Athlete Endorsements: Negotiating deals between brands and athletes, such as Jannik Sinner’s partnerships with Gucci, Nike, and Rolex. Sponsorship Activation: Creating campaigns that integrate brands into sports culture, like Starbucks and Seattle Seahawks’ co-branded merchandise.

Digital and Social Media Campaigns: Leveraging platforms for influencer-driven marketing, as seen with Nike’s #BetterForIt or Red Bull’s extreme sports content.

Global Reach: Connecting brands with international markets, such as Allsport Promotion’s campaigns for global brands across Europe and beyond.

Notable Sports Promotion

Agencies

Several agencies specialize in facilitating these brand partnerships:

Octagon: A global leader in sports and entertainment, representing talent and brands across multiple sports.

SPORTFIVE: Creates value for brands through partnerships with rights holders and media platforms.

rEvolution: Focuses on authentic campaigns that connect brands with passionate fans.

Excel Sports Management: Manages high-value contracts for athletes in basketball, baseball, and golf, with $3.4 billion in contracts.

IMG: Specializes in rights, data, and digital strategies for sports organizations and brands.

CSM: Known for creating memorable experiences through partnerships, like Red Bull Racing’s F1 activations.

Trends in Sports Promotion:

Influencer Marketing: Brands like Nike and Red Bull use athletes and influencers to create authentic, engaging content.

Sustainability and Social Causes: Over 80% of consumers prefer brands supporting environmental or diversity initiatives, prompting promoters to align brands with such values.

The world's top sports brands include Nike, Adidas, Lululemon, Puma, and Under Armour.

Nike: A global leader in athletic footwear, apparel, and equipment, known for its iconic swoosh logo and strong brand recognition.

Adidas: A major competitor to Nike, offering a wide range of sports apparel, footwear, and accessories.

Lululemon: Specializing in athletic apparel, particularly yoga wear, but expanding into other areas like running shoes and personal care.

Puma: A well-known sportswear brand with a strong presence in football and other sports.

Under Armour: A prominent brand known for its performance apparel and innovative technologies.

Other notable brands: ASICS, Fila, New Balance, Skechers, Decathlon, and more, each with their own niche in the market.

Sports Brands: News

Nike: Nike has launched a new soccer campaign, “Scary Good,” focusing on talented players redefining the sport. This aligns with their “Sport Offense” strategy, emphasizing performance wear and storytelling in key sports like running and basketball, following a quarter of underwhelming financial results. CEO Elliott Hill aims to differentiate Nike, Jordan Brand, and Converse by sport for sharper brand distinction. Additionally, tennis player Carlos Alcaraz debuted Nike’s retro-inspired 2025 London Collection cardigan at Wimbledon, blending classic tennis tradition with modern flair.

New Balance: The 119-year-old brand is making waves by signing young superstars like Cooper Flagg, Shohei Ohtani, and Coco Gauff, aiming to redefine its position in the sports hierarchy. This move has shifted its image from “dad shoe” to a top contender, notably with Flagg as the No. 1 NBA Draft prospect.

Adidas: Adidas unveiled the new Team India T20 jersey, available since May 2024, ahead of the T20 World Cup, reinforcing its presence in cricket sponsorships.

Several well-known brands dominate the combat sports market, offering a wide range of equipment and apparel for various disciplines. Some of the most popular brands include Venum, Adidas, Everlast, Fairtex, Hayabusa, Rival, and Ringside. These brands are recognized for their quality, innovation, and unique designs, catering to both professional athletes and enthusiasts.

These brands cater to various combat sports, offering specialized gear for different disciplines and skill levels. For beginners, brands like Everlast and RDX Sports are budget-friendly, while Hayabusa and Fairtex appeal to advanced practitioners seeking premium quality. Always consider your discipline, budget, and needs (e.g., durability, fit) when choosing gear. Hayabusa: A premium brand specializing in MMA, boxing, and BJJ gear. Known for advanced technology, ergonomic designs, and durable gloves, shin guards, and training equipment. Highly regarded for performance and comfort.

Fairtex: A renowned Thai brand focused on Muay Thai and MMA gear, particularly gloves and shin guards. Trusted for durability and quality, widely used by Muay Thai practitioners.

Combat Sports International: Offers affordable, high-quality MMA gear, including gloves, grappling dummies, and heavy bags. Based in Kansas City, known for innovation and catering to all skill levels.

Fuji Sports: A top choice for BJJ and judo, known for high-quality gis that prioritize comfort and fit. Favored by grapplers for durability and performance.

Twins Special: Another Thai brand excelling in Muay Thai and MMA gear, particularly gloves and shin guards. Renowned for durability and quality, a go-to for striking arts.

Leone 1947: An Italian brand specializing in boxing and kickboxing gear, offering affordable, high-quality gloves, shin guards, and accessories. Popular among professional fighters.

Elite Sports: Offers affordable, premium-quality fight wear for BJJ, MMA, boxing, and more. Known for stylish gis, rashguards, and gloves, catering to men, women, and kids.

Revgear: A California-based brand since 1996, recognized for innovative, durable equipment for boxing, MMA, Muay Thai, and BJJ. Trusted by athletes for high-performance gear. (Grok)

Sports Promoters: Brands

Sports promoters are critical in bridging brands like Nike, Adidas, Red Bull, and emerging players like YouTube with sports ecosystems. They craft partnerships that resonate with fans, leveraging events, athletes, and digital platforms to drive engagement and revenue. For brands seeking to enter or expand in sports, working with agencies like Octagon, SPORTFIVE, or rEvolution ensures strategic alignment and impactful campaigns.

Sports promoters are key players in connecting brands with sports events, athletes, and fans to create mutually beneficial partnerships. They facilitate sponsorships, endorsements, and marketing campaigns that amplify brand visibility while enhancing the sports experience. Below is an overview of notable brands involved in sports promotion, based on their prominence in the industry and partnerships, as well as the role of sports promoters in these collaborations.

Key Brands in Sports Promotion

Sports promoters often work with global brands across various industries, leveraging the emotional and cultural appeal of sports to drive engagement. Some prominent brands include:

Nike: A leader in sports marketing, Nike partners with athletes and teams worldwide, using campaigns like #BetterForIt to promote inclusivity and fitness through influencer and athlete endorsements.

Example: Nike’s campaigns often feature athletes as brand ambassadors, such as their work with social media influencers and everyday athletes to motivate active lifestyles. Adidas: Known for high-profile collaborations with teams, athletes, and designers, adidas merges sports and lifestyle through partnerships like those with Ivy Park, Bad Bunny, and Gucci.

Promoters facilitate these deals, ensuring alignment with events like soccer tournaments or fashion-driven campaigns. Red Bull: Specializes in extreme sports and high-energy branding, Red Bull works with promoters to create visually stunning campaigns, such as those featuring snowboarder Travis Rice, aligning with their adventurous brand image.

Promoters manage event sponsorships and athlete endorsements to maximize Red Bull’s reach. Gatorade: A staple in sports hydration, Gatorade signs college athletes like Cooper Flagg, Paige Bueckers, and JuJu Watkins for endorsement deals, expanding its influence in youth markets.

Promoters negotiate these contracts to ensure brand alignment with emerging talent. Reebok: Recently extended a multiyear endorsement with Chicago Sky’s Angel Reese, including a signature shoe release planned for 2026.

Promoters handle such deals to integrate Reebok’s branding into WNBA events and fan engagement. Under Armour, Puma, and New Balance: These brands compete in the athleisure and performance markets, often collaborating with promoters to secure sponsorships for events like marathons or partnerships with rising stars.

Example: New Balance’s revival through collaborations with designers and athletes highlights promoter-driven strategies. Non-Traditional Brands: Companies like YouTube (partnering with Mr. Beast for NBA jersey patches) and luxury brands like Hugo Boss and Gucci (F1 and tennis sponsorships) are increasingly entering sports through innovative partnerships.

Promoters bridge these brands with sports audiences, crafting campaigns that appeal to diverse demographics.

Role of Sports Promoters

Sports promoters act as intermediaries, orchestrating partnerships that benefit brands, athletes, and events.

Their roles include:

Event Promotion: Organizing and marketing events like tournaments, matches, or festivals, ensuring brands gain visibility through sponsorships (e.g., Sports Marketing Australia’s work with AusTriathlon).

Athlete Endorsements: Negotiating deals between brands and athletes, such as Jannik Sinner’s partnerships with Gucci, Nike, and Rolex. Sponsorship Activation: Creating campaigns that integrate brands into sports culture, like Starbucks and Seattle Seahawks’ co-branded merchandise.

Digital and Social Media Campaigns: Leveraging platforms for influencer-driven marketing, as seen with Nike’s #BetterForIt or Red Bull’s extreme sports content.

Global Reach: Connecting brands with international markets, such as Allsport Promotion’s campaigns for global brands across Europe and beyond.
