text:
$ANT starts trading on Nasdaq today. Largest IPO ever.

$83 a share. $81.3B raised, plus a $26.0B private placement. ~$1.5T fully diluted.

18 months ago Anthropic did $376M of revenue in a quarter. Last quarter: $16.96B. Run-rate hit ~$81B on Oct 31.

And it has already signed $900.9B of compute...

Here is what you need to know for $ANT. All from the 424B4, plus what its 1-hop neighbors told their own investors (pulled out of nodus42):

1. The deal

- Priced at $83 last night. The roadshow range was $70 to $78 for 825M shares. They upsized to 980M and priced above the top
- 956M shares are new (primary). The 7 co-founders sell ~23.6M combined
- Greenshoe: 147M more shares
- Concurrent private placement: $26.0B of non-voting stock at $83, bought by the chip and cloud vendors (more on that below)
- Lead left $GS, then $MS. 22 banks total
- Part of the deal goes to retail through $SCHW, Fidelity, $HOOD, $SOFI and E*TRADE
- Orders reportedly ~$500B, 6-7x covered (Reuters)
- Gray market this morning: indicated 20-26% above $83 (Bloomberg)

2. The numbers (424B4)

Revenue by quarter:
- Q1'25: $376M
- Q2'25: $787M
- Q3'25: $1.38B
- Q4'25: $2.04B
- Q1'26: $4.73B
- Q2'26: $11.56B
- Q3'26: $16.96B (12x Y/Y)

Full years: $41M (2023) → $386M (2024) → $4.59B (2025). First nine months of 2026: $33.2B.

Run-rate revenue (trailing 28 days of usage x 13 + subscriptions x 12): ~$81B on Oct 31, up $10B from Sep 30.

Margins... there is no gross margin line. Compute is an operating expense:
- compute + infrastructure = 58% of revenue in Q3'26 (48% in Q2'26, 144% in Q4'25)
- Q2'26 was operating profitable. Q3'26 was -3% operating margin, +15% adjusted
- operating cash flow: +$6.6B in the first nine months of 2026 (vs -$2.0B a year earlier)
- the 9M'26 net loss of $104B is almost all non-cash fair value marks on notes, SAFEs and derivatives
- cash: $131.8B on Sep 30, ~$232B pro forma for the IPO

3. The customers

- "More than 11,900 customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis" (up from 950+ a year earlier)
- 1,900+ customers above $1M, ~250 above $10M
- "Net Revenue Retention of approximately 900%"
- no customer above 10% of revenue in 9M'26, top 5 ~25%
- Opus 5.5 "reduced customer costs per task by approximately 40% compared to Opus 5"

900% NRR is absurd. The average $100k+ customer spends 9x what it did a year ago.

4. The compute bill (this is the part that matters for the supply chain)

"aggregate committed spend of approximately $900.9 billion, substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure"

- $451.6B of it lands before end-2030, the rest 2031-2045
- $70.7B is due in the next 12 months

Who gets paid (424B4):
→ $AVGO: five-year equipment leases, ~$161.2B of rent excl. interest. Broadcom is "supplier and lessor"
→ $GOOGL: TPU cloud, at least ~$121.3B, Apr 2026 to Jul 2033, "regardless of actual usage"
→ SpaceXAI ($SPCX): up to $120.5B into 2029, ~$3.1B a month once all capacity lands (expected Dec)
→ $AMZN: at least $110.0B, May 2026 to Apr 2036, regardless of usage
→ $MSFT: at least $47.2B, up to $49.2B, Nov 2026 to Jun 2033
→ Nscale: up to ~$44.6B (NVIDIA GPUs)
→ Lambda: ~$41.3B into 2034
→ $AMD: Helios racks with MI450, first tranche in 2027

That's ~$646B across seven names before AMD, Akamai and the landlords.

5. The 1-hop neighbors (Nodus42 map: ~68 direct neighbors, 20 chains)

What the neighbors told their own investors, verbatim:

Chips →
- $AVGO Hock Tan (Q3 call): "Anthropic is on track to become our largest XPU customer in 2027 and sustain that in 2028." 1 GW of Ironwood in 2026, 5 GW of TPU v8i in 2027, another 10 GW in 2028. Asked if that 10 GW is one number: "10 GW is just for Anthropic."
- Broadcom also: "We closed the first $35 billion tranche in June for Anthropic's 1 GW deployment"
- $NVDA Jensen at Goldman (Sep 10): "Anyhow, our share of Anthropic is growing very quickly". NVIDIA put in $10B earlier this year and buys another $10B today. On its Nov 17 call NVIDIA cited "Anthropic's annualized revenue reaching $81 billion at the end of October."
- $AMD: "a company like Anthropic has ambitions to do up to 2 gigawatts with us in the first generation". First GW in H1'27. AMD agreed to buy up to $5.0B of Anthropic stock as GPU deliveries hit milestones (424B4). So AMD pays Anthropic in equity to take its racks...
- $TSM: board approved buying up to $500M of Anthropic "at its per share initial public offering price" (6-K, Nov 10)

Cloud →
- $AMZN Q1 call: "the recent deal that we announced with Anthropic for over $100 billion." Project Rainier = 500k Trainium2 and growing
- Alphabet Q3 call: "our work with Anthropic, both directly and via Broadcom"
- $MSFT booked "a $3.2 billion gain from our investment in Anthropic" (Q4 FY26)
- $AKAM Q3 call: "we signed an $11.6 billion commitment over seven years with Anthropic to support their CPU workloads". Akamai also gave Anthropic a warrant for up to ~5% of Akamai

Neoclouds →
- SpaceXAI: Anthropic paid just over $5B in Q3, 34.5% of SpaceX revenue (per CNBC)
- $CRWV: "Signed multi-year agreement with Anthropic" (Q1 8-K)
- Nscale (Vera Rubin NVL72, West Virginia), Lambda, Fluidstack (runs its own sites)

Power + sites →
- $WULF: 401 MW in Kentucky, "approximately $19 billion of contracted revenue over the initial 20-year lease term". Google signed credit support agreements to backstop Anthropic's leases (8-K, Nov 4)
- $RIOT: 910 MW at Corsicana. "The Frontier AI Lab will pay base rent of $130.0 per kilowatt of critical IT load capacity per month", +3% a year (10-Q names it Anthropic)
- $HUT: River Bend, Louisiana, 15-year lease, up to 2,295 MW with the options
- $EROC: "We contracted with Anthropic for 470 MW of generation capacity for a new data center."

Memory (2-hop) →
- no direct edge in the map. The 424B4 says HBM is "largely manufactured by SK hynix Inc., Samsung Electronics Co., and Micron Technology, Inc." SK Hynix (000660.KS), Samsung (005930.KS), and $MU buys $1.0B of stock at the IPO

Customers →
- $CRM: "Anthropic is one of our biggest users of CRM, of Sales Cloud, and obviously Slack"
- IT services building on Claude: $ACN, TCS, $EPAM, $CTSH
- software paying for it: $NOW, $SNOW, $WDAY, $FIS
- security (Project Glasswing): $CSCO, $ZS and others

The circle here is kinda wild:
→ Amazon and Google sell it compute, own ~28% of it, buy its models and compete with it
→ Broadcom leases it the chips Google designs, Google backstops its rent to TeraWulf
→ NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC all buy stock at $83 today

The 424B4 says it straight: Amazon, Google and Microsoft "simultaneously serve as our investors, customers, distribution partners, and competitors"

6. Who owns it, who controls it

- Amazon 14.6%, Google 13.4% of capital stock, both non-voting Class N
- Class F (one share, the Founder LLC of the 7 co-founders) = 50.1% of the total vote, no economic rights
- Class T (the Long-Term Benefit Trust) elects a majority of the board
- Delaware public benefit corp + Nasdaq "controlled company"
- a public benefit fund got ~847M shares and can get up to 2% more each time the stock rises 50% past the last milestone, starting from $83

So public buyers get the economics. Founders + the Trust keep the steering wheel.

7. Valuation + the Street

- ~13.2B A+N shares after the deal → ~$1.1T basic, ~$1.5T fully diluted at $83
- ~$1.5T / $81B run-rate = ~18.5x. On Q3 annualized ($67.8B) it's ~22x
- Initiations today: Citizens $125, Wolfe $135, Needham $150, Melius $155 (+51% to +87%)
- Citizens models $137.0B of revenue in 2027
- Nasdaq-100 fast entry reportedly on track for Dec 21 (Bloomberg, not final)

For reference, OpenAI is reportedly at ~$50B annualized revenue and still private.

8. What could go wrong

- the compute bill: $70.7B due in 12 months, most of it owed "regardless of actual usage". If growth stalls, the commitments don't
- compute was 58% of Q3 revenue. One bad quarter of pricing and the operating line goes red again (it was -3% in Q3)
- supply: lock-up is up to 180 days (365 for founders and 0.5%+ holders), but non-founder employees can sell up to 10% of locked shares from day one, plus staggered early releases
- the safety brakes are a real line item: the company says it has delayed or limited model releases (Mythos via Project Glasswing) and could again
- data centers: states and towns are "considering or have approved moratoriums on new data center construction"
- governance: you get no say. 50.1% of the vote sits with the founders' one share
- the vendors are the shareholders. Good for alignment, but every big supplier is also a competitor

TLDR:
- Largest IPO ever, $83, ~$1.5T fully diluted, trades on Nasdaq today
- $16.96B revenue last quarter, ~$81B run-rate, 900% NRR, cash flow positive
- $900.9B of compute signed. The bill lands on Broadcom, Google, SpaceXAI, Amazon, Microsoft, AMD and the landlords (TeraWulf, Riot, Hut 8)
- Founders hold 50.1% of the vote, the Trust picks the board majority

My take is that $ANT is the single biggest demand signal in the whole AI supply chain. Every GW above is somebody's TPU, GPU, HBM stack, optic, transformer or turbine order... and it is now public, with a quarterly print.

I am extremely bullish on the entire AI buildout. Today it gets a ticker.

text:
An Open Letter to @elonmusk 

From a disabled British citizen of Chinese origin, whose family suffered decades of political persecution under the Chinese Communist Party, and who has invested almost all his personal investment wealth in Tesla and SpaceX.

Please Do Not Mistake China's Material Prosperity for the Legitimacy of Authoritarian Power

Dear Mr Musk,

I am a British citizen of Chinese origin living in York, England. I am a disabled man, a father, and an investor in Tesla and SpaceX.

Let me begin by making one thing clear: I am not writing this letter because I oppose you. Quite the contrary.

For many years, I have regarded you as one of the most creative, courageous and consequential figures of our time.

From electric vehicles and reusable rockets to artificial intelligence and brain-computer interfaces, you have repeatedly challenged what humanity once considered impossible.

I believe your contributions to human civilisation will be remembered for generations.

I admire your creativity, leadership and willingness to challenge established thinking. I have also appreciated your public defence of free speech, individual autonomy and the importance of resisting excessive government power.

Such has been my confidence in your vision that I have invested almost all of my personal investment wealth in businesses associated with you, particularly Tesla and SpaceX.

That is why your recent comments about China, President Xi Jinping and former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have left me deeply disappointed.

I would like to explain why, beginning with my family's history.

1. I Come from a Family That Suffered Decades of Political Persecution

I was born in China in 1973.

Both of my parents experienced political persecution under the Chinese Communist Party.

In 1957, my father was labelled a "Rightist" after writing an article calling for fundamental reform of China's deeply hierarchical system.

He was expelled from the Communist Party, demoted and subjected to other political punishments.

During the Cultural Revolution, he suffered further persecution, including public denunciation, detention for political investigation and confinement in what was known as a "cowshed", a place used to hold people targeted by political campaigns.

In 1969, he was sent to a May Seventh Cadre School in Shanggao, Jiangxi Province, where he was required to perform manual labour. He did not return to Beijing until 1977.

My mother's family suffered a similarly devastating fate.

She was born in 1937 in Neijiang, Sichuan Province.

Around 1952, during the political campaigns of the early Communist period, my maternal grandfather was arrested, publicly denounced and eventually executed. The family's property was confiscated.

Because of her family background, my mother was deprived of normal educational opportunities and experienced years of hardship.

Political persecution was not an isolated experience involving my father alone. It affected both sides of my family and left consequences that extended across generations.

When I was born in 1973, my mother experienced an extremely difficult delivery. I suffered severe oxygen deprivation and survived only after several hours of resuscitation.

The result was permanent brain damage.

To this day, I live with significant hand tremors and impaired motor coordination.

Writing by hand is extremely difficult for me. Even using a computer requires considerable effort, and I rely heavily on voice input, assistive devices and specialised software to manage everyday tasks.

In my family's understanding of our history, the circumstances surrounding my birth cannot be separated from the years of political persecution and instability my parents endured.

I share this history not to seek sympathy, but to explain why the consequences of unchecked political power are deeply personal to me.

What I am asking is that, when evaluating a political system, we look beyond the roads, bridges, factories and skyscrapers it has built.

We must also consider what political power has done to ordinary families.

Some forms of suffering never appear in GDP figures.

Some injuries last a lifetime.

2. I Once Hoped That Your Neuralink Technology Might Help Me

There is something deeply personal I would also like to share with you.

When I first learned about Neuralink and its progress towards human clinical trials, I was genuinely excited.

I have already undergone deep brain stimulation surgery, yet I continue to experience serious hand tremors.

At one point, I seriously considered contacting Neuralink to describe my medical condition and ask whether your technology might one day offer any possibility of helping someone like me.

I understand that Neuralink's current clinical studies primarily focus on people with severe paralysis, rather than treating the kind of tremor I experience.

Nevertheless, I remain hopeful about the future of brain-computer interface technology.

In the end, I never made contact.

I felt that the distance between an ordinary disabled man and one of the world's wealthiest and most influential entrepreneurs was simply too great.

I had little confidence that my voice would ever be heard.

Yet that did not diminish my admiration for your work.

I believe that using technological innovation and extraordinary resources to help disabled people regain independence is a profoundly valuable humanitarian endeavour.

And that is precisely why I hope you can understand something important.

For people whose families have suffered political persecution, freedom, dignity and individual rights are not abstract political concepts.

They concern real human lives.

3. China's Visible Prosperity Is Being Used to Justify Political Power

I do not deny China's extraordinary achievements in infrastructure.

Its high-speed railways, bridges, airports, industrial facilities and impressive urban landscapes are real accomplishments.

I understand why they impress you.

But that is precisely where my concern begins.

For decades, the Chinese Communist Party has presented economic development and infrastructure construction as major sources of legitimacy for its rule.

Magnificent buildings are easy to see.

High-speed trains are easy to experience.

Modern factories are naturally impressive to visiting business leaders.

But the difficulties facing ordinary Chinese families, the restrictions placed upon political freedoms, and the experiences of those who cannot speak openly are much less visible.

Under Xi Jinping, political power has become increasingly concentrated.

The severe restrictions imposed during the COVID-19 pandemic, followed by the prolonged property downturn, difficulties in youth employment and weak household confidence, have placed substantial pressure on many Chinese families.

Consider some recent economic evidence.

According to the World Bank's October 2026 report, real house prices in China were approximately 23 per cent below their 2021 peak, while housing sales remained far below their previous high.

For a family that has committed years of savings and taken on a substantial mortgage, such a decline is not an abstract economic adjustment.

It represents a real loss of household wealth.

The Mercator Institute for China Studies reported that property investment had fallen by approximately 20.6 per cent during the first three quarters of 2026, while unemployment among 16-to-24-year-olds not in education reached 18.9 per cent in August.

I acknowledge that China's economy continues to grow and that its manufacturing and technology sectors remain formidable.

But those achievements do not erase the economic pressures experienced by ordinary households.

I would also like to draw your attention to a fact that is both more immediate and directly relevant to you personally.

To this day, ordinary internet users in mainland China cannot freely access X, the social media platform you own, through a normal internet connection.

Nor is X the only example. Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, WhatsApp and many other internationally used social media and communication platforms remain blocked in mainland China.

An ordinary Chinese citizen cannot simply log in to these platforms, as someone in Britain or the United States can, to exchange ideas with people around the world, share news or participate freely in international public discussion.

I believe you are well aware of these restrictions.

You have repeatedly emphasised the importance of free speech, and you have described X as an important platform for global public discourse.

So I would like to ask you:

How do you assess the state of political freedom in a country where ordinary citizens cannot freely use your own social media platform or routinely access a broad range of independent international information?

When you praise China's modern development and its political leadership, why do you not express equal concern about the internet censorship and information restrictions experienced by ordinary Chinese people?

A country can possess world-class high-speed railways and spectacular modern cities while denying its citizens ordinary access to the world's major social media platforms. Should that not concern you at least as much as its impressive skyline?

My concern is not that every social media platform is beyond criticism. It is whether political authorities should have the power to determine what information citizens may access, which discussions they may join and which differing views they may hear.

Under a highly centralised political system, who can independently scrutinise the allocation of public resources?

Who can hold political leaders accountable for harmful policies?

Can ordinary citizens freely criticise their government and organise independently to defend their interests?

Should these questions not matter just as much as railways, skyscrapers and industrial output?

When you described Xi Jinping as a great leader and associated China's prosperity with his leadership, I could not help asking:

Have you examined with equal seriousness the economic and social costs of his policies?

Have you listened to those who lost their income during prolonged lockdowns, those whose family wealth was devastated by the housing crisis, or those who faced repression for expressing dissent?

China's development has depended upon the creativity and labour of hundreds of millions of workers, engineers, entrepreneurs and scientists.

Why should their achievements automatically become a tribute to the country's supreme political leader?

The ability to build an impressive modern economy does not, by itself, establish the legitimacy of those who govern it.

4. I Once Felt Deeply Moved by What I Understood to Be Your Concern for the Chinese People

Several years ago, I remember reading a report about you.

As I recall it, you had expressed a wish that people in China should be treated well.

I cannot now independently verify the exact wording of that report or to whom your remarks were addressed.

I therefore do not wish to attribute a direct quotation to you without reliable evidence.

But I clearly remember how moved I felt at the time.

I believed that someone with your wealth and international influence was showing genuine concern for ordinary Chinese people.

That earned my respect.

Today, however, when I see you praising Xi Jinping's leadership in an interview with Chinese state media and pointing to the prosperity achieved during his tenure, I find it difficult to reconcile those remarks with the values I had admired.

Concern for ordinary people should not be measured solely by how many cars a country produces or how many factories it builds.

It should also involve whether its people enjoy freedom, dignity and the right to criticise and hold political authority accountable.

5. Your Public Support for Jensen Huang Raises Serious Questions for Me

I am also concerned about your recent public support for Jensen Huang, the former chief executive of Nvidia.

The United States Department of Justice has investigated and prosecuted cases involving the illegal diversion of advanced artificial intelligence chips to China.

Such cases demonstrate that advanced semiconductor exports are not merely a commercial matter. They also concern legal compliance, technological security and American national security.

Mr Huang has recently faced serious public controversy concerning his personal conduct and related corporate governance questions, and he has stepped down as Nvidia's chief executive.

I want to be absolutely clear: I have not seen conclusive evidence establishing that Mr Huang personally directed illegal chip exports or engaged in espionage.

Allegations are not convictions. Personal criminal responsibility must be determined through proper evidence and due process.

Nevertheless, the seriousness of the wider questions demands rigorous, independent scrutiny.

That is why I was troubled by your public support for Mr Huang's return to Nvidia, and by your response that hiring him would be "an honor".

I understand that you admire his extraordinary technical abilities.

But should technical brilliance alone determine whether someone is suitable for a position of exceptional corporate responsibility?

Should integrity, legal compliance, corporate governance and national security considerations not carry equal weight?

This is particularly important for a company such as SpaceX, whose activities involve advanced aerospace technology and sensitive regulatory responsibilities.

As an investor, I do not want potential compliance or security concerns to be overlooked because of personal admiration.

If Tesla or SpaceX were ever seriously to consider employing Mr Huang in a senior position, I would hope that the decision would be subject to rigorous, independent due diligence consistent with applicable law.

Your companies' long-term credibility and security deserve nothing less.

6. My Investment Decisions Have Always Reflected My Values

I have committed substantial personal capital to the American stock market.

In selecting investments, I consider more than profitability, technological strength and growth prospects.

I also care about the values and public positions of corporate leaders.

For example, I have deliberately avoided investing in Meta, the parent company of Facebook, as well as Microsoft and Apple.

I disagree with aspects of these companies' conduct and public positions in political controversies, particularly those involving Donald Trump, freedom of expression and the influence of major technology companies over public debate.

I recognise that these companies have different records and that reasonable people may interpret their actions differently.

Nevertheless, these considerations have influenced my investment decisions.

By contrast, I have long admired your willingness to defend free expression and challenge established institutions.

I have also welcomed your public support for certain political positions associated with President Trump.

However, I have never expected the executives of companies in which I invest to agree with every one of my political opinions.

What matters to me is consistency of principle.

If we oppose excessive government power, should that principle not also apply to China?

If we believe in freedom of speech and individual liberty, should those values not extend beyond national borders?

If we object to excessive control over public discussion by large technology companies, should we not also scrutinise the far greater power of a state to restrict the speech of an entire population?

These are the questions at the heart of this letter.

My decision to invest almost all of my personal investment wealth in businesses associated with you reflects both my confidence in their commercial prospects and my longstanding trust in your judgement.

Your recent statements have made me wonder whether the principles by which you judge freedom and political power change when the subject is China.

For me, that question is more troubling than short-term movements in share prices.

7. I Still Respect You, but I Hope You Will Reconsider What Deserves Our Admiration

Elon, you have made extraordinary contributions to human civilisation.

You have helped make reusable rockets a reality, transformed the electric vehicle industry and given new hope to people living with severe disabilities through Neuralink.

I sincerely hope your work continues to succeed.

I do not oppose your doing business in China.

Nor do I object to your admiration for Chinese engineers, the dedication of Chinese workers or the technological achievements of the Chinese people.

But I hope you will recognise several essential distinctions.

Admiring the Chinese people does not require admiring the Chinese Communist Party.

Appreciating a country's infrastructure does not require endorsing its political system.

Respecting economic achievement does not require overlooking the freedom and dignity of those who live under that system.

Political authority should not be judged solely by the scale of what it builds or produces.

It should also be judged by whether it is constrained by law, subject to meaningful accountability and respectful of fundamental individual rights.

I hope you will see not only the skyscrapers of Shanghai and the advanced factories of Shenzhen, but also the ordinary families who have lost wealth, freedom or opportunities because of harmful political decisions.

I hope you will look beyond China's economic statistics to the lives of people who cannot speak freely about their own government.

I still believe technological innovation can change the world.

But I also believe that freedom, the rule of law, human dignity and limits upon political power are indispensable foundations of genuine civilisational progress.

As a disabled man, I know how much personal independence matters.

As the son of a family that experienced political persecution, I know how devastating unchecked power can be.

As a long-term investor in your businesses, I still want them to succeed and help humanity move forward.

But admiration for your achievements cannot require me to suspend my independent judgement of your public statements.

Please do not look only at the lights of China's great cities.

Look also at the people living in their shadows.

I admire your ability to change the world. But I hope you will never confuse a nation's material achievements with the legitimacy of the political power that governs it.

Yours sincerely,

A British citizen of Chinese origin, a disabled man, and a long-term investor in Tesla and SpaceX

York, United Kingdom

19 November 2026

Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe, Nigeria’s first President, offered a profound tribute to Dr. Joseph Boakye Danquah following his death in detention at Nsawam Medium Security Prison on February 4, 1965.

His words remain a damning indictment of Kwame Nkrumah 

“If independence means the substitution of indigenous tyranny for alien rule, then those who struggled for the independence of former colonial territories have not only desecrated the cause of freedom, they have betrayed their peoples.”

He further observed:

“If the lessons of history mean much, then the sacrifice of West Africa’s pioneer scholar, lawyer, journalist, poet, statesman and fighter in the cause of human freedom will not be in vain.”

The man widely regarded as the doyen of Ghanaian politics was reduced to a prisoner in his own country and died in detention under the watch of an emotionally imbalanced leader whose government had become increasingly intolerant of dissent.

Danquah was imprisoned without trial, not for a crime he had committed, but under a regime that treated political opposition as a threat to be crushed and perceived future intentions as grounds for punishment.

The greatest irony of independence is that a people can overthrow colonial tyranny only to become victims of tyranny imposed by their own.

Dr. Kwame Nkrumah may have led Ghana to independence, but history must also hold him accountable for the repression, political persecution and human tragedy that stained his administration.

Independence without liberty is merely a change of masters. And no political legacy, however celebrated, should be allowed to erase that truth.

EVENSTAD FOR U.S. SENATE BLASTS GOVERNOR TIM WALZ AND SENATOR AMY KLOBUCHAR FOR REFUSING TO MEET ON MINNESOTA’S THREE CURRENT PUBLIC SAFETY EMERGENCIES
Charges leadership with willful indifference while preventable violence continues and the only structural solution remains ignored
EDINA, MN — Thomas Evenstad, Republican candidate for the United States Senate seat being vacated by Amy Klobuchar and architect of the Violently Dangerous Persons Act (VDP Act / Mariah’s Law / Iryna’s Law), today issued a direct and blistering condemnation of Governor Tim Walz and Senator Amy Klobuchar for their continued refusal to meet with him regarding Minnesota’s three interlocking public safety emergencies.
“Governor Walz and Senator Klobuchar have had every opportunity to sit down, review the record, and confront the failures that keep producing dead women and children,” Evenstad said. “They refuse. That refusal is not a scheduling problem. It is a choice. While they protect their political comfort, Minnesota families bury the predictable victims of a system that will not remove the most violently dangerous offenders before they kill again.”
Evenstad identifies the three current public safety emergencies as follows:
The continuing wave of domestic-related and preventable violent deaths across Minnesota communities, including recent incidents in Lindstrom, North St. Paul, Cottage Grove, Inver Grove Heights, and other locations where killers had documented prior courses of violence, protective-order violations, and repeat domestic abuse histories.
The systemic failure to identify, detain, and civilly commit the most violently dangerous repeat offenders before they kill again — the precise gap the VDP Act is designed to close by expanding Minnesota’s existing civil-commitment framework (modeled on Chapter 253D) to cover violently dangerous persons who have engaged in a course of harmful violent behavior, manifest a relevant mental disorder or dysfunction, and are likely to reoffend. Modeling projects a 50–64 percent reduction in overall violence if applied aggressively.
Institutional capture and selective enforcement that treats genuine accountability efforts and structural reform as radioactive while rewarding photo-ops, task-force theater, coordination memos, and party loyalty over results that actually lower the body count.
“These are not random tragedies and they are not acts of God,” Evenstad stated. “They are the direct, foreseeable result of leadership that has refused for years to engage the one proposal on the table that targets the small number of people driving the majority of serious violence. I proposed GPS monitoring of high-risk offenders in January 2003 — months before Dru Sjodin was murdered. I have refined the VDP Act for more than twenty years. Walz and Klobuchar know it exists. They have refused every request for a meeting. That is not bipartisanship. That is institutional stonewalling.”
Evenstad renewed his demand for an immediate, public, on-the-record meeting with both Governor Walz and Senator Klobuchar (or Governor-elect Klobuchar, as the case may be) to discuss:
Immediate legislative consideration and advancement of the VDP Act / Mariah’s Law
Appointment of a Public Safety Commissioner focused on measurable violence reduction rather than rhetoric
Full accountability for the institutional failures that have left victims unprotected
“I am not asking for a favor or a photo opportunity,” Evenstad said. “I am demanding that the highest elected officials in this state stop ignoring the blood on the floor. Meet. Debate the record in public. Or explain to every grieving family why their loved one’s death was an acceptable cost of your silence.”
Evenstad is running as a public-safety-first Republican populist in the 2027 special election for the open U.S. Senate seat (Republican primary August 10, 2027; general election November 2, 2027). His platform centers on results: expanded civil-commitment authority against violently dangerous repeat offenders, real accountability for institutional failure, secure borders, protection of Minnesota families, and an end to the soft-on-crime and selective-enforcement policies that have defined the current era.

text:
EDINBURGH 

International Arts Festival plans more for 80th birthday, funds permitting; Nicola Bernadetti's contract extended two more years.

In an early taster of next year’s programme, Benedetti said Glyndebourne Festival Opera, which provided the backbone of the first festival in 1947, would return with a new interpretation of Leoš Janáček’s unflinching 1904 opera Jenůfa, which examines infanticide and redemption.

Three other productions announced early include a world premiere of Scottish Ballet’s new multidisciplinary treatment of William Shakespeare’s 'A Midsummer Night’s Dream', performed by Jessica Wright and Morgann Runacre-Temple. Simon Rattle will conduct the Bavarian Radio Symphony Orchestra, featuring Berlioz and Brahms – two composers whose work also featured in 1947.

It will also stage a new theatrical adaptation of Harry Macqueen’s film Supernova, featuring Ewan McGregor and Alan Cumming performing together on stage for the first time. It “beautifully explores how a lifetime of love is changed irrevocably when memory starts to fray”, the festival said.

Despite this trail, the EIF has abandoned a short-lived experiment with selling tickets to some of its headline shows earlier than normal. 

Last year it put some tickets for shows including San Francisco Ballet and Wagner Moura’s recasting of Henrik Ibsen’s An Enemy of the People on sale in November, in an attempt to test whether that boosted publicity and audiences.

Benedetti indicated that despite anxieties about the festival’s funding, EIF will continue heavily subsiding its events, she said, selling some tickets for Jenůfa below the entry-level prices set for Glyndebourne’s festival in East Sussex.

In her five-year tenure, extended by two more years to 2029, Benedetti expanded the festival’s cut-price ticketing offer, guaranteeing £10 seats for every performance; pricing half of all seats at £30 or less, increasing free tickets for the young.

“I would say our commitment to affordability, accessibility and that societal involvement that allows all of those barriers to be broken down, we’re doubling down on that,” she said.

Previous real-terms cuts to the EIF’s core funding, a decline in funding from donors and private foundations and rising inflation meant its spending power had fallen by 26% in real terms between 2019 and 2024.

The 2027 Edinburgh international festival runs from 6 August to 4 September, with the full programme to be announced in March.

text:
'The Wailing Wall' (1880) by Jean-Léon Gérôme

Jean-Léon Gérôme’s 'The Wailing Wall' offers an illusion of almost photographic immediacy. The extraordinary precision with which the artist renders the masonry lends the surface of the painting an arresting material presence: each stone appears singular, bearing the distinctive marks of time, erosion and exposure to the elements. An intricate palette of ochre and sandstone hues, punctuated by fissures and tufts of vegetation emerging from the crevices, contributes to the impression that we are contemplating not a painted representation but a fragment of reality itself. The work exemplifies the principles of Academic Realism, a tradition to which Gérôme remained deeply committed throughout his career. Drawing extensively on the observations gathered during his numerous travels, the French painter cultivated an exceptionally meticulous pictorial language, frequently turning to historical, Orientalist and mythological subjects.

At the centre of the composition, a solitary Jewish figure stands before the ancient stones, holding a small piece of paper, presumably bearing a prayer, an invocation or a personal wish. In accordance with a religious custom that has endured for centuries, he appears about to slip the note into one of the wall’s crevices. Beside him rests a walking staff, while a modest bundle on the ground suggests that he may be travelling, carrying with him the few possessions he needs. His attire is equally distinctive: a dark top hat contrasts with the green robe that envelops his figure. Yet the circumstances of his presence remain deliberately indeterminate. Is he preparing to embark on a journey, entrusting his fate to divine protection, or has he returned safely and come to express his gratitude? Gérôme offers no narrative clues that might resolve this ambiguity, leaving the viewer to imagine the personal history concealed behind this moment of silent devotion.

Historically, the so-called Wailing Wall constitutes the western retaining wall of the platform built under Herod the Great as part of the expansion of the Second Temple in Jerusalem. Although originally a structure with no independent religious function, it gradually acquired profound spiritual significance in Jewish tradition. Its emergence as a site of prayer and pilgrimage is generally traced to the centuries following the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE. Significantly, Jewish usage traditionally refers to it as the Western Wall (Ha-Kotel Ha-Ma'aravi), rather than by the designation «Wailing Wall», a term that reflects an external perception of Jewish lamentation. For many Jews, the wall embodies the enduring bond between God and the people of Israel, as well as the historical continuity of their religious and cultural identity. The practice of inserting written prayers and supplications into its crevices, documented from at least the early eighteenth century, lends Gérôme’s painting an additional ethnographic and historical dimension: the artist captures not merely an architectural monument, but a ritual gesture through which individual hopes and anxieties become inscribed in a place of collective memory.

text:
Chris Hayes: Donald Trump clearly admires dictators, and he wants to be one himself. He's basically said as much over and over. He once infamously joked that he wants his people to sit up at attention like North Korean officials do for Kim Jong Un. We saw this on display in China today, where Trump spent the day greeting and fawning over Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, both of whom he will meet with tomorrow. But here's the thing, try as he might, Donald Trump is not a dictator. That is simply not the way things work in this country. And voters drove that point home two weeks ago in the midterms. When you step back and take stock of the rebuke of Trump and his party, it is truly historic. I mean, Democrats are rocketing towards 14-point national House vote margin. That is the largest victory for either political party since the post-Watergate era. That's 52 years. With last night's call for Democrat Mary Peltola in Alaska, the Democratic Party has officially flipped nine Senate seats, the most since the 1958 midterms under President Dwight Eisenhower almost 70 years ago. When all the races are called, we're still waiting on a few outstanding House races, it's now looking like Democrats will wind up with something like 260 seats in the House. That's an absolute shellacking for the Republicans and Donald Trump. I mean, the hard floor for one of the two major parties in this country is about 40 percent of the vote. It's just the way partisanship works in a two-party society. It's roughly what Herbert Hoover got in 1932 and what Barry Goldwater got in 1964. Two historic losers. Right now it's looking like the Republicans got about 43 percent of the national vote this time. Not quite a Hoover-esque disaster, but pretty close. You just don't see margins like that very often. But the fact that Democrats won such a historic victory should not distract us from the fact they had to overcome some real structural hurdles, not just the ones baked into our Constitution, but also the anti-democratic agenda that the wannabe dictator and his party undertook ahead of this election, specifically their unprecedented mid-cycle redistricting scheme to redraw the electoral maps in their favor. The fact that Democrats were able to overcome those rigged maps shouldn't excuse the fact they were rigged in the first place. That's not how this should work. As the economist Owen Winter points out, thanks to Republican gerrymandering, Democrats won 53 percent of the vote in Texas, but only 37 percent of its House seats. They won 45 percent of the vote in Tennessee, but only 11 percent of its House seats. In Oklahoma, they won no House seats, despite earning 41 percent of the vote. We saw some similar trends in Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, Louisiana, and Utah. They won a majority of votes for Congress in Utah, of all places. All told, elections analyst G. Elliott Morris estimates that with fair maps, Democrats could have won more than 280 House seats instead of 260. That's approaching new deal-level majorities like we saw following the Great Depression. And in just two years, we're going to see a bunch of Democrats defending seats with these gerrymandered maps in very red districts. That is to say nothing of the larger structural issue that we all labor under of the Electoral College, which has, twice just in my lifetime, handed the presidency to the Republican presidential candidate who got fewer votes. It's the only election in the whole country that works that way. And in both cases, it was a person who was unqualified to be the president at moments of incredible peril and challenge. It led to a disaster both times. George W. Bush during 9/11 and Donald Trump during the COVID pandemic. Both men sent the country into a reeling set of crises despite the majority of voters choosing the other person. There's a real question of whether Republicans want to continue with that system. They say they do. They love the Electoral College because of that, because it's benefited them twice. But here's a question I have for them and for you at home. Do Republicans really want to roll the dice in a world where Texas is a swing state? Think about this. A world where Democrats can win all 40 electoral votes despite a narrow victory in the state of, say, a few thousand vote win? Do you want to give the Democrats all 40 electoral votes from Texas if the top of the ticket carries it by 5,000 votes? Or do Republicans just want to try to win the national popular vote, something they managed to do twice since 2004, something that Donald Trump did in the last election? I think there's an open question setting to 2028. But right now, we should just not let the fact that Democrats managed to overcome a death initially unfair system distract from the fact that the system is unfair and anti-democratic in the first place.

SOURCE: MS NOW, Nov. 18, 2026

text:
A woman from the US Democratic Party, which won the election, for the 2028 presidential race 

A week after an unprecedented number of left-wing candidates won in the American midterm elections, nearly 600 individuals joined a Zoom discussion with the aim of fielding New York Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez for the 2028 presidential election. The discussion was organized by 'Ready for AOC,' a new organization comprising progressives and union organizers, who focused on future plans rather than celebrating the Democratic Party's victory.
"People across the country are ready for a very different and better future. We are more ready for it than ever," stated Genevieve Rand, an organizer for the group.

Within 24 hours of the 'Ready for AOC' movement launching last Monday, over 10,000 people from all 50 US states had signed a pledge to support her, and nearly 4,000 had registered for organizational discussions to kickstart a grassroots campaign to ensure her victory. Ravi Sahay, an organizer for the group who also worked on New York City Councilman Zohran Mamdani's election campaign last year, said their sole aim was to get her to run. Emphasizing that this was an independent volunteer effort not connected to her team, he stated, "This is clearly a very personal decision. We respect that, and we want to show that there is real and broad support behind such a candidacy."

Ocasio-Cortez, a millennial congresswoman who eight years ago unexpectedly defeated a traditional candidate, paving the way for a new renaissance in American left-wing politics, has not yet officially announced her presidential candidacy. She recently mentioned that she would take some time to make a personal decision on the matter. It is also reported that she is considering running in a primary challenge against Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer. Nevertheless, efforts to build a grassroots campaign for her have already begun, and the New York City branch of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), which supported many left-wing candidates who won in the midterm elections, passed a resolution at its biennial convention last Saturday encouraging her to run for president. The resolution passed 291 to 123, stating that in the face of rising fascism and historic levels of inequality, the 2028 presidential election will have a decisive impact on the direction of American politics and world history.

Amidst rising living costs, endless wars, and a widening gap between a small wealthy elite and the rest of the population, American left-wing politics has been revitalized. Since Bernie Sanders' historic presidential campaign in 2016, demands for universal healthcare, affordable housing, free childcare, and getting money out of politics have become more mainstream than ever. With the recent electoral victories, six new democratic socialists, including pro-Palestinian activists, labor, and community organizers, are set to join Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib in Congress by next January. Additionally, four new democratic socialist mayors will join Mamdani in governing American cities, and over 100 socialists will serve in state and local offices across the country.

However, not everyone in the left-wing camp is waiting for Ocasio-Cortez's decision. Two days after the midterm elections, former Democratic Socialist Congressman Jamaal Bowman and progressive activist Nomiki Konst together formed a committee to field California Congressman Ro Khanna for president. On the other hand, New York City Councilman Mamdani, who has become a pivotal figure on the left through his support for other democratic socialist candidates, is also holding discussions with union leaders to advocate for a pro-labor left-wing leader. Shawn Fain, president of the United Auto Workers (UAW), and Sara Nelson, president of the Association of Flight Attendants (CWA), were among the leaders he met.

Nevertheless, political activists point out that Ocasio-Cortez's popularity, fundraising ability, and deep connections within Washington and with working-class movements are unmatched by any other viable candidate in the left-wing camp. "Her victory in 2018 shook national politics in a way we hadn't seen before. There's really no one else with that kind of profile," said Ravi Sahay. When she first ran for Congress in 2018, she stated that she was running not "from the left" but "from the bottom." With the victory of both progressive and moderate Democratic candidates this month, her supporters are once again highlighting that grassroots populist message. They focus more on policies like Medicare for All, the Green New Deal, and raising the minimum wage, rather than ideology. However, this approach may clash with the DSA, the largest national organization on the left, which shows little inclination to change its stances or vocabulary to suit mainstream audiences.

Socialists, who have prioritized local elections and grassroots organizing for years, say that now is the best opportunity to elect a socialist president, and if this opportunity is missed, it may not come again. By 2028, anyone entering the race will face a completely different political landscape. Currently, the DSA has over 130,000 dues-paying members nationwide and more than 200 local chapters, and the number of Americans who view socialism positively is also growing. "Democratic socialism is becoming a mainstream part of American politics. Now we have an opportunity to do something much bigger and bolder," said Eric Blanc, a member of Rutgers University and the DSA, on election night.

Although socialist candidates have previously run for American president, they always ran as a third party. The highest percentage of votes a socialist candidate received in a presidential election was 6% by Eugene Debs in 1912, a founding member of the Socialist Party of America, labor organizer, and anti-war activist. In that year, the socialist movement reached its peak with 120,000 members, but it was later pushed to the fringes of American politics due to anti-communist scares (Red Scares), the Cold War, and internal conflicts. The DSA surpassed that 120,000-member record last summer. The dormant socialist movement was revived in 2016 when Bernie Sanders came very close to securing the Democratic Party's presidential nomination. This served as a catalyst for many newcomers like Ocasio-Cortez and Mamdani to enter politics, and DSA membership rapidly increased under the theme, "We have a world to win."

However, as the organization grew, internal disagreements also emerged between pragmatism and ideological rigidity, as well as on issues concerning Israel, policing, and other matters. Even some dedicated members have on several occasions distanced themselves from the organization's more radical stances, such as abolishing borders or the US Senate. While a group is rallying around Ocasio-Cortez, internal opposition against her remains strong. One group, in particular, accuses her of betraying the organization's values, especially concerning Israel. The DSA national leadership also maintains a highly critical stance towards her and has not yet taken any official position regarding her presidential candidacy. The national DSA organization withdrew its official endorsement for her in 2024 due to her failure to vote against funding for Israel's Iron Dome missile defense system and for organizing a discussion that included supporters of a controversial interpretation of antisemitism.

Furthermore, it is still unclear whether other parts of the Democratic Party are ready to accept a socialist candidate. Moderate Democratic funders, fearing the potential impact of the DSA in the 2028 election, have already pledged to spend millions of dollars to combat it. Although the last midterm election was a historic victory for leftists, many of their wins occurred in reliably Democratic states, while moderate Democratic candidates advanced in other areas. A successful presidential candidate must be able to gain broad popular appeal, at least in crucial swing states. Ravi Sahay points out that Ocasio-Cortez is the only candidate in the left-wing camp with the ability to communicate with such a large segment of the population, stating, "She has a vision, experience, and connections with the movement that no other candidate possesses."

text:
They Have a Fight. You Don't.

You do not have a fight with anyone in Russia. The fight is kept on by the offices that will not end it, the commands that still give the order, and the contracts that get paid either way.

The United States is not in a declared war with Russia. It is in a nine-month war with Iran. The bill arrives anyway, as fuel, as tax, and, on the other side of other borders, as a draft notice. That is not a mood. It is this month's record.

The Manual Already Named the Job

Buried in the fifteenth chapter of the Book of Jubilees is a sentence that reads like a job description. The nations belong to God, it says, "and over all hath He placed spirits in authority to lead them astray from Him." Then the exemption: "But over Israel He did not appoint any angel or spirit, for He alone is their ruler."

Deuteronomy 32 draws the same map. When the Most High divided the nations, he set their borders by the number of the sons of God, in the Dead Sea Scroll reading. The next verse holds one people back: "For the LORD's portion is his people; Jacob is the lot of his inheritance."

The earlier reading of those lines was simple. The nations were assigned to managers. The managers were given a brief. The brief was misdirection. And every flock was told it was the portion held back, so none of them ever compared notes.

That is still the architecture. This month is the log file.

Each government talks as if it were the exception. Washington talks as if its wars were regrettable necessities that somehow never reach the kitchen table. Moscow talks as if a "special operation" were a duty the public already blessed. Jerusalem talks as if another raid were the only language left. Beijing can run a hundred ships around Taiwan and call the carrier activity routine. Each side is told it is the one that cannot afford to stop. That is how a quarrel gets made for people who do not have one.

What the People Said

In October the Levada Center asked 1,601 Russians, in their homes, across 50 regions, what should happen now. Sixty-five percent said it was time to move to peace talks with Ukraine. Twenty-six percent wanted the fighting to continue. That is not a country demanding another year of war.

It is also not a country that has turned on its army. Sixty-nine percent still said they supported the Russian forces' actions in Ukraine. Twenty-one percent said they did not. Fifty-seven percent said they feared a general mobilisation. Seventy-two percent said a second wave was not needed in the coming months. Only nine percent said it was.

A month earlier, Levada had already measured the hook inside that fatigue. Eighty-one percent said they would support the president if he ended the conflict that very week. Only thirty-five percent would support him if ending it meant giving back the taken land. The public wants the shooting to go to the table. It does not, in the main, want to surrender the prize. The Kremlin has given it neither talks that stop the dying nor a reason to send the men home.

Americans were just as clear about the war they are actually in. In July the Chicago Council on Global Affairs found that 68 percent said the Iran war had not been worth fighting, against 31 percent who said it had. Eighty-six percent said the war was bad for the cost of living in the United States. In late October, with the midterms days away, an Institute for Global Affairs / YouGov poll found that 56 percent wanted the country to avoid higher prices even if that meant military goals in Iran were not fully met. Only 22 percent took the other side. Forty-four percent said a candidate who supported the war would make them less likely to vote; 13 percent said more likely.

On November 3, Democrats took both the House and the Senate. The war did not end.

Even the quieter conflict shows the same split. In mid-October, Economist / YouGov found that 46 percent of registered voters still favored sending military aid to Ukraine, down from 56 percent in July, and 34 percent said the United States should not. Forty-eight percent called Russia an enemy. Thirty percent called it unfriendly. A public can dislike a government and still not want to own its war.

Israelis, in mid-September, did not think they had won. The Institute for National Security Studies asked a representative sample about the Gaza war and the war with Iran. Fifty-five percent said neither side had won in Gaza. Sixty percent said the war with Iran had no decisive winner. Only 34 percent were satisfied with the government's handling of Gaza. Seventy-five percent wanted a state commission of inquiry. That is not pacifism. It is a public that has already started keeping the books, while the offices keep writing new entries.

In China the last published Pulse survey, fielded in the spring by the Carter Center and Emory University and released in the fall, found no mandate for a preemptive full-scale invasion of Taiwan. Most respondents favored cultural exchange, economic exchange, and official talks. Forty percent said Taiwan should not be unified by force under any circumstances. If Taiwan declared independence, 24 percent favored a full-scale attack. The public's warmth toward Taiwan was the highest of any place in the survey. The navy, in early November, still went to sea.

What the Offices Did

On November 19, in Shenzhen, the presidents of the United States, China, and Russia issued a "Declaration toward Peace." The text has four points. They will reform the United Nations. They will increase the supply of refined petroleum and keep energy flows stable. They will respect the immunities of state officials, and the International Criminal Court and "other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction." They repeated that "a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought."

The document does not mention Ukraine. It does not mention Iran. It does not mention Taiwan. It does not mention Gaza. That is not an oversight. That is the function of the text: peace among the managers, with the wars left off the page.

The same day, in Vienna, the United States, Britain, France, and Germany told the International Atomic Energy Agency's board that inspectors have "lost continuity of knowledge" on Iran's previously verified stock of highly enriched uranium for a year and a half. Only the Bushehr power plant is being inspected. Iran said access cannot resume while attacks and the threat of more attacks continue. Both statements can sit on the same table. The material is unaccounted for. The doors stay closed. The war that closed them is in its ninth month.

The day before, Israeli tanks crossed Gaza's "yellow line" in the first ground operation across that boundary since the October 2025 ceasefire. The military said the raid was completed about 24 hours later. Hamas called it a violation. The Board of Peace, the American-led body overseeing the truce, had just told the U.N. Security Council that both sides were failing to honor their commitments. Its line was plain: "a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely."

In the first days of November, Taiwan's national security chief, Joseph Wu, reported more than 100 Chinese navy and coast-guard ships in the western Pacific, with dozens of military aircraft near the island. Analysts read the pattern as a rehearsal for isolation: ships close in, and a carrier group between Taiwan and Guam. China did not give the drill a name. Officials in Taipei later called it silent intimidation. Beijing called the carrier activity routine.

So lay the week out. A peace declaration that will not name the wars. A uranium stock the inspectors cannot see. A ceasefire line crossed. A fleet large enough to practice a blockade, sent out without a title. And a public, in country after country, that had already said it wanted the bill to stop growing.

The Truce They Forbade

This is not a new invention. It is an old habit with better stationery.

Late on Christmas Eve, 1914, British soldiers in the trenches heard Germans singing carols and saw lanterns and small fir trees along the parapet. Messages started crossing the mud. One German voice, remembered later, made the offer in broken English: "Tomorrow you no shoot, we no shoot."

On Christmas Day, in some sectors, they met in no-man's-land. They exchanged gifts, took photographs, buried the dead, and in some places kicked a football around. It was not universal. Elsewhere the killing continued. Some officers hated it on sight, because a man who has shared a cigarette with the person opposite him is harder to send over the top in the morning.

After Boxing Day the meetings dwindled. After 1914, the high commands on both sides moved to make sure a truce on that scale did not happen again. A German veteran recalled the sequel in one sentence: a strict order came that no fraternisation was allowed, and they had to stay back in their trenches. Later in the war, in quiet sectors, soldiers still sometimes practiced a tacit "live and let live," pausing long enough to repair a trench or gather the dead. The commands kept trying to stamp even that out.

The control is sitting in the Imperial War Museum's letters and photographs. Ordinary men, given a night and a hymn, stopped shooting. The offices made sure they started again. The flocks found each other. The shepherds pulled the leash.

Who Gets Paid

You do not need a theory about motives to read an invoice.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration reported that in September, American retail gasoline averaged $4.35 a gallon. Diesel averaged $6.29. A year earlier, the annual gasoline average had been $3.10. In July, 86 percent of Americans already said the Iran war was bad for the cost of living. They were not guessing. They were looking at the pump.

On October 22, Lockheed Martin reported third-quarter sales of $20.7 billion, up 11 percent from a year earlier, and net earnings of $1.8 billion, up 14 percent. Its backlog hit a record $292 billion. That number included a $52.5 billion multi-year award for PAC-3 interceptors. The Missiles and Fire Control backlog alone rose from $46.7 billion at the end of 2025 to $142.5 billion. The company raised its dividend for the 24th year in a row.

That backlog is not an abstract cloud. It is tax money, already committed, sitting in a queue of missiles. It is also a reason the fight is easy to keep on. A truce does not grow a $292 billion book. A new year of operations does.

On the Russian side of the ledger the currency is not only money. It is men. Fifty-seven percent of those Levada asked in October said they feared being called up. Seventy-two percent said the country did not need another mobilisation. The war continued anyway. A family that has no personal quarrel with a family in Kharkiv or Donetsk still lives inside the risk of a telegram at the door.

You can dislike a government in Moscow and still see the symmetry. You have no fight with the people there. They, in the main, have no fight they want to keep with you. The assigned leaders keep writing the war as if both sides had asked for it. The pump, the tax bill, and the draft notice are how the assignment reaches the house.

Keep the Books

The old texts did not say the managers would look like demons to their own flocks. They said each flock would be taught that the other flocks' shepherds were the demons, and that its own was the exception. Watch the speeches this month and you will hear that firmware humming in every capital at once.

Do not take their word for the exception. Take their receipts.

When a summit issues a peace declaration, read whether it names the war, and then check whether the shooting stopped. When a government calls a raid a completed operation, write down whether the ceasefire line moved back. When executives and ministers talk about necessity, look at the backlog and the price of diesel. When a poll says the public wants talks, look at who is still being sent.

The test is older than any of these offices. Keep the ledger. Write down what was promised and when. Then write down what came. Do it for the president and the general, the company and the ministry, the church and the feed.

You will notice the same gap in each column. The people keep saying they are tired. The offices keep finding a reason to continue. The invoice keeps arriving at the house.

You do not have a fight with anyone in Russia. You do not have to pretend the quarrel started at your table. The only duty that follows from that is a plain one: watch what the assigned leaders do, and stop confusing their fight with yours.

text:
Everything that happened in the data center world today (Nov 19, 2026)

Anthropic just raised $107B to pay its compute bill. Taiwan had its 7th-worst point drop ever the same morning.

ANTHROPIC IPO
- Priced at $83, above the $70-78 range. 980M shares, $81.3B raised, the largest IPO on record. About $1.5T fully diluted. Trades today as ANT. (Anthropic, CNBC)
- A $26B private placement at the same price lifts the total to ~$107B. Nvidia and AMD are among the placement buyers. (https://t.co/qptOQaaEZU)
- The filing shows ~$900B of compute and infrastructure commitments, including ~$121B with Google for TPU hosting and ~$110B with AWS for Trainium. It warns contracted capacity "may be delayed, repriced, reduced, or not delivered" if partners' chip financing dries up. (Anthropic filing, DCD, Semi Doped)

NVIDIA
- Closed -2.89% at $150.96 a day after the beat. Kress told staff "let's move forward" at the first all-hands without Huang and pulled annual reviews up to December. (CNBC)
- Heidrick & Struggles has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas about the CEO job. He's one of several candidates. (Bloomberg Law, Guardian)
- Kress says Nvidia's guarantees only kick in after a customer lines up its own financing. Land, power and shell is the top priority, and it will be choosier about which companies it backs. (TechCrunch)

CHINA RULES
- TSMC is halting affected Chinese orders at 16nm and below without US licenses. Those customers get 28/40nm, with no HBM and no advanced packaging. Samsung also paused some shipments, per the FT. (Reuters)
- Alibaba capex rose 60% to 50.5B yuan, and AI cloud revenue grew 53%. It says the new US rule will hit its access to overseas compute. (Alibaba)

CHIPS, MEMORY & PACKAGING
- Micron: 75% of 2027 output is sold and customers are already negotiating 2028. It has 26 multiyear deals with $32B upfront, take-or-pay terms and price bands. (Micron at TomorrowX)
- Google wants to buy HBM directly for the TPUs it builds with MediaTek. (Digitimes)
- Microsoft will package Azure chips with Intel's EMIB and locked in multiyear Xeon supply, including Diamond Rapids. (Intel)
- Kulicke & Soffa Q4 revenue up 131% to $410.3M. (K&S)
- ASE broke ground on a NT$248.9B high-end test campus in Kaohsiung. (Economic Daily News)
- AAOI fell 9% on a $550M at-the-market stock sale. Coherent and Lumentum rose ~4%. (24/7 Wall St.)

POWER & POLICY
- Fed minutes: "most" officials said AI debt grew fast through "complex and opaque" financing. Staff flagged off-balance-sheet leases and circular deals. Waller wants a possible 50bp hike in December. (CNBC)
- Texas resumed data center air permits. Salt Lake City passed a 180-day ban on new data centers. (Reuters, Axios)

$SLNH | Dorothy 3A: the Microsoft connection looks strong. The delivery schedule and lease economics still need explaining.
ChronoScale’s November 18 SEC presentation identifies Silverton, Texas, as the location for its 49.5 MW Microsoft deployment. The Texas Comptroller lists ChronoScale as Dorothy 3A’s occupant, while Soluna describes a planned 50 MW critical IT facility—approximately 75 MW gross—with Applied Digital.

The evidence strongly points to Dorothy 3A, although ChronoScale does not explicitly name Dorothy in its presentation. https://t.co/0HK20ZLdXt

Several important questions remain.

1. The delivery schedule is extremely tight.

ChronoScale signed its Microsoft agreement on August 6, 2026. Its presentation schedules:

• February 28, 2027: 12,600 GPUs / 24.3 MW IT
• March 31, 2027: 13,104 GPUs / 25.2 MW IT

That totals 25,704 GPUs and 49.5 MW IT, approximately seven to eight months after signing. These are ChronoScale’s planned deliveries; Soluna has not announced a corresponding rent commencement date. https://t.co/5UQM4xY0B0
Soluna says construction started in October, leaving roughly four to six months of site construction before those deliveries. Earlier design, procurement and off-site manufacturing could help, but we need evidence showing how this schedule is achievable.

For context, Applied Digital describes standardized construction cycles of approximately 12–18 months for larger 100–150 MW facilities. Dorothy’s smaller, phased deployment has different requirements, but its schedule still appears exceptionally aggressive. https://t.co/cZFZYvpnBk

2. How much of the building actually exists?

Soluna’s progress chart indicates initial vertical construction at Dorothy. The building image on its Dorothy slide is explicitly illustrative.

We have not independently verified a completed shell or the current state of electrical, cooling and commissioning work. That leaves a critical gap in assessing delivery readiness. https://t.co/cZFZYvpnBk

3. The JV closing and definitive lease remain outstanding.

Soluna and Applied signed a binding subscription agreement on October 20, but closing and the definitive ChronoScale lease remain unfinished in the disclosures reviewed.

Applied is already funding development and long-lead equipment before closing. Nevertheless, if the site transaction fails, we have no basis to assume another facility could meet the same Microsoft schedule. https://t.co/sBRiUncjin

4. The lease terms will determine the project’s financing and Soluna’s economics.

Microsoft’s disclosed GPU services agreement runs for approximately three years. The Dorothy 3A lease must establish its own duration, rent, delivery obligations and payment guarantees. Those terms have not yet been disclosed.

We need to know whether ChronoScale’s rental obligations will carry an Applied Digital guarantee, prepaid rent or other security. Microsoft’s involvement alone should not be treated as a guarantee of the JV’s rental income. https://t.co/sBRiUncjin

ChronoScale’s presentation allocates approximately $200 million of equity funding to the Microsoft GPU contract and describes Silverton fit-out work. It also anticipates additional financing for remaining capital expenditure. This does not establish that all funding for the GPUs and facility is committed.

Soluna’s planned 49% interest is in the landlord JV. Its returns will depend on the lease, project expenses, financing and distribution terms. That interest does not represent 49% of ChronoScale’s Microsoft GPU revenue.

5. Delivery extensions are not a blanket escape clause.

ChronoScale discloses possible extensions, excluded delays and force majeure provisions. The precise qualifying events, extension periods and approval mechanism have not been disclosed in the material reviewed.

Its filings also describe daily delay credits and Microsoft termination/refund rights under specified circumstances. Financing or construction difficulties should not be assumed to qualify for a penalty-free extension. https://t.co/sBRiUncjin

6. Microsoft delay credits are ChronoScale’s obligations.

No direct Soluna guarantee of those credits has been disclosed. Any delivery liability of the landlord JV would need to arise under its own agreements, whose final terms remain unknown.

Soluna does have a separate disclosed exposure if the JV transaction terminates: reimbursement of 80% of specified Applied-funded development costs, capped at $45 million, plus applicable interest. That obligation relates to transaction termination, rather than automatically arising from a late Microsoft delivery. https://t.co/sBRiUncjin

7. Expansion remains potential.

The disclosed Microsoft deployment is approximately 50 MW. I have not found a publicly disclosed capacity expansion option beyond that initial deployment. Dorothy’s broader campus potential should therefore remain separate from confirmed Microsoft demand. https://t.co/sBRiUncjin

The Microsoft connection materially strengthens Dorothy 3A’s commercial case. The next proof points are the completed JV closing, signed lease with credible credit support, committed financing and a construction-to-service schedule supported by actual site progress.

Until those are clearer, a full quarter of project rental income in Q2 2027 remains a conditional scenario.

The lawsuit, filed in February, asked a judge to declare CAIR and the Muslim Brotherhood foreign terrorist and transnational criminal organizations and bar them from operating, fundraising, recruiting or owning property in the state.
