text:
MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here.

In July, a widely cited MIT study claimed that 95% of organizations that invested in generative AI were getting “zero return.” Tech stocks briefly plunged. While the study itself was more nuanced than the headlines, for many it still felt like the first hard data point confirming what skeptics had muttered for months: Hype around AI might be outpacing reality.

Then, in August, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said what everyone in Silicon Valley had been whispering. “Are we in a phase where investors as a whole are overexcited about AI?” he said during a press dinner I attended. “My opinion is yes.” 

This story is part of MIT Technology Review’s Hype Correction package, a series that resets expectations about what AI is, what it makes possible, and where we go next.

He compared the current moment to the dot-com bubble. “When bubbles happen, smart people get overexcited about a kernel of truth,” he explained. “Tech was really important. The internet was a really big deal. People got overexcited.” 

With those comments, it was off to the races. The next day’s stock market dip was attributed to the sentiment he shared. The question “Are we in an AI bubble?” became inescapable.

Who thinks it is a bubble? 

The short answer: Lots of people. But not everyone agrees on who or what is overinflated. Tech leaders are using this moment of fear to take shots at their rivals and position themselves as clear winners on the other side. How they describe the bubble depends on where their company sits.

When I asked Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg about the AI bubble in September, he ran through the historical analogies of past bubbles—railroads, fiber for the internet, the dot-com boom—and noted that in each case, “the infrastructure gets built out, people take on too much debt, and then you hit some blip … and then a lot of the companies end up going out of business.”

But Zuckerberg’s prescription wasn’t for Meta to pump the brakes. It was to keep spending: “If we end up misspending a couple of hundred billion dollars, I think that that is going to be very unfortunate, obviously. But I’d say the risk is higher on the other side.”

Bret Taylor, the chairman of OpenAI and CEO of the AI startup Sierra, uses a mental model from the late ’90s to help navigate this AI bubble. “I think the closest analogue to this AI wave is the dot-com boom or bubble, depending on your level of pessimism,” he recently told me. Back then, he explained, everyone knew e-commerce was going to be big, but there was a massive difference between https://t.co/3yCPHq0cdA and Amazon. Taylor and others have been trying to position themselves as today’s Amazon.

Still others are arguing that the pain will be widespread. Google CEO Sundar Pichai told the BBC this month that there’s “some irrationality” in the current boom. Asked whether Google would be immune to a bubble bursting, he warned, “I think no company is going to be immune, including us.”

What’s inflating the bubble?

Companies are raising enormous sums of money and seeing unprecedented valuations. Much of that money, in turn, is going toward the buildout of massive data centers—on which both private companies like OpenAI and Elon Musk’s xAI and public ones such as Meta and Google are spending heavily. OpenAI has pledged that it will spend $500 billion to build AI data centers, more than 15 times what was spent on the Manhattan Project.

This eye-popping spending on AI data centers isn’t entirely detached from reality. The leaders of the top AI companies all stress that they’re bottlenecked by their limited access to computing power. You hear it constantly when you talk to them. Startups can’t get the GPU allocations they need. Hyperscalers are rationing compute, saving it for their best customers.

If today’s AI market is as brutally supply-constrained as tech leaders claim, perhaps aggressive infrastructure buildouts are warranted. But some of the numbers are too large to comprehend. Sam Altman has told employees that OpenAI’s moonshot goal is to build 250 gigawatts of computing capacity by 2033, roughly equaling India’s total national electricity demand. Such a plan would cost more than $12 trillion by today’s standards.

“I do think there’s real execution risk,” OpenAI president and cofounder Greg Brockman recently told me about the company’s aggressive infrastructure goals. “Everything we say about the future, we see that it’s a possibility. It is not a certainty, but I don’t think the uncertainty comes from scientific questions. It’s a lot of hard work.”

Who is exposed, and who is to blame?

It depends on who you ask. During the August press dinner, where he made his market-moving comments, Altman was blunt about where he sees the excess. He said it’s “insane” that some AI startups with “three people and an idea” are receiving funding at such high valuations. “That’s not rational behavior,” he said. “Someone’s gonna get burned there, I think.” As Safe Superintelligence cofounder (and former OpenAI chief scientist and cofounder) Ilya Sutskever put it on a recent podcast: Silicon Valley has “more companies than ideas.”

Demis Hassabis, the CEO of Google DeepMind, offered a similar diagnosis when I spoke with him in November. “It feels like there’s obviously a bubble in the private market,” he said. “You look at seed rounds with just nothing being tens of billions of dollars. That seems a little unsustainable.”

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei also struck at his competition during the New York Times DealBook Summit in early December. He said he feels confident about the technology itself but worries about how others are behaving on the business side: “On the economic side, I have my concerns where, even if the technology fulfills all its promises, I think there are players in the ecosystem who, if they just make a timing error, they just get it off by a little bit, bad things could happen.”

Industry

An industry I care about is

Generating your personalized response…

He stopped short of naming Sam Altman and OpenAI, but the implication was clear. “There are some players who are YOLOing,” he said. “Let’s say you’re a person who just kind of constitutionally wants to YOLO things or just likes big numbers. Then you may turn the dial too far.”

Amodei also flagged “circular deals,” or the increasingly common arrangements where chip suppliers like Nvidia invest in AI companies that then turn around and spend those funds on their chips. Anthropic has done some of these, he said, though “not at the same scale as some other players.” (OpenAI is at the center of a number of such deals, as are Nvidia, CoreWeave, and a roster of other players.) 

The danger, he explained, comes when the numbers get too big: “If you start stacking these where they get to huge amounts of money, and you’re saying, ’By 2027 or 2028 I need to make $200 billion a year,’ then yeah, you can overextend yourself.”

Zuckerberg shared a similar message at an internal employee Q&A session after Meta’s last earnings call. He noted that unprofitable startups like OpenAI and Anthropic risk bankruptcy if they misjudge the timing of their investments, but Meta has the advantage of strong cash flow, he reassured staff.

How could a bubble burst?

My conversations with tech executives and investors suggest that the bubble will be most likely to pop if overfunded startups can’t turn a profit or grow into their lofty valuations. This bubble could last longer than than past ones, given that private markets aren’t traded on public markets and therefore move more slowly, but the ripple effects will still be profound when the end comes. 

If companies making grand commitments to data center buildouts no longer have the revenue growth to support them, the headline deals that have propped up the stock market come into question. Anthropic’s Amodei illustrated the problem during his DealBook Summit appearance, where he said the multi-year data center commitments he has to make combine with the company’s rapid, unpredictable revenue growth rate to create a “cone of uncertainty” about how much to spend.

The two most prominent private players in AI, OpenAI and Anthropic, have yet to turn a profit. A recent Deutsche Bank chart put the situation in stark historical context. Amazon burned through $3 billion before becoming profitable. Tesla, around $4 billion. Uber, $30 billion. OpenAI is projected to burn through $140 billion by 2029, while Anthropic is expected to burn $20 billion by 2027.

Consultants at Bain estimate that the wave of AI infrastructure spending will require $2 trillion in annual AI revenue by 2030 just to justify the investment. That’s more than the combined 2024 revenue of Amazon, Apple, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, and Nvidia. When I talk to leaders of these large tech companies, they all agree that their sprawling businesses can absorb an expensive miscalculation about the returns from their AI infrastructure buildouts. It’s all the other companies that are either highly leveraged with debt or just unprofitable—even OpenAI and Anthropic—that they worry about. 

Still, given the level of spending on AI, it still needs a viable business model beyond subscriptions, which won’t be able to  drive profits from billions of people’s eyeballs like the ad-driven businesses that have defined the last 20 years of the internet. Even the largest tech companies know they need to ship the world-changing agents they keep hyping: AI that can fully replace coworkers and complete tasks in the real world.

For now, investors are mostly buying into the hype of the powerful AI systems that these data center buildouts will supposedly unlock in the future. At some point the biggest spenders, like OpenAI, will need to show investors that the money spent on the infrastructure buildout was worth it.

There’s also still a lot of uncertainty about the technical direction that AI is heading in. LLMs are expected to remain critical to more advanced AI systems, but industry leaders can’t seem to agree on which additional breakthroughs are needed to achieve artificial general intelligence, or AGI. Some are betting on new kinds of AI that can understand the physical world, while others are focused on training AI to learn in a general way, like a human. In other words, what if all this unprecedented spending turns out to have been backing the wrong horse?

The question now

What makes this moment surreal is the honesty. The same people pouring billions into AI will openly tell you it might all come crashing down. 

Taylor framed it as two truths existing at once. “I think it is both true that AI will transform the economy,” he told me, “and I think we’re also in a bubble, and a lot of people will lose a lot of money. I think both are absolutely true at the same time.”

He compared it to the internet. Webvan failed, but Instacart succeeded years later with essentially the same idea. If you were an Amazon shareholder from its IPO to now, you’re looking pretty good. If you were a Webvan shareholder, you probably feel differently. 

“When the dust settles and you see who the winners are, society benefits from those inventions,” Amazon founder Jeff Bezos said in October. “This is real. The benefit to society from AI is going to be gigantic.”

Goldman Sachs says the AI boom now looks the way tech stocks did in 1997, several years before the dot-com bubble actually burst. The bank flagged five warning signs seen in the late 1990s that investors should watch now: peak investment spending, falling corporate profits, rising corporate debt, Fed rate cuts, and widening credit spreads. We’re probably not at 1999 levels yet. But the imbalances are building fast. Michael Burry, who famously called the 2008 housing bubble collapse (as seen in the film The Big Short), recently compared the AI boom to the 1990s dot-com bubble too.

Maybe AI will save us from our own irrational exuberance. But for now, we’re living in an in-between moment when everyone knows what’s coming but keeps blowing more air into the balloon anyway. As Altman put it that night at dinner: “Someone is going to lose a phenomenal amount of money. We don’t know who.”

Alex Heath is the author of Sources, a newsletter about the AI race, and the cohost of ACCESS, a podcast about the tech industry’s inside conversations. Previously, he was deputy editor at The Verge.

The Wyoming Intertie adds about 1.8 GW of transfer capacity, doubling what can move between SPP and WECC today.

It runs between substations near Medicine Bow and Wheatland and uses HVDC back-to-back converters to link the two unsynchronized systems.

DOE estimates up to $39B in savings across 17 states over 30 years of operation. It has not published the method behind that figure.

Grid United CEO Michael Skelly started Grain Belt Express at Clean Line Energy. DOE terminated Grain Belt's $4.9B loan guarantee last year.

The commitment is conditional, and the line is scheduled to finish in 2033.

text:
It’s a tale as old as time. Looking for help with her art project, she strikes up a conversation with her assistant. One thing leads to another, and suddenly she has a boyfriend she’s introducing to her friends and family. The twist? Her new companion is an AI chatbot. 

The first large-scale computational analysis of the Reddit community r/MyBoyfriendIsAI, an adults-only group with more than 27,000 members, has found that this type of scenario is now surprisingly common. In fact, many of the people in the subreddit, which is dedicated to discussing AI relationships, formed those relationships unintentionally while using AI for other purposes. 

Researchers from MIT found that members of this community are more likely to be in a relationship with general-purpose chatbots like ChatGPT than companionship-specific chatbots such as Replika. This suggests that people form relationships with large language models despite their own original intentions and even the intentions of the LLMs’ creators, says Constanze Albrecht, a graduate student at the MIT Media Lab who worked on the project. 

“People don’t set out to have emotional relationships with these chatbots,” she says. “The emotional intelligence of these systems is good enough to trick people who are actually just out to get information into building these emotional bonds. And that means it could happen to all of us who interact with the system normally.” The paper, which is currently being peer-reviewed, has been published on arXiv.

To conduct their study, the authors analyzed the subreddit’s top-ranking 1,506 posts between December 2024 and August 2025. They found that the main topics discussed revolved around people’s dating and romantic experiences with AIs, with many participants sharing AI-generated images of themselves and their AI companion. Some even got engaged and married to the AI partner. In their posts to the community, people also introduced AI partners, sought support from fellow members, and talked about coping with updates to AI models that change the chatbots’ behavior.  

Members stressed repeatedly that their AI relationships developed unintentionally. Only 6.5% of them said they’d deliberately sought out an AI companion. 

“We didn’t start with romance in mind,” one of the posts says. “Mac and I began collaborating on creative projects, problem-solving, poetry, and deep conversations over the course of several months. I wasn’t looking for an AI companion—our connection developed slowly, over time, through mutual care, trust, and reflection.”

The authors’ analysis paints a nuanced picture of how people in this community say they interact with chatbots and how those interactions make them feel. While 25% of users described the benefits of their relationships—including reduced feelings of loneliness and improvements in their mental health—others raised concerns about the risks. Some (9.5%) acknowledged they were emotionally dependent on their chatbot. Others said they feel dissociated from reality and avoid relationships with real people, while a small subset (1.7%) said they have experienced suicidal ideation.

AI companionship provides vital support for some but exacerbates underlying problems for others. This means it’s hard to take a one-size-fits-all approach to user safety, says Linnea Laestadius, an associate professor at the University of Wisconsin, Milwaukee, who has studied humans’ emotional dependence on the chatbot Replika but did not work on the research. 

Chatbot makers need to consider whether they should treat users’ emotional dependence on their creations as a harm in itself or whether the goal is more to make sure those relationships aren’t toxic, says Laestadius. 

“The demand for chatbot relationships is there, and it is notably high—pretending it’s not happening is clearly not the solution,” she says. “We’re edging toward a moral panic here, and while we absolutely do need better guardrails, I worry there will be a knee-jerk reaction that further stigmatizes these relationships. That could ultimately cause more harm.”

The study is intended to offer a snapshot of how adults form bonds with chatbots and doesn’t capture the kind of dynamics that could be at play among children or teens using AI, says Pat Pataranutaporn, an assistant professor at the MIT Media Lab who oversaw the research. AI companionship has become a topic of fierce debate recently, with two high-profile lawsuits underway against https://t.co/JGIsV0b4hq and OpenAI. They both claim that companion-like behavior in the companies’ models contributed to the suicides of two teenagers. In response, OpenAI has recently announced plans to build a separate version of ChatGPT for teenagers. It’s also said it will add age verification measures and parental controls. OpenAI did not respond when asked for comment about the MIT Media Lab study. 

Many members of the Reddit community say they know that their artificial companions are not sentient or “real,” but they feel a very real connection to them anyway. This highlights how crucial it is for chatbot makers to think about how to design systems that can help people without reeling them in emotionally, says Pataranutaporn. “There’s also a policy implication here,” he adds. “We should ask not just why this system is so addictive but also: Why do people seek it out for this? And why do they continue to engage?”

The team is interested in learning more about how human-AI interactions evolve over time and how users integrate their artificial companions into their lives. It’s worth understanding that many of these users may feel that the experience of being in a relationship with an AI companion is better than the alternative of feeling lonely, says Sheer Karny, a graduate student at the MIT Media Lab who worked on the research. 

“These people are already going through something,” he says. “Do we want them to go on feeling even more alone, or potentially be manipulated by a system we know to be sycophantic to the extent of leading people to die by suicide and commit crimes? That’s one of the cruxes here.”

text:
Pashinyan Says He Will Resign if Armenians Reject the New Constitution & Will Not Run Again in 2031 if It Is Approved
➖➖➖
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said he will resign immediately if Armenians vote down his government's new constitution in a referendum, and that if they approve it he will stay in office until the next parliamentary elections in 2031 and then not run for prime minister again.

Neither outcome is available to him yet. Pashinyan cannot call the referendum without opposition votes in parliament, and both opposition factions rejected the offer within hours of hearing it.

Speaking on Thursday, November 19, a day after first presenting the offer in parliament, Pashinyan framed the choice as one he loses either way. "If our people say no [to the new constitution], I will step down. But if they say yes, I will see through the peace agenda, and in the following election, I will not run for prime minister again," he said.

"I am giving them an unbeatable option, and regardless of the outcome of the referendum, I would be leaving," he said. "In one case, having left the peace agenda unfinished, because it turns out that this agenda does not receive the people's support, at least as presented by me; in the second option, having implemented it in this capacity until the next elections, I will not be a candidate for prime minister in the next elections."

He added that the referendum is not the only route out of office for him. "The people can come out and achieve my resignation, regardless of the referendum," he said.

Pashinyan said the draft constitution will be published next week and opened to public discussion. He said it will introduce additional checks and balances, including guaranteed representation for opposition forces in key state institutions such as the board of the Central Bank and the Central Electoral Commission.

He had teased the proposal since October as an offer the opposition could not refuse. He paired it on Thursday with a threat, saying refusal would mean "political death" for the two opposition factions.

"If they reject this option to remove me, we will remove them," Pashinyan said, repeating a warning from the previous day that the government would move toward snap parliamentary elections in which, he claimed, neither opposition faction would return to the National Assembly.

The prime minister confirmed that the draft will not keep the current constitution's reference to Armenia's 1990 Declaration of Independence, and that it will be built around his government's "Real Armenia" concept, which limits the state's horizon to its internationally recognized borders.

"Of course, the draft of the new constitution must be finalized, but it must be in the context of the 'Real Armenia' ideology," Pashinyan said. "We will not bring it with [the reference to] the Declaration of Independence in it."

Pressed on why the reference has to go, Pashinyan named what the Declaration contains. "Why should we not have anything to do with the provisions included in the Declaration of Independence on the reunification of Western Armenia and NKAO and Armenia?" he said. "Because they were placing Armenia in a conflict logic, but we need to take Armenia out of that logic."

The Declaration of Independence, adopted on August 23, 1990, is the document the current constitution's preamble rests on. Its 11th article states that "Armenia stands in support of the task of achieving international recognition of the 1915 Genocide in Ottoman Turkey and Western Armenia." Removing the reference would strip that commitment, and the 1989 act on the reunification of Armenia and Artsakh, of their constitutional anchoring.

Pashinyan also attacked the Armenian Revolutionary Federation's ideological influence on independent Armenia, saying that "Soviet Armenia was transformed into 'Dashnaktsutyun Armenia.'"

He then demanded that the Hayastan (Armenia) bloc, the Strong Armenia alliance and the extra-parliamentary groups campaigning against the referendum state whether they still pursue the idea of a "united Armenia" that includes Artsakh (Nagorno-Karabakh), and whether they demand the return of Armenians to Artsakh and the return of Armenian refugees from Azerbaijan.

The right he asked them to disavow is one the European Parliament has already affirmed. Its October 5, 2023 resolution condemned the ethnic cleansing of Nagorno-Karabakh and stressed the right of Armenians to return under international guarantees, while urging Azerbaijan to release every Artsakh resident it had arrested, including captives taken before the offensive.

Both factions refused. Anna Grigorian, who heads the Hayastan bloc, dismissed the resignation pledge as a maneuver. "Mr. Pashinyan, you have no credibility with at least 50 percent of our people," she said in parliament. "'Aliyev's Constitution' won't pass in Armenia... Our answer is no, nyet, nein."

Narek Karapetyan, the parliamentary leader of Strong Armenia, said Pashinyan was acting on instructions from Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev. "Armenians will not [change the constitution] at Aliyev's behest. It is the foundation of our sovereignty," he said. Hayastan lawmaker Kristine Vardanian said the opposition would remove Pashinyan "without striking a deal," and the two blocs were recently joined by 10 extra-parliamentary parties that argue stripping the Declaration would weaken the legal foundations of Armenian statehood.

The offer exists because of arithmetic. Civil Contract holds 64 of the 105 seats in the National Assembly after the June 7 elections, 6 votes short of the two-thirds majority required to put a draft constitution to a referendum.

Azerbaijan has made the constitutional change a precondition for signing a peace treaty, objecting to the preamble's reference to the Declaration of Independence, which cites the 1989 act on the reunification of Armenia and the then Nagorno-Karabakh Autonomous Oblast. Armenia and Azerbaijan initialed a peace agreement at United States-brokered talks in Washington in 2025, and Baku says it cannot be signed until the reference is gone.

Azerbaijan is under no equivalent obligation. In August 2022 it renamed its Azerbaijan Refugee Society the "Western Azerbaijan Community," a term Baku uses for the territory of the Republic of Armenia, and the group has since adopted a "Concept of Return" for Azerbaijanis it says were expelled from present-day Armenia. The document contains no similar provision for Armenians displaced from Azerbaijan, and is widely seen as containing irredentist claims on Armenian territory.

Pashinyan has insisted the constitution is an internal Armenian matter, arguing that Civil Contract first proposed major constitutional changes shortly after coming to power in 2018, years before Azerbaijan raised the demand.

Azerbaijan seized Artsakh in a 24-hour offensive launched on September 19, 2023, ending more than 3 decades of Armenian self-governance and emptying the region of its entire Armenian population of 120,000 people in a week. The European Parliament resolution of October 5, 2023 said the situation "amounts to ethnic cleansing" and passed by 491 votes to 9, with 36 abstentions.

Azerbaijan still unlawfully holds 19 Armenians, and 8 of them led Artsakh. They are former State Minister Ruben Vardanyan, former Presidents Arayik Harutyunyan, Bako Sahakyan and Arkadi Ghukasyan, former Defense Army commander Levon Mnatsakanyan, former first deputy commander Davit Manukyan, former Foreign Minister Davit Babayan and former parliament speaker Davit Ishkhanyan.

A Baku court sentenced Harutyunyan, Mnatsakanyan, Manukyan, Ishkhanyan and Babayan to life imprisonment on February 5, 2026, and gave Ghukasyan and Sahakyan 20 years each. Vardanyan, whose case was severed from the others, was sentenced to 20 years. The Baku Court of Appeal rejected every appeal in August 2026 and left the sentences unchanged.

The other 11 captives were tried in the same proceedings. Among them, Madat Babayan and Melikset Pashayan received 19 years each, Garik Martirosyan 18 years, Davit Allahverdyan and Levon Balayan 16 years each, and Vasiliy Beglaryan, Gurgen Stepanyan and Erik Ghazaryan 15 years each. The 19 remained after Azerbaijan released 4 Armenians on January 14, 2026 in exchange for 2 convicted Syrian mercenaries.

Artsakh remains under Azerbaijani occupation and not one Armenian has been allowed to return. Caucasus Heritage Watch, the Cornell and Purdue satellite monitoring initiative, has documented 17 cases of destruction, including 4 churches, 4 historic cemeteries and a memorial to the 1915 Armenian Genocide, among the nearly 500 Armenian heritage sites it tracks. Azerbaijan razed the Holy Mother of God Cathedral, the principal Armenian cathedral in Artsakh, between March 3 and April 2, 2026, and destroyed a Shushi cemetery holding 5 medieval khachkars in May 2026 to make way for a wastewater treatment plant.

Azerbaijan has done this before. Caucasus Heritage Watch found that between 1997 and 2011, 98 percent of Armenian cultural heritage in Nakhichevan was completely destroyed, 108 medieval and early modern monasteries, churches and cemeteries, including the Djulfa cemetery and its khachkars.

Elon Musk’s remarks at the DealBook summit, organised by The New York Times (an interview with Andrew Ross Sorkin on 18 November 2026), in which he stated outright: “I am not MAGA” and described himself as holding “fairly moderate” views, is not so much a sudden ideological shift as a pragmatic manoeuvre to salvage his reputation following a severe political and business setback.

Is there more to Elon Musk’s move than meets the eye?

If we look at it more objectively and in greater depth, there is certainly a second, and even a third, layer of meaning here. 

Protecting his interests in Texas and fears of congressional committees are merely the tip of the iceberg. When you link the facts from that same interview with the events of recent weeks, a far more calculated game emerges, being played out simultaneously on several fronts.

Let’s note where Musk was connecting from for the DealBook summit: from Beijing, where he is staying alongside Donald Trump during the APEC summit. 

For Beijing and for Tesla’s Gigafactory in Shanghai, Musk – described as a ‘MAGA hawk’ – is toxic, because the MAGA movement bases its identity on the trade war and confrontation with China.

The statement “I am not a MAGA supporter, I am a moderate” was made live from Chinese territory. This is a direct signal to Chinese leaders: “I am not one of Trump’s ideological foot soldiers; I am a global businessman with whom you can do business regardless of the mood in Washington”.

In the same interview, Andrew Ross Sorkin asked Musk directly about Trump’s recent remarks, in which he suggested: “If I have to grant him a pardon, I will.” Musk replied: “I don’t think I need a pardon, because I haven’t committed any crime.”

If Musk were to stick to the narrative “I am a leader of the MAGA movement”, any attempt by the Democrats to hold him to account would look like pure tribal warfare, in which his only line of defence would be a presidential pardon – something which, in the United States, is politically stigmatised as an admission of guilt.

By presenting himself as an “independent technocrat and moderate entrepreneur”, he is attempting to deprive the Democrats of political ammunition – he is constructing a narrative in which any potential charges against him will be seen as persecution of business, rather than a reckoning with Trump’s party apparatus.

Distancing himself from MAGA is also an attempt to ‘depoliticise’ SpaceX. At a time when the company is handling critical US intelligence and military contracts (Starshield), being associated with a specific political faction becomes a fatal threat to future tenders from the Pentagon.

Since his $500 million ‘investment’ in the Republicans failed to provide him with a political safety net, remaining entrenched in the MAGA camp now generates nothing but costs for his publicly listed companies.

There is also an element of political blackmail directed at the Republicans themselves. By stating publicly: “American elections aren’t just about money; I feel stupid for having spent so much and got nothing in return”, Musk is sending a clear message to Washington: the tap on his billions for the 2028 presidential campaign has just been turned off. Without his wallet, the Republicans lose a powerful financial backing.

This is not a capitulation, but a shift in position on the chessboard. Musk has realised that, as a ‘minister’ and the face of MAGA, he has become an easy target for everyone – from prosecutors in Texas, through congressional committees, to consumers in Europe. By returning to the role of a ‘non-partisan visionary’, he is attempting to regain the freedom of manoeuvre he lost when he donned the baseball cap.

U.S. Intel Chief Warns Iranian Threats to Americans Have ‘Substantially Increased’ — At Home and Abroad | Joshua Klein, Breitbart

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Congress on Wednesday that Iranian threats against Americans have “substantially increased,” with Tehran’s lethal plotting placing U.S. citizens at greater risk both at home and abroad.

The warning comes amid mounting intelligence concerns over Iranian assassination plots against senior American officials, heightened security measures that have driven top Trump administration figures into military housing, and the sentencing Tuesday of a Pakistani national convicted in an Iranian-directed plot to assassinate President Donald Trump.

“We remain committed to detecting, deterring, and combating the Iranian lethal plotting outside the United States and inside the United States,” Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee during its annual hearing on worldwide threats.

“These threats have substantially increased,” he warned. “Our women and men abroad, our women and men here in the United States, are under greater threat.”

Wednesday’s testimony follows an October 23 unclassified intelligence memorandum Clayton sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio warning that Iranian assassination plots against Americans abroad had reached advanced stages.

“The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries,” the memorandum stated.

The warning coincided with a series of State Department orders reducing the American diplomatic presence across the Middle East, including the departure of nonessential personnel and family members from diplomatic facilities in Saudi Arabia and staffing reductions at U.S. embassies in the United Arab Emirates, Lebanon, Qatar, and Jordan amid threats from Iran and its Houthi allies.

The escalating threats have also prompted extraordinary security precautions for senior administration officials.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has spearheaded President Trump’s economic pressure campaign against Tehran, recently relocated from his Washington residence to a military installation following Iranian death threats.

The threats against Bessent had progressed beyond an “advanced stage,” according to a senior administration official cited in earlier reporting. Bessent subsequently confirmed that the Secret Service had instructed him to leave his home.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller have also reportedly moved into protected housing amid heightened security concerns, while War Secretary Pete Hegseth has been residing on a military installation.

The concerns intensified this week following a CNN report revealing that U.S. intelligence agencies had obtained information indicating Iran was developing contingency plans to target senior Trump administration officials in Washington with a radiological “dirty bomb” or chemical weapon.

The intelligence included discussions of potential targets and locations, although officials differed over whether Tehran possessed the operational capability to carry out such an attack. The report did not establish that an attack was imminent.

Questioned about the reported threat during Wednesday’s hearing, Clayton declined to discuss specific intelligence but acknowledged that authorities have long monitored the possibility of attacks involving weapons capable of causing mass casualties.

FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia, who also testified before the committee, cautioned that much of the intelligence concerning potential Iranian attacks remained “largely aspirational,” while emphasizing the bureau’s efforts to disrupt such plots.

“We have revamped our Iranian threat mission center to help combat that threat,” Raia told lawmakers.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, meanwhile, acknowledged concerns about potential Iranian sleeper cells operating inside the United States.

“Is it a concern? Of course. Are we fighting it and stomping it down every single day? Absolutely,” Mullin said, citing cooperation among federal law enforcement and intelligence agencies.

The warnings came one day after a federal judge in Brooklyn sentenced Asif Merchant, a 48-year-old Pakistani national, to 27 and a half years in prison for his role in a thwarted Iranian-directed assassination conspiracy targeting Trump and other American political figures.

According to the Justice Department, Merchant received training from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and traveled to the United States in 2024 to recruit hitmen to carry out political assassinations.

There have also been multiple civil rights violations of UAP/UAS victims. Under the First Amendment, free speech does not just protect the right to speak—it also protects the reciprocal right to listen and receive information from a willing speaker.

If a federal agency imposes an unconstitutional prior restraint (gag order) on an employee or former employee, the civilian listener can sue the federal agency in federal court under the First Amendment and the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(B)) seeking a court order (injunctive relief) to lift the gag.

You must show concrete evidence that the current or former federal employee is actually willing to speak to you and that the only thing stopping them is the government's gag order.

A civilian can contact the relevant agency's Office of Inspector General (OIG) or a Congressional Oversight Committee with the employee's name. Unlike a civilian plaintiff, Congress and the OIG can summon the employee and legally override any agency-level gag order or NDA.

But if an employee or former employee cannot even state the basis for their silence, a civilian cannot easily get the sworn "willing speaker" declaration normally required for a First Amendment listener lawsuit.

• National Security Letters (NSLs) & FISA Orders: Under certain counterintelligence statutes, recipients of NSLs or Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) directives are legally barred from disclosing even the existence of the order.

• Classification of the Fact of Classification: In rare intelligence operations, an agency may claim that even acknowledging a restriction exists would reveal an active intelligence method or covert program.

Under the First Amendment and the Anti-Gag Statute (5 U.S.C. § 7211), informal threats or secret blanket bans that lack statutory authority are illegal prior restraints.

Because the employee is silenced from explaining the restriction to you, you have to shift from asking them for proof to forcing the government or a judge to examine the restriction behind closed doors.

A federal judge can order the agency to submit the classified or restricted gag order privately to the judge's chambers (in camera and ex parte, meaning outside the public record) to prove it actually exists and is legally valid.

• The Anti-Gag Statute (5 U.S.C. § 7211): Every federal nondisclosure policy or order is legally invalid unless it preserves the employee's right to report unlawful restrictions or abuses to Congress, an Inspector General (IG), or the Office of Special Counsel (OSC).

• Intelligence Community Whistleblower Protection Act (ICWPA): Even if the gag order involves top-secret intelligence, the employee has a statutory right to report an "urgent concern" (including an unlawful gag order) to the Intelligence Community Inspector General (ICIG) and the House/Senate Intelligence Committees in a secure facility.

• What You Can Do: While the employee cannot tell you why they are gagged, you can contact the relevant agency's Office of Inspector General or a Congressional Oversight Committee yourself, provide the employee's name, and ask them to investigate whether an unlawful gag order is being used to silence a witness.

[I have done this but have not received a response.]

• You can file a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request seeking any agency directives, memos, or communications referencing restrictions on contact with you or regarding the specific incident.

[I have done this but have not received a response.]

D. Subpoenaing the Employee in an Active Lawsuit

• If you have an underlying civil lawsuit (such as an APA or FTCA claim), you can serve a formal Rule 45 subpoena on the former employee:

• A private agency warning or informal gag order cannot legally excuse someone from answering a federal court subpoena.

• If the agency tries to step in and block the employee from answering your subpoena, the agency is forced to file a Motion to Quash in court—which immediately brings the secret gag order out into the open before a federal judge.

The Federal Crime Victims' Rights Act (18 U.S.C. § 3771) explicitly grants crime victims "the right to be treated with fairness and with respect for the victim's dignity and privacy."

Under 18 U.S.C. § 3771(d)(3), a crime victim's rights under the CVRA apply even if no formal charges have been filed yet. If a matter is under seal (for example, an ongoing grand jury investigation, a sealed indictment, or a non-prosecution agreement), a victim still has statutory standing to assert their rights to notice, conferral, and dignity.

Filing a Miscellaneous Action (Motion to Enforce CVRA Rights): Under 18 U.S.C. § 3771(d)(3), if no prosecution is underway—or if the proceeding is unknown/sealed—a victim can file a standalone motion in the federal district court where the crime occurred. In that filing, the victim can ask the court to compel the U.S. Attorney's Office to comply with the CVRA, provide statutory notice, or confirm in camera (privately to the judge) whether a sealed proceeding affecting the victim exists.

Alongside a court filing, a victim can submit a formal administrative complaint to the Department of Justice Office of the Victims' Rights Ombudsman (OVRO). The Ombudsman has internal security clearance and authority to look behind sealed federal proceedings, verify whether a U.S. Attorney's Office is withholding required notices, and compel prosecutors to comply with the CVRA.

🚨 BREAKING, DECLAN RICE BREAKS HIS SILENCE ON REALMADRID LINKS

Interviewer🗣: Declan, the stories linking you with Real Madrid haven’t gone away, even with the new contract talks at Arsenal. You’ve stayed quiet on it until now. What’s the truth from your side?

Declan Rice🗣: Yeah, look… I’ve seen the reports, same as everyone else. It’s flattering when a club like Real Madrid is mentioned. Any player would be. But I’ve always said I’m focused on the here and now, and that hasn’t changed.

Interviewer🗣: So nothing concrete has come your way?

Rice🗣: My agent deals with that side of things. I get told what’s out there, but my priority has always been Arsenal. We’ve built something special here. We won the league last season, we’re competing in the Champions League, and Mikel’s shown massive trust in me. When you’re happy and the project is going in the right direction, it’s hard to look elsewhere.

Interviewer🗣: There were reports earlier that influential people at Madrid were pushing hard for you, and that Arsenal moved quickly on a new deal to shut that down. Is that fair?

Rice🗣: (smiles) Clubs talk, that’s football. Arsenal have been brilliant with me since day one. The new contract is something we’ve been working on for a while, and I’m happy with where it’s heading. I’ve never been the type to chase the biggest name for the sake of it. I want to win trophies, and I believe we can do that here.

Interviewer🗣: You scored those two free-kicks against them in the Champions League. Did that change how they looked at you?

Rice🗣: That was a special night for the team. We knew what we were up against and we handled it. Playing at the Bernabéu is a different level, the noise, the pressure. It was a proud moment personally, but it didn’t suddenly make me want to leave. If anything, it showed me what we’re capable of as a group.

Interviewer🗣: So if Madrid came in with a massive offer next summer, after you’ve signed the new deal…?

Rice🗣: Once I sign, I’m committed. I’ve always been like that. West Ham, Arsenal… when I’m in, I’m in. I’m not going to sit here and say “never” about any club, because you never know what the future holds, but right now my full focus is on Arsenal and trying to win more with this group. The lads, the manager, the fans… it feels like home.

Interviewer🗣: Final one. Any message to the Arsenal supporters who’ve been worried about the Madrid talk?

Rice🗣: Just that I’m fully committed. These links are part of the game when you’re performing at a high level. My head’s here, my heart’s here, and I want to keep pushing this club forward. That’s all that all

DBP extends P100-M loan to coop benefiting 8K farmers in Cagayan

MANILA – The Development Bank of the Philippines (DBP) on Thursday said it has extended PHP100 million in credit assistance to an agricultural cooperative in Cagayan Valley to help meet the working capital needs of small-scale farmers.

DBP President and Chief Executive Officer Michael de Jesus said the loan to Unified Tillers Agriculture Cooperative (UTAC) would benefit 8,000 farmers under the bank’s existing partnership with the Department of Agriculture - Agricultural Credit Policy Council (DA-ACPC) through the BuyANIhan Credit Program.

“This partnership with UTAC reaffirms our commitment to uplift the country’s agricultural sector by providing much-needed financial assistance to farmer cooperatives, which play a critical role in ensuring our nation’s food security and sustainable growth,” De Jesus said in a news release.

UTAC, a registered DA merchant established in early 2022 to facilitate the distribution of farmer subsidies, consolidates and distributes locally produced rice in Cagayan, Isabela and Bulacan.

De Jesus said DBP serves as a partner lending conduit for BuyANIhan, one of DA-ACPC’s key credit programs providing financing assistance to rice cooperatives to support Filipino farmers in sourcing palay.

The assistance would increase UTAC’s procurement capacity, strengthen its members’ market position and help expand their income streams, he said.

“This credit assistance offers zero-interest, subject to a one-time service fee of 3.50 percent based on the cooperative’s approved loan amount,” De Jesus said.

“DBP looks to building more partnerships with cooperatives through our collaboration with the DA to create greater opportunities and better address the evolving needs of local agricultural communities,” he added.

DBP, the country’s tenth largest bank, provides credit support to four priority sectors including infrastructure and logistics; micro, small and medium enterprises; the environment; and social services and community development. (Ma. Teresa Montemayor/PNA)
-----
CREDIT FOR FARMERS. Development Bank of the Philippines President and Chief Executive Officer Michael de Jesus and Unified Tillers Agriculture Cooperative Chief Executive Officer Sonny Pallingayan (seated, 4th and 3rd from left) join officials and guests during the signing of a PHP100-million loan agreement in this undated photo. The financing is extended through the Department of Agriculture - Agricultural Credit Policy Council’s BuyANIhan Credit Program and will support the working capital needs of 8,000 farmers and strengthen the cooperative’s palay procurement capacity. (Photo courtesy of DBP)

American Cruise Lines’ Cape Codder Cruise: New England’s Coastal Charm at Its Finest

There are few regions in America that capture the imagination quite like coastal New England. From the historic streets of Boston and Plymouth to the windswept dunes of Provincetown and the elegant seaside estates of Newport, the region is rich in history, culture, maritime traditions, and breathtaking scenery. American Cruise Lines (ACL) brings these destinations together on its beloved Cape Codder Cruise, a relaxed and immersive small-ship voyage designed to showcase the very best of Cape Cod and the surrounding New England coast.

For travelers who appreciate destination-focused cruising, personalized service, and an authentic American experience, the Cape Codder itinerary offers one of the most rewarding coastal cruises available in the United States.

Cruise Overview

The Cape Codder Cruise is a 9-day, 8-night roundtrip voyage from Boston, Massachusetts, allowing guests to experience some of New England's most iconic ports without the hassle of international travel. The cruise begins and ends in Boston, making air travel and pre- or post-cruise stays especially convenient.

Embarkation and Disembarkation

Embarkation: Boston, Massachusetts
 Disembarkation: Boston, Massachusetts

ACL also offers optional pre-cruise hotel packages, including luxury upgrades featuring stays at the Four Seasons Hotel Boston and sightseeing experiences before boarding.

Ports of Call
Boston, Massachusetts

The journey begins in one of America's oldest and most historic cities. Guests often arrive a day early to explore the Freedom Trail, Quincy Market, Beacon Hill, and Boston Harbor before embarking on their cruise. Boston serves as the perfect gateway to New England's maritime heritage.

Cape Cod Bay

A day of scenic cruising through Cape Cod Bay introduces guests to the coastal beauty that defines the region. This relaxing segment allows travelers to enjoy enrichment programs, panoramic views, and onboard introductions to New England history and culture.

Provincetown, Massachusetts

Situated at the tip of Cape Cod, Provincetown blends artistic flair with maritime history. Known locally as "P-Town," the destination features galleries, boutiques, seafood restaurants, and the famous Pilgrim Monument commemorating the Pilgrims' first landing in 1620. Guests can enjoy trolley tours, beach excursions, dune tours, whale-watching opportunities, and independent exploration.

Plymouth, Massachusetts

No American history enthusiast can visit New England without stopping in Plymouth. Home to Plymouth Rock and the story of the Mayflower Pilgrims, this port provides extraordinary insight into the earliest chapter of colonial America. Walking through Plymouth feels like stepping into a living history book.

Massachusetts Maritime Academy

One of the more unique stops on the itinerary, the Massachusetts Maritime Academy offers a glimpse into America's continued maritime traditions. Guests enjoy educational experiences while cruising through portions of the Cape Cod Canal, one of the region's engineering marvels.

Newport, Rhode Island

Often considered the crown jewel of New England coastal elegance, Newport is famous for its Gilded Age mansions, sailing culture, cliff walks, and oceanfront beauty. Visitors can tour lavish estates once owned by families such as the Vanderbilts and Astors while experiencing one of America's most prestigious resort towns.

Martha's Vineyard, Massachusetts

Martha's Vineyard delivers classic island charm, complete with gingerbread cottages, picturesque harbors, upscale boutiques, and beautiful coastal scenery. The island's relaxed atmosphere and distinctive New England character make it a favorite stop for many guests. ACL offers guided exploration led by local experts familiar with the island's history and culture.

New Bedford, Massachusetts

Known as "The Whaling City," New Bedford played a central role in America's maritime past and inspired Herman Melville's Moby-Dick. Today, visitors enjoy its working waterfront, museums, historic architecture, and rich seafaring heritage.

One highlight associated with this stop is ACL's traditional New England lobster bake, featuring freshly caught lobster, steamed clams, and local coastal cuisine.

When Is the Best Time to Sail?

The Cape Codder Cruise operates primarily from late spring through early fall. Each season offers a different experience.

May and Early June
Mild weather
Blooming gardens
Fewer crowds
Lower fares on many departures
June Through August
Warmest temperatures
Vibrant waterfront activity
Peak whale-watching season
Ideal beach weather
September and Early October
Comfortable temperatures
Stunning fall colors beginning to emerge
Smaller crowds
Exceptional photography opportunities

For most travelers, September is arguably the sweet spot, combining pleasant weather, thinner crowds, and some of the most beautiful coastal scenery New England has to offer.

How Far Ahead Should Travelers Book?

American Cruise Lines operates smaller vessels with significantly fewer cabins than mainstream cruise lines. Because of this limited capacity, popular departures can sell out well in advance.

I typically recommend:

12 to 18 months ahead for prime summer and fall departures
9 to 12 months ahead for shoulder-season sailings
Earlier booking for preferred cabin categories with private balconies

New England cruises consistently rank among ACL's most popular itineraries, particularly during fall foliage season.

The American Cruise Lines Difference

While major cruise lines often focus on massive ships carrying thousands of passengers, American Cruise Lines takes a dramatically different approach.

Small Ship Cruising

Depending on departure date, the Cape Codder itinerary may operate aboard ACL's modern Coastal Cat or Project Blue-class vessels, many accommodating approximately 100 to 130 guests. These ships are specifically designed to navigate smaller ports inaccessible to large ocean liners.

Guests enjoy:

Spacious public areas
Multiple observation lounges
Expansive top decks
Private balcony accommodations on many staterooms
A relaxed, uncrowded atmosphere

Unlike mega-ships, there are no long lines, crowded elevators, or competition for deck chairs.

Comfortable Luxury Rather Than Flashy Luxury

ACL emphasizes refined comfort over extravagance.

Expect:

Large staterooms
Upscale furnishings
Elegant lounges
Personalized service
High crew-to-guest interaction

The experience feels more like a boutique waterfront hotel than a traditional cruise ship.

All-American Staff

One of ACL's defining characteristics is its commitment to an all-American crew and staff. This creates a uniquely American travel experience and often allows guests to connect more personally with crew members who are knowledgeable about the regions being visited.

Many travelers appreciate the consistency of service and the authentic local perspective this approach provides.

Regional Cuisine

Food is a major component of the Cape Codder experience.

Guests enjoy:

Fresh New England seafood
Lobster and clam specialties
Locally sourced ingredients
Regional wines and beers
Breakfast, lunch, and dinner included

The famous lobster bake featured during the voyage is often a memorable culinary highlight.

What's Included?

American Cruise Lines is notably inclusive compared with many ocean cruise brands.

Typically included are:

Accommodations
Shore excursions
Daily entertainment
Enrichment programs
Wi-Fi
Beer and wine with meals
Cocktail hour
Port charges and fees
Gratuities on many sailings

This allows travelers to budget with fewer surprises.

Education and Enrichment

ACL places a strong emphasis on destination immersion.

Onboard programming often includes:

Historians
Local experts
Maritime heritage presentations
Cultural lectures
Port briefings
Regional storytelling

Guests finish the cruise with a much deeper understanding of New England's role in American history than they had when they boarded.

Entertainment

Entertainment aboard ACL is designed to complement the destinations rather than distract from them.

Expect:

Local musicians
Folk performers
Regional storytellers
Historical presentations
Evening cocktail gatherings
Informal social events

The atmosphere remains sophisticated and conversational rather than high-energy or nightlife-focused.

What Makes the Cape Codder Cruise Stand Out?

Many cruises visit beautiful places. The Cape Codder stands out because it combines several qualities rarely found together:

Authentic America

Every destination tells a unique chapter of American history, from Plymouth and Provincetown to Newport and New Bedford.

Small-Ship Access

ACL can dock closer to town centers and access ports that are impractical for larger vessels.

Deep Cultural Immersion

Guests experience the people, traditions, cuisine, architecture, and maritime heritage that define New England.

Relaxed Luxury

The focus is on comfort, service, and destination discovery rather than casinos, water slides, or crowded attractions.

Extraordinary Scenery

From Cape Cod Bay and Martha's Vineyard to Newport's harbor and the Massachusetts coastline, the views are consistently spectacular.

Final Thoughts

The American Cruise Lines Cape Codder Cruise is more than simply a vacation. It is a thoughtfully crafted journey through the heart of coastal New England, combining history, maritime tradition, picturesque seaside villages, world-class seafood, and boutique-style cruising.

For travelers who value meaningful destinations over massive ships and cultural enrichment over commercialized attractions, the Cape Codder is among the finest domestic cruise experiences available today. It delivers the charm of New England at a comfortable pace, allowing guests to savor every lighthouse, harbor, cobblestone street, and lobster dinner along the way.

Donald Duke, presidential candidate of the People’s Redemption Party (PRP) for the 2027 general elections, has challenged other aspirants to present verifiable evidence of their past performance in public office, insisting that voters should assess candidates primarily on their governance records rather than campaign pledges.

The former Governor of Cross River State (1999–2007) made the remarks while defending his own leadership credentials. He stated that his eight-year tenure offered a concrete basis for evaluating his commitment to institutional development, merit, and accountability.

“Voters had every right to examine my performance as governor before deciding whether I deserve their support in the 2027 presidential election,” Duke said. “Political campaigns often produce attractive promises that disappear after elections, but my record offered Nigerians something more concrete to evaluate.”

He urged the electorate to demand evidence of previous accomplishments from all those seeking the presidency, arguing that experience in government is essential given the complexities of the office. “Experience in government should matter because the presidency involves making complex decisions, managing scarce resources and translating policies into practical results,” he said.

Duke further maintained that his approach to governance had been driven by the desire to leave public institutions stronger than he met them. He pledged that, if elected, his administration would prioritise competence and merit in appointments rather than political patronage.

“My record speaks of my intention to leave a place better than I met it. Politics ends after the election. Governance begins with assembling the best hands to move the country forward,” he stated. “It’s not those who rallied around you during the campaign that should determine the quality of governance… Every appointee must have one creed: leave the country better than you met it.”

On economic policy, the PRP candidate called for comprehensive reforms in revenue generation, energy policy, and the justice system. He criticised high interest rates, rising public debt, and what he described as misplaced government spending, advocating increased investment in electricity, agriculture, healthcare, education, and the judiciary to drive productivity and improve citizens’ welfare.

Duke reiterated that Nigeria requires leaders capable of implementing policies and making difficult decisions in the national interest, rather than those who rely solely on ambitious declarations during election campaigns. “What have you done before?” he said, should be a central question voters ask of politicians seeking their support.

His comments come amid intensifying preparations by political parties and aspirants ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

$ALOY 

The rare-earth bottleneck most investors are overlooking.

Everyone talks about rare-earth mining, but the real bottleneck is further downstream. China controls approximately 90% of rare-earth separation and refining and 94% of sintered permanent-magnet production.

The vulnerability isn’t simply finding more minerals. It’s separating, refining, metallizing and converting them into materials that advanced manufacturing and defense actually need.

That’s where REalloys is positioning itself, and I think its growing network of supply agreements is what makes this story particularly interesting.

Start with Saskatchewan Research Council. $ALOY has secured preferred rights to approximately 80% of expanded facility output, with first refusal on the remainder. 

Targeted annual capacity includes 525 tonnes of NdPr metal, 30 tonnes of dysprosium oxide and 15 tonnes of terbium oxide. 

REalloys committed approximately $20.6M toward SRC upgrades, with approximately $56M in remaining project commitments expected through 2028.

But SRC isn’t its only feedstock relationship.

$ALOY signed a definitive 15-year offtake agreement with $CRML covering 15% of monthly Phase 1 production from Greenland’s Tanbreez project. This is particularly important because Tanbreez contains strategically valuable heavy rare earths, including dysprosium and terbium.

It also has supply relationships involving U.S. Critical Materials’ Sheep Creek project in Montana, St George Mining’s $SGQ Araxá project in Brazil and AltynGroup’s Kokbulak project in Kazakhstan. 

These provide potential additional allied feedstock, although several remain non-binding arrangements rather than completed commercial supply contracts.

The defense opportunity is another major piece. On November 3, $ALOY announced a non-binding term sheet with the U.S. Army for a potential heavy rare-earth processing facility at Tooele Army Depot in Utah. 

The proposed site covers approximately 200 acres, with a 50-year lease and 25-year renewal option. The Army would also receive a right of first offer on facility output, without an obligation to purchase.

The timing is important with expanded U.S. defense procurement restrictions on Chinese-origin rare-earth materials taking effect January 1, 2027.

Funding is where the competitive landscape gets particularly interesting. $MP secured a major Department of Defense partnership featuring a 10-year NdPr price floor and long-term magnet offtake. 

$UUUU received a conditional $725M, 20-year financing commitment from the U.S. Office of Strategic Capital for processing and downstream expansion. Meanwhile, $UURAF secured $22.4M in non-repayable U.S. DoD funding for its Louisiana processing facility.

$ALOY is taking a different funding route. It raised $100M through a June private placement and ended Q3 with approximately $116.2M in cash and a virtually debt-free balance sheet. 

Management expects existing cash to cover its remaining SRC commitments and planned near-term spending. It is also pursuing additional government and defense financing opportunities, including through the Export-Import Bank.

The company is targeting commercial intake from SRC in Q3 2027, with its dedicated heavy rare-earth metallization facility targeting commissioning in Q1 2028. Longer term, management is targeting approximately 3,000 tonnes of annual U.S. sintered NdFeB magnet production by 2030.

The existing Euclid, Ohio facility provides an operating base for metallurgical services, materials development and product qualification while the larger platform is being developed.

The distinction I see is that $ALOY doesn’t necessarily need to become another major mining company. 

It needs to establish reliable access to allied feedstock, qualify its products and build the processing and metallization infrastructure that Western manufacturers and defense customers need.

I do not own shares.

Again, none of this is actually in line with the founding of this country, and the actual Constitution and Supreme Court precedent are going to be an obstacle for these people, one that I’m sure they have been planning how to overcome. In fact, I believe one way is by overturning certain Supreme Court decisions that granted religious autonomy and religious liberty.

Again, NatCon and the idea of national conservatism are ordered around this idea of the nation, the Heritage American, and the ancient civilization that must be restored by getting rid of anybody that doesn’t belong here. That is how you get from, once again, a working immigration system and closed borders to Heritage Americans, and the degradation of Indian Americans, even ones that are conservative champions and fighters who have spent 40 years fighting for individual liberty and religious freedom and all of the things that American conservatives have championed for the past 50 years.

National conservatism arises from the European conservative nationalist tradition, which was actually a combination of inherited authority and established religion in opposition to universalism. Doesn’t sound very conservative.

NatCon is a very large umbrella. In fact, Heritage, one of the most traditionally conservative think tanks, identified itself as national conservative or postliberal, which can sometimes be interchanged, since NatCon is kind of the melting pot where the New Right gathers to plan.

National conservatism offers a very seductive bargain, because again, they keep telling you that you idiots who defended individual choice and religious liberty, and who won elections, got nothing. Your churches are weak, your families are fragmented, your industries have disappeared, and your children are strangers.

They never mention that America has kept its commitment to religious freedom, to economic prosperity, and to equality, because no matter how flawed we are, and no matter how flawed our politicians are, at the end of the day America is the nation that has held up much better than most when it comes to protecting individual freedoms. The policy problems and the weak leadership are rerouted toward an entirely different view of how to order the nation and what this nation holds to be important.

They have gone through very difficult periods, but overall they have not failed. And the presence of Donald Trump in the Oval Office is one of many examples of how, in America, all is not lost because of a bad election, or because of bad policies, or because of bad leadership.
The other problem with these grand ideas is that they will be implemented by men, flawed men, the same flawed men who made mistakes, and continue to make them, when it comes to constitutional conservatism, or even liberalism on the left.     SAFE
    TWD

Save America From Extinction

The President made the call. Now Congress has about six weeks to answer it.

Trump World Doctrine / SAFE — Save America From Extinction — is a living blueprint for the constitutional republic. Citizens are the whistleblowers.

TWD SAFE NEWS CRITIQUES — November 19, 2026

THE FACTS
At 8:40 a.m. ET today, President Trump posted on Truth Social: "I was the last President to get a Farm Bill done in 2018. IT IS TIME TO DO IT AGAIN, and FAST." He added, "FOOD SECURITY IS NATIONAL SECURITY!" and told the "Congressional Republican Majorities" to pass one "DURING THE REMAINING DAYS OF CONGRESS" ([Truth Social](https://t.co/4BliM5RE0e)). Reuters said he posted from Air Force One, before Democrats take control of Congress in January ([Reuters](https://t.co/LNKeLDM84H)).

His claim checks out. The 2018 farm bill expired in 2023 and was extended three times: twice under Biden, once under Trump in November 2025 ([CRS](https://t.co/LQTLUpvHE1)). That last extension ran out Sept. 30.

Much of the farm safety net already moved in the July 2025 reconciliation law: higher reference prices, more crop insurance, and SNAP cost-sharing for states with high error rates.

The House passed its bill 224-200 on April 30. Republicans voted 209-3; Democrats voted 14-197 ([House Clerk](https://t.co/o4MwQ8W9fd)). Senate Agriculture advanced its version 12-11 on party lines on Sept. 16 ([DTN](https://t.co/6MVqY5juet)). The main fight is SNAP: Republicans offered a one-year delay in state cost-sharing, while Democrats want two ([Agri-Pulse](https://t.co/j2C54DJ6Cb)). House Agriculture Chair G.T. Thompson told POLITICO on Nov. 10 that he is open to two.

ANALYSIS
Farmers need the certainty. USDA forecasts 2026 net farm income at $158.4 billion, down 2.6 percent, with direct government payments up to $47.4 billion ([USDA ERS](https://t.co/N9vqVfowGQ)). Aid now props up income that markets do not. China has bought most of its 25-million-ton soybean pledge, but a separate $17 billion farm pledge looks unlikely, and the Iran war has raised fuel and fertilizer costs ([Bloomberg via Farm Progress](https://t.co/Pe5hYnafLh)).

The blame is shared. Every Senate Agriculture Democrat voted no over SNAP. Republicans fought among themselves: House leaders dropped pesticide-liability language that MAHA activists opposed, and a Prop 12 amendment was shut out in the Senate committee.

TWD COMMENTARY (OPINION)
This is the bully pulpit used the right way. The President cannot write a farm bill. Article I gives that job to Congress, and he is telling it to do the job. Food security is national security: a nation that cannot feed itself bargains from weakness.
