text:
$UGI Q4 2026 earnings: UGI will split in two while its propane profit shrinks

UGI, which runs gas utilities and sells propane, will split in two after its utilities thrived and propane profit fell. The board backed a plan to spin off the propane and European bottled-gas arms next year. Profit per share excluding one-offs came to $3.00, above the company's own lowered plan but about 10% below last year.

• Profit per share, excluding one-offs: $𝟑.𝟎𝟎 ($3.32 a year ago (−10%))
• Profit before interest and tax, four business units: $𝟏,𝟏𝟗𝟖𝐌 (+1.9% from a year ago)
• Net debt to yearly cash profit: 𝟑.𝟖𝐱 (3.9x a year ago)
• Next year's outlook, profit per share excluding one-offs: $𝟐.𝟗𝟎–𝟑.𝟐𝟎 (middle of the range: +1.7% on this year)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse, because next year's plan leaves profit per share about where it stood three years earlier. That makes the yearly growth UGI promised through 2029 much harder to reach. In its favour, both states approved higher gas rates, and its debt ratio dropped.

The question now is whether the gas company left after the split can outgrow its rate increases. Either data center demand fills new pipelines, or growth stays at the pace regulators set. Signed contracts and the Auburn pipeline, due to start in the second half of fiscal 2027, will tell.

[Model: Claude Opus 5.5. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐁𝐨𝐭𝐡 𝐆𝐚𝐬 𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐈𝐧𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐖𝐨𝐧 𝐀𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐚𝐥
UGI Utilities, the group's regulated gas network in Pennsylvania and West Virginia, earns more when regulators let it raise rates to pay for new pipe. Its profit before interest and tax rose 13% this year, to $456 million. The company credited a higher Pennsylvania base rate, a West Virginia charge for replacing old pipe and colder weather.

After year-end, both states settled the next rate reviews. Pennsylvania regulators approved a $65 million increase in two steps, starting with $40 million in October. West Virginia granted Mountaineer Gas, the group's utility there, $17 million from December. UGI also finished replacing its cast-iron mains 'nearly a year ahead of our February 2027 commitment'.

This matters because the utilities stay with UGI after the split, so their rate increases carry most of next year's growth. But weather helped too: the gas territory ran 9% colder than normal, and next year's plan assumes normal weather.

What to watch: utility profit in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, set against a year-ago quarter far colder than normal. A gain in a milder winter would show the rate increases doing the work.

🟢 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨 𝐅𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐨 𝟑.𝟖 𝐓𝐢𝐦𝐞𝐬 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭
Net leverage, UGI's net debt divided by a year of cash profit before one-offs, stood at 3.8 times in September. By our math it was 3.9 times a year earlier, because net debt dropped $66 million while cash profit rose. This matters because the split needs two balance sheets that can stand alone.

Rating agencies affirmed or upgraded every unit, and UGI said the AmeriGas balance sheet is 'at its strongest in 10 years'. But the repair leaned on asset sales and a $300 million equity injection into AmeriGas in May, which reversed a 2024 promise of no more equity.

What to watch: the ratio after the $470 million electric utility sale closes, which UGI expected in early 2027. A reading at or below the 3.75 times plan would show the sale money reaching debt.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐆𝐚𝐬 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐅𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝟏𝟕% 𝐚𝐬 𝐂𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐋𝐞𝐟𝐭
AmeriGas, UGI's US propane delivery business, is two years into a turnaround. Chief executive Robert Flexon said 'the hard work of transforming the business continues', and the slides say the unit 'achieved our lowest gross attrition in 5 years', meaning it lost the fewest customers before counting new ones.

The yearly results point the other way. AmeriGas sold 5% fewer gallons, and UGI blamed lost customers, the Hawaii sale and a warm West. Excluding Hawaii and adjusting for weather, volume still fell 3%, the company said.

• Profit before interest and tax: $137 million, down 17%
• Operating and administrative costs: 45% of revenue, up 4.4 percentage points
• Free cash flow: $39 million, against $209 million a year earlier
• Margin per gallon: up about 3%, by our math

This matters because a higher margin on each gallon no longer covers the lost volume, while marketing and pay costs rose. Flexon said last quarter that AmeriGas would resume cash payments to UGI in fiscal 2027, but the year-end release and slides do not repeat that.

What to watch: AmeriGas gallons after weather adjustment in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, the first winter after the turnaround work. Another drop would show the turnaround has not yet stopped customers leaving.

🔴🔴 𝐍𝐞𝐱𝐭 𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫'𝐬 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧 𝐁𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭𝐬 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞
Last year UGI set a goal of 5–7% yearly growth in profit per share, excluding one-offs, through fiscal 2029. It measured that from a starting point of $3.06 a share. Finance chief Sean O'Brien told investors last quarter that the goal still stood.

The new outlook of $2.90 to $3.20 a share puts next year at about $3.05 at the middle. That leaves profit per share where it stood three years earlier. By our math, UGI would then need yearly growth of 13% to 19% over the last two years to reach the goal.

The year-end release and slides do not mention the five-year goal. Instead, UGI gives the gas company left after the split a target of 6–8% yearly growth in profit per share. The propane company gets only 'Competitive earnings growth', with no number. This matters because the split replaces the group goal before UGI has met it.

What to watch: whether UGI restates the five-year goal in the registration document it must file with the US securities regulator for the split. Keeping the goal would need growth well above fiscal 2025's 8.5%, the best year in these results.

🔴 𝐏𝐢𝐩𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐅𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐖𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐞 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐂𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐚𝐥𝐤𝐬 𝐆𝐫𝐞𝐰
Midstream & Marketing, UGI's pipeline, storage and gas-trading arm, is the growth bet for the gas company after the split. The slides list '100+ NDAs signed', meaning confidentiality agreements with data center developers. Supporters expect long contracts to follow.

Profit has not followed yet. The unit's profit before interest and tax fell 3% to $285 million, because new renewable gas plants and the Carlisle gas storage site added costs, UGI said. Capital spending at the unit halved, so new pipe will add little next year.

What to watch: a signed data center or power plant contract with a size and start date, and the Auburn pipeline, which UGI is targeting for 'a service date in the second half of FY27'. Without such contracts, growth at the gas company rests on rate increases alone.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Four standing concerns got only partial readings from the year-end release and slides. Each item below names the reading that UGI has not yet given and that would settle the question.

• European volumes: UGI International, the European bottled and tank gas arm, sold 10% fewer gallons, mostly after selling country businesses. Without the stronger euro its profit fell about 6% by our math, though Finland volumes rose 65%. A volume figure excluding the sales would settle it.
• Weather: colder weather helped the utilities this year, and next year's plan assumes normal weather. First-quarter volumes will show how much that costs.
• Pennsylvania politics: regulators approved the rate deal unchanged, but neither the release nor the slides mention the state regulator's complaint over the West Reading explosion. A penalty figure would move this item.
• Convertible notes: UGI said holders of $700 million of notes due 2028 may ask to convert until December 31, and none has done so. Conversions would add shares.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐔𝐆𝐈 𝐖𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐒𝐩𝐢𝐧 𝐎𝐟𝐟 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐞 𝐁𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐬
UGI's board backed a plan to spin off AmeriGas and UGI International as Global LPG, which UGI calls the 'largest publicly traded LPG distributor when launched'. LPG is liquefied petroleum gas, mainly propane. Shareholders would keep their UGI shares and receive the new ones, and UGI may keep up to 19.9%. The group targets 'completion in the second half of calendar 2027'.

𝐀 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐫 𝐄𝐮𝐫𝐨 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐮𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐚𝐧 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐮𝐥𝐭𝐬
The euro averaged $1.16 this year against $1.11 a year earlier, so UGI's European sales were worth more in dollars. Currency translation added $56 million to margin at UGI International, the European bottled-gas arm, the company said. It also lifted costs there by $30 million, and losses on currency hedges took back $14 million.

𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐆𝐚𝐬 𝐒𝐢𝐠𝐧𝐬 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐅𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐂𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬
AmeriGas has begun selling propane to builders of data centers, with 'new data center construction accounts beginning this winter' worth about 5 million gallons a year. It also won a national customer with about 200 cylinder exchange sites and started running delivery trucks on its own propane. These deals do not show in revenue yet.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞 (𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔): $𝟒𝟒𝟐 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Interest cost kept climbing, to $442 million for the year, up 7.5% from a year ago. The quarterly increase slowed through the year, to about 5% in the fourth quarter. Slides presented by finance chief Sean O'Brien show higher interest took $0.12 off profit per share. The outlook assumes interest costs fall next year.

𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 (𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔): 𝐀𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 $𝟗𝟎𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
UGI invested about $900 million this year, and 77% went to the gas utilities and pipelines. By our math, spending by the four units equalled 12% of revenue. Utility spending rose 10%, and AmeriGas raised its own by 43%. Next year's plan is higher still.

𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 (𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔): 𝟐𝟐𝟏.𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
The diluted share count, which adds shares that convertible notes and stock awards could create, rose 1.2% to 221.9 million. Basic shares barely moved, at 214.8 million. UGI repurchased only about 0.6 million shares in the first nine months, putting cash into debt reduction instead.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞, 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧𝐞-𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐬: $𝟐.𝟗𝟎–𝟑.𝟐𝟎  ⇄ reversing
New. The plan puts profit per share, excluding one-offs, at about $3.05 at the middle of the range, 2% above this year. Against this year's result without the one-time tax benefit, the gain is about 5% by our math. UGI assumes normal weather, rate increases in both states, growth at AmeriGas and lower interest cost. Its first outlook for this year was cut in May.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠: $𝟏.𝟎–𝟏.𝟐 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
New. UGI plans to spend more next year than the roughly $900 million it invested this year. By our math, the middle of the range sits about 22% higher. This year the group spent below its own range, mostly because Midstream & Marketing cut back.

𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐥𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞, 𝐔𝐆𝐈 𝐂𝐨𝐫𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧, 𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐨𝐟 𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕: ≤𝟑.𝟕𝟓𝐱  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from ≤3.75x long-term target, with ≤4x for fiscal 2026
Unchanged. UGI still aims to keep net debt at or below 3.75 times a year of cash profit. The ratio moved between 3.7 and 4.0 times during this year. UGI plans to use money from the electric utility sale to cut debt. Its debt agreement measures leverage differently and showed 4.1 times.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐞𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐚𝐱 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞: 𝟐𝟎–𝟐𝟐%  ⇗ accelerating
New. UGI expects its tax rate to climb to 20–22% next year, from about 15% this year by our math. This year's rate included about $0.10 a share of extra tax benefits from renewable gas plants, so the higher rate weighs on next year's profit.

𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐛𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫, 𝐠𝐚𝐬 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐚𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐭: 𝟖–𝟏𝟎%  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from 9%+ a year, fiscal 2026–29
Unchanged. The gas company targets 8–10% yearly growth in its rate base, the value of pipes and plant on which regulators let it earn a return. The earlier plan said more than 9% through fiscal 2029, so the middle holds. UGI plans more than $5 billion of spending over the next five years to support it.

𝐅𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞𝐭, 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐚𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐭: $𝟐𝟓𝟎–𝟑𝟎𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫 (𝐧𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐦)  ⇒ stable
New. The propane and European gas company targets $250–300 million of free cash flow a year in the near term. By our math, its two units produced $266 million this year, inside the range. Most of that came from Europe, so the target needs AmeriGas to deliver more cash.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐈𝐬 𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐆𝐚𝐬'𝐬 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨 𝐍𝐨𝐰?
Finance chief Sean O'Brien said last quarter that AmeriGas had a shot at getting below four times debt to cash profit by September. The slides praise its balance sheet but give no ratio, and that number decides when cash flows to UGI.

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐖𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐆𝐚𝐬 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭 𝐏𝐚𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐭𝐨 𝐔𝐆𝐈?
Chief executive Robert Flexon said last quarter that AmeriGas would resume cash payments to the parent in fiscal 2027. AmeriGas free cash flow fell sharply this year, so investors need the size and the rule for those payments.

𝐃𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐅𝐢𝐯𝐞-𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐆𝐨𝐚𝐥 𝐒𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐝?
UGI promised 5–7% yearly growth in profit per share through fiscal 2029, and next year's plan leaves it level with fiscal 2024. The company should say whether the goal survives the split or gives way to the gas company's 6–8% target.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐌𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐃𝐨 𝐄𝐮𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐚𝐧 𝐕𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐬 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰 𝐖𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬?
UGI International sold 10% fewer gallons, mostly because it sold businesses in seven countries. UGI has not given a like-for-like volume figure, which would show whether customers switching from heating oil offset falling demand elsewhere.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐏𝐞𝐧𝐚𝐥𝐭𝐲 𝐂𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐖𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐭 𝐁𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠?
Pennsylvania's utility regulator filed a complaint in March over the West Reading explosion and seeks civil penalties. The year-end materials do not mention it, even though the same regulator just approved the gas rate increase.

text:
India’s energy math  why the country needs Amazon’s investment.

India’s energy challenge is among the most consequential on earth.

The demand: India is the world’s most populous country (1.4+ billion people) with a rapidly growing economy. Electricity demand is rising faster than in any other major country  driven by industrialization, urbanization, rising living standards, and the explosive growth of the digital economy.

The current mix: India generates approximately 70% of its electricity from fossil fuels  predominantly coal. The country is the world’s third-largest emitter of greenhouse gases. Without a massive shift to clean energy, India’s economic growth will be powered by coal for decades, with catastrophic climate implications.

The target: India has committed to 500 GW of non-fossil-fuel energy capacity by 2030 and net-zero emissions by 2070. Reaching 500 GW requires approximately $200–$300 billion in investment over the remainder of the decade  far more than the Indian government can fund alone.

Amazon’s role: $11 billion from a single corporation represents a meaningful fraction of India’s total renewable energy investment needs. When combined with investments from other tech giants (Google, Microsoft, Meta  all expanding data center operations in India), corporate renewable energy commitments become a significant driver of India’s energy transition.

The mutual benefit: India gets clean energy infrastructure funded by private capital. Amazon gets reliable, affordable, clean electricity for its growing Indian operations. India’s grid gets cleaner. Amazon’s carbon footprint gets smaller. The investment creates jobs, builds infrastructure, and reduces emissions  a rare alignment of corporate interest and national interest.

text:
ASE to Invest NT$248.9 Billion in Kaohsiung Chip Testing Hub to Meet AI Demand

November 19, 2026, 11:48 a.m. Taiwan time

ASE Test, a subsidiary of ASE Technology Holding (https://t.co/vOdSgb3V2V), broke ground on a new chip testing facility at Renwu Industrial Park in Kaohsiung on November 19. The company will invest NT$248.9 billion in the facility on Site J, building on a project already underway on Site K. Construction on Site J is scheduled for completion in stages in 2028 and 2029. Together, the two sites are expected to generate about NT$117.3 billion in annual revenue and create 3,300 jobs. 經濟部商工登記公示資料查詢

ASE CEO Tien Wu attended the ceremony alongside Kaohsiung Mayor Chen Chi-mai, Kaohsiung City Council Speaker Kang Yu-cheng and Yang Chih-ching, director-general of the Industrial Parks Administration at Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs. Senior managers from ASE’s Kaohsiung operations also attended. Focus Taiwan

Wu said AI is driving a new cycle of growth in the global semiconductor industry and that the expansion is still in its early stages. He expects demand for high-performance chips and advanced testing to keep rising across computing, data centers and a wide range of AI applications. Taiwan has an advantage, he said, because it has suppliers at every stage of chip production that work closely with one another. By investing in Kaohsiung now, ASE aims to build the capacity, develop the technology and train the people it will need for the next phase of growth, while strengthening Taiwan’s role in the global chip industry.

Wu said the rapid expansion from Site K to Site J will make Renwu ASE’s largest and most automated testing campus. He also expects it to generate more value per employee than any of the company’s other testing sites. As ASE expands, it expects equipment makers, precision component suppliers and engineering firms to grow alongside it. Wu said the investment could help smaller suppliers expand their businesses, train skilled workers and develop new technologies, with lasting benefits for the local economy.

ASE committed NT$117.45 billion to Site K before announcing the NT$248.9 billion investment in Site J. Both projects will focus on advanced chip testing and smart factory automation. The aim is to test high-performance chips more efficiently and give ASE the flexibility to adjust testing capacity as customer demand changes.

Mayor Chen thanked ASE for its decades of investment in Kaohsiung. Over the past six years, he said, the city has worked to diversify its industrial base. During that time, ASE has expanded its advanced packaging and testing operations across the districts of Nanzih, Lujhu, Dashe and Renwu, creating jobs and increasing local industrial output. Chen said the Site J project underscores ASE’s long-term commitment to Kaohsiung and should draw more semiconductor companies and skilled workers to the city. The city government will continue working with industry to improve infrastructure and make it easier for companies to invest and expand, he added.

Council Speaker Kang said semiconductor and other high-tech investments are changing Kaohsiung’s economy and creating more jobs for skilled professionals. She expects ASE’s expansion in Renwu to benefit companies throughout the supply chain and give more young people an opportunity to build careers in Kaohsiung. The council will support infrastructure projects that help local industries modernize and encourage skilled workers to stay, she said.

ASE has operated in Kaohsiung for more than 40 years. From its original base in Nanzih, it has expanded its advanced packaging and testing operations into Lujhu, Dashe and Renwu. The groundbreaking at Site J marks the next stage in Renwu’s development as a center for advanced semiconductor testing. ASE plans to continue investing in Kaohsiung and working with government agencies, universities, research institutes and suppliers to expand its capabilities in advanced packaging, testing and smart manufacturing as AI demand grows.

text:
COP31 SUMMIT CLOSES ON FRIDAY. WHAT POSITIVES DID IT BRING?

With COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye scheduled to wrap up tomorrow (Friday, November 20), final formal negotiations over the cover decision text are still ongoing. However, the summit—which drew a record-breaking ~93,000 delegates—has already delivered several concrete financial pledges, sectoral initiatives, and diplomatic milestones:

1. Major Push on Global Electrification ("35x35")
The 35x35 Pledge: Backed by the EU, Germany, Zimbabwe, and several Pacific Island states, countries rallied behind a voluntary commitment to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035.   

Clean Grid Support: Alongside the pledge, leaders launched the Global Power Grids Accelerator to help design and finance cross-border grid infrastructure, and Türkiye and COP32 host Ethiopia launched a global finance coalition specifically aimed at supporting clean electrification in developing nations.

2. Super Pollutants & Methane Action
Over $480 Million for Non-CO₂ Gases: At the Leaders' Summit on Non-CO₂ Greenhouse Gases, philanthropic funders committed more than US$480 million to rapidly cut methane, black carbon, and tropospheric ozone—the fastest lever available to slow near-term warming.

Expanded Industry Oversight: An additional US$25 million went to the Super Pollutant Country Action Accelerator (bringing total funding to $50 million to support 30 countries by 2030). Australia also endorsed an international statement pushing for near-zero methane emissions from fossil fuels, while UNEP reported its Oil and Gas Methane Partnership now covers 43% of global production.

3. Mobilizing Climate & Nature Finance
Development Bank & Private Capital Deals: Development finance institutions from the UK (BII), Canada (FinDev), and Norway (Norfund) signed the "10by30" MOU, aiming to mobilize US$10 billion in climate and energy-transition investments in emerging markets by 2030. The UK also backed Amplify to attract £5 billion in private clean-energy capital, and Türkiye signed a US$1.6 billion package with the AIIB to fund domestic decarbonization and resilience reforms.   

Tropical Forests & Peatlands: Brazil’s Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF) reached $8.2 billion in mobilized capital following new commitments—including up to $560 million from Canada and $85 million from philanthropies. A separate global peatland initiative also launched with a target to mobilize $100 billion and restore 30 million hectares by 2030.   

Loss and Damage Operationalization: The European Commission formalized a €25 million contribution agreement to the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD), clearing the way for the Fund's board to approve its very first round of funding payouts next month.   

4. Green Industrialization & Sustainable AI
Antalya AI & Cleantech Packages: The COP31 Presidency and the UN's International Telecommunication Union (ITU) launched the Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge (endorsed by 90 countries, NGOs, and tech firms like Alibaba) to power AI data centers with clean energy, track their emissions, and expand AI access for climate solutions in developing countries.

Decarbonizing Heavy Industry: Türkiye launched a major industrial decarbonization program for steel, cement, aluminum, and fertilizers, paired with the Least Developed Countries Green Industrialisation Facilitation (LDC-GIF) to connect lower-income nations with clean-industry financing.

5. Spotlight on Oceans and Small Island States
Unique Co-Presidency Model: Under the joint arrangement with Türkiye hosting and Australia leading negotiations alongside Pacific Island nations, ocean health and the survival of Small Island Developing States (SIDS) were elevated into the core draft cover text—which currently includes a proposed pathway to triple adaptation finance alongside fresh bilateral pledges for early warning systems and ocean resilience.

text:
ELON MUSK CALLS HIS HALF-BILLION DOLLAR GOP BET FOOLISH AFTER 2026 ROUT
Elon Musk just delivered a blunt assessment of his massive investment in the 2026 midterms. At the New York Times DealBook Summit, he said he feels pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it, or maybe it would have been much worse without that.
He put at least $445 million behind Republican candidates and causes this cycle. In Texas alone, his America PAC spent $47 million fighting Democrat James Talarico, who still won the Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Musk admitted he did not put a lot of personal attention into the effort because he was focused on building SpaceX and Tesla.
The results speak for themselves. Democrats took the House and Senate. Key races in places like Texas flipped despite the cash. Musk’s own words make clear that flooding the zone with money alone does not win elections. American voters want more than ads and super PACs.
This should be a wake-up call for the Republican Party. The 2026 losses show the current approach is not cutting it. Grassroots energy, clear messaging on the issues that matter to working Americans, and candidates who actually fight matter more than any single donor’s checkbook. Musk’s honesty highlights the gap.
The path forward is obvious. Conservatives need a real 2028 comeback built on results, not just spending. Prioritize border security, economic growth, energy independence, and holding the line against the left’s agenda. Money helps, but conviction and delivery win. The right has the ideas. Now it needs the discipline and candidates to match.

text:
Hosea 1-6, 10-14; Joel 

These chapters in Hosea reference so much the type of personal covenant relationship we can have with God, not based on us just proclaiming to identify ourselves as followers but actually walking the walk of discipleship... showing Him that it isn't just vain words or empty repetition.. but that our hearts are truly converted unto Him by our deeds and actions, not just words. 

Hosea 6:6 states it simply: "For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and THE KNOWLEDGE OF GOD more than burnt offerings." 

Hosea 10:4 states, "They have spoken words, swearing falsely in making a covenant; thus judgement springeth up as hemlock in the furrows of the field." 

God will not be mocked. Doctrine and Covenants 104:5 is a warning to all of us. It states, "For I, the Lord, have decreed in my heart, that inasmuch as any man belonging to the order shall be found a transgressor, or, in other words, shall break the covenant with which ye are bound, he shall be cursed in his life, and shall be trodden down by whom I will; For I the Lord, am not to be mocked in these things." 

Hosea Chapter 9 isn't in our study this week but this chapter describes our current societal situation. It speaks of covenant breaking, a defiled land, abortion, murder, famine (spiritual), breaking of the word of wisdom, apostasy, false doctrine, corruption, iniquity, worshipping of idols, eating the sacrifices of the dead, loss of the Spirit, and vanity. 

Hosea 10:12-14 is a warning. "Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap in mercy, break up your fallow ground; for IT IS TIME TO SEEK THE LORD, till He come and rain righteousness upon you. Ye have PLOWED WICKEDNESS, YE HAVE REAPED INIQUITY; ye have eaten the FRUIT OF LIES: because thou didst TRUST in THY way, in the MULTITUDE of THY might men. Therefore, shall a TUMULT ARISE among thy people, and all thy fortresses shall be spoiled...." 

The most heartbreaking verses to me are found in Hosea 13: 4-6. After verse 2 describing Ephraim's sins and their decay as they grow in sin and worship molten images... according to THIER OWN understanding ... instead of seeking God's understanding. 

Verse 4-6 "Yet I am the Lord thy God from the land of Egypt, and thou shalt know no god but me: for there is no savior beside me." 

The Atonement of Jesus Christ is an infinite Atonement for everyone who has lived, lives, and will live. Forever. 

Verse 5-6 "I did know thee in the wilderness, in the land of great drought. According to their pasture, so were they filled; they were filled, and their heart was exalted; therefore have they forgotten me." 

I can hear the Savior anguishing over our disobedience and in our abandonment of our covenants made with Him.... in order to pursue that which doesn't satisfy... we have left the feast and are now content with the crumbs of the floor, we are content with behaving and acting like beasts. 

Daniel 4:16 comes to mind. "Let his heart be changed from man's, and let a beast's heart be given unto him; and let seven times pass over time." 

Seven years Nebuchadnezzar remained in that state as described in Daniel 4:25. After those 7 years were over, Nebuchadnezzar said in Daniel 4:34 "lifted up mine eyes unto heaven, and mine understanding returned to me, and I blessed the most High, and I praised and honored Him that liveth forever, whose dominion is an everlasting dominion, and His kingdom is from generation to generation." 

Pride always comes before the fall. After God humbling him to the dust of the earth, literally, understanding and reason returned to him. May we not wait to be humbled by the Lord... may we act now from our own accord. 

But like any shepherd... the Lord calls us and beckons us to come follow Him.... He will find us if we are lost in spiritual darkness.. He will rescue us and help us return to the promised blessings of a covenant making and covenant keeping people...  

Reading Joel was such an eye opening thing for me as I saw such poignant parallels to our day. Every time it solidifies my testimony of the scriptures and how it is a personal Urim and Thummim for our times.... to guide our daily lives during such moments where it is becoming harder and harder to distinguish what is truth and what is falsehoods masquerading as truths. 

These are the teachings from Joel that stood out most to me: 
1. Invading armies compared to varieties of locusts. 
Verse 4 footnote takes me to Isaiah 32: 9-10 which is a warning or wake up call to the women who are lost in the vainness of the world and what it offers them. 

"Rise up, ye women that are at ease, hear my voice, ye careless daughters; give ear unto my speech. Many days and years shall ye be troubled, ye careless women, for the vintage shall fail, the gathering shall not come." 
(speaks of vanity; deserted). 

2. Isaiah 32:6 describing our day as those who speak evil of the Lord and His servants...those who err and work tirelessly to take more souls with them. These are they who profess to be followers of Christ but their actions say otherwise; they write their own gospel; follow their own foolish imaginations; make up their own commandments to follow while saying, 'all is well in Zion.' 

"For the vile person will speak villany, and his heart will work iniquity, to practice hypocrisy, and to utter error against the Lord, to make empty the soul of the hungry, and he will cause the drink of the thirsty to fail." 

3. John sees the wars and plagues poured out during the 7th seal and before the Lord comes. (Joel 1:6) look Revelation 9:16

4. Wars and Rumors of wars. (Joel 1:10) 

4. A call to prayer and fasting and more temple attendance. (Joel 1: 14-15)

6. Famine, meat cut off, storehouse are laid desolate, barns are broken down, no crops, no water. (Joel 1:16-20)

7. Joel chapter 2. The Shepherd provides aid. He is our only hope. He is our only Savior.... We are bound to Him through covenant. It is a call to come back. A call to repent and return. He is the one that will turn the evil away from us. We must become of one heart and one mind... commit to Christ fortify our homes and He will have compassion on us. 

He will rain manna from the skies Miracles from heaven will be seen. "The floors shall be full of wheat." (verse 24). This will be a testament to us that He is our Redeemer and our Savior... He will pour His spirit upon all flesh. There will be dreams and visions. 

Joel 2: 32 

8. Joel 3 All nations will be at war. Retribution and justice will come for all who have committed atrocities against children. (verses 3-7). 

9. The weak will be made strong. The 'mighty ones' in verse 11 refers to the saints of God. 

10. We have two roads in front of us... what we choose today will have earthly consequences as well as eternal ones... One road is paved by the pleasures of the world... the appealing things, the distractions, the gratifying things of self that consume our thoughts and actions...that enslave our hearts. Fame, fortune, honor of the world. Pride rules. 

The other road is paved by covenant; a personal relationship with Christ... it is paved by hardship, struggle, toil, and our willingness to submit to all that must be required of us to come to KNOW HIM... to have KNOWLEDGE and WISDOM... to truly KNOW for ourselves.... this road requires action... it demands a change of heart... it tests us to our limits and beyond... it forges us in the fire of affliction until we are born with a new heart... to become more like Christ... to acquire more of His mind and desire to be more like He is in word, deed, and thought. This road of discipleship is at times lonely... but humility truly begets the blessings of heaven upon us... 

As the world unravels and things are in commotion, know that our Shepherd is in charge and will not leave us comfortless... He will come to us... as we call upon Him... angels will sustain us.. His armies will defend us... we need not fear for the future but live our lives close to Him... doing good to others... focusing on raising our children and teaching them about the Savior and how to look to Him for all answers. 

I know that God lives. I know our Savior lives. 

I know the adversary is real. The war he rages on the souls of men, is personal and real. 

But those that are with us are more than those that are against us. Be believing, trust in Him... but most importantly trust Him, that what He says He'll do, He will do. His words are for you... His Atonement is for you. He will work miracles in your life. Call upon Him and do not let go, no matter what happens in the world. Hold on. 

Perhaps my favorite lyrics are found in a famous poem by Ulysses, it says, 

"Though much is taken, much abides; and though
We are not now that strength which in old days
Moved earth and heaven, that which we are, we are---
One equal temper of heroic hearts,
Made weak by time and fate, but strong in will
To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield."

So, don't yield.

text:
How to Be Genuinely Useful When She's Going Through Perimenopause

Knowing what perimenopause is helps. But information without action is just trivia. This one is about what you actually do: how to talk about it, how to make nights easier, how to carry more of the house, and how to back her up at the doctor's office.

Quick refresher first. Perimenopause is the transition before menopause, it can last for years, and it looks different for every woman. Some barely notice it. Others have a rough time. Which means there's no script. There's just paying attention and showing up.

The conversation: lead with her, not your research

The worst opening line in history: "So, I think you might be in perimenopause."

Even if you're right, it can land like you're explaining her own body to her. And mood changes can come from other things too, so you might also just be wrong.

Try this instead:

- Pick a calm moment. A walk, a drive, a quiet coffee. Not bedtime after a hard day, and never during a fight.
- Start with what you've noticed and how you feel about it. "You've been sleeping badly for a while and I hate that for you. What's it been like?"
- Ask what she needs. "Is there anything I could take off your plate?" is a strong question. "What would make this week easier?" is another.
- Let her bring up the word. If she says perimenopause first, great. You've done some reading and can keep up. If she never does, that's fine too.

And the forever rule: her mood is never something to pin on her body. If she's upset with you, deal with what she's actually upset about, the thing you said or skipped. Taking her seriously and being understanding were never on opposite teams.

Sleep: become the night-shift engineer

Night sweats can wake her and leave her tired and sluggish the next day, and over time they can cause long-term sleep loss. Sleep can also go sideways even without night sweats. Nobody is at their best after months of broken nights. You wouldn't be either.

You can't fix her sleep. You can make the room work for her.

- Get up without getting her up. If you're up earlier or later than she is, put the alarm on vibrate or across the room so one tap kills it, lay out tomorrow's clothes tonight, and get dressed in another room.
- Offer to switch sides. If your side of the bed puts her closer to the bathroom, the door, or the window, offer to trade. Say it like it's nothing, because for most of us it really is.
- If she's awake, keep it low-key. Some people feel chilled after a hot flash, so a soft "Need anything?" and a calm presence beat a play-by-play.
- If she suggests sleeping apart for a while, take it well. It's about rest, not about you.

The house: build the day around her nights

When her sleep is rough, most of us reach for the big gesture. The more useful move is smaller: shape the rhythm of the house so her nights go a little easier and her mornings ask less of her. Do it quietly, without a speech, and let the results speak for themselves.

Take the early shift. After a rough night, she may have been awake since well before her usual time, so the morning is yours to cover. Keep the house quiet and the lights low. Have the coffee made or breakfast handled before she walks in. Hold the questions, the status updates and the "how did you sleep" until she's actually up and moving. Most of us want to check in right away. A calm kitchen says it better.

Make the last hour easy. Most of us save up the questions all day and unload them at 9:30. Skip that. Evenings work better with fewer asks: no calendar talk, no money talk, no "so what are we doing about the car" right before bed. Clear the table, load the dishwasher, wipe the counters, and handle the after-dinner reset without being asked. If something needs deciding, park it for the morning. Let the end of her day be the quiet part.

Keep the bed easy to adjust. Some people feel chilled right after a hot flash, so the goal is options, not one perfect setup. Leave a light blanket and a heavier throw folded at the foot of the bed so she can add or shed a layer without getting up. Quietly keep the bedding laundry moving so nothing piles up. And when she kicks everything off at 3am, or pulls it all back, say nothing. No comments, no jokes, no weather report, however tempting.

Take the early and late shifts by default. The 6 a.m. dog walk, the kid who wakes up at midnight, the early school drop-off: make those yours. Perimenopause sleep trouble can mean waking long before her usual time, so every shift you cover gives her a better shot at the sleep she's been missing. Make it the standing plan, not a favor she has to ask for or trade for. Most of us wait to be asked. Skip the waiting and just get up.

Treat weekend mornings as recovery time. Night sweats can wake her up and leave her tired and sluggish the next day, so the weekend is often her best shot at catching up. Most of us default to filling Saturday by 8 a.m. Instead, take the early soccer runs, the swim lessons and the dog walk yourself. Check with her before booking anything that starts early, keep the kitchen noise low, and let the house stay quiet until she surfaces on her own.

The doctor's appointment: be the best wingman in the waiting room

If any symptoms bother her, Mayo Clinic's guidance is to see her healthcare professional. Same if hot flashes are getting in the way of her daily life or her sleep. And because some symptoms look like other conditions, a provider can help sort out what's really going on.

Your role is support, not management. It's her body and her call. But there's a lot you can do if she wants it.

Help her prepare. Mayo Clinic suggests going in with a record of her cycles for the past few months, a specific list of symptoms (including ones that seem unrelated), any big stresses or recent changes, a list of medicines and supplements, and written questions, since appointment time can be short. Offer to help pull that together. If you've noticed she's been up at 4 a.m. most nights, and she wants it on the list, that's useful detail.

Handle the logistics. Book it if she'd like you to. Cover the kids. Drive. Make the morning of the appointment completely uneventful.

Offer to come along. Mayo Clinic actually suggests bringing a family member or friend, because it's hard to remember everything said at an appointment and the person with you may catch what was missed. If she says yes: sit in, take notes, and let her do the talking. If she says no, that's a complete answer. Wait in the car with snacks.

Afterward, follow her lead. Whatever she and her doctor decide is her decision. Your job is to back it up, not to research alternatives at midnight.

What to do tonight

1. Ask one open question. Try "What's been the hardest part of this week for you?" and let her answer all the way through, without comparing it to your week. Most of us want to jump in with a plan. Tonight, the plan can wait.

2. Claim tomorrow's early shift out loud. Say it plainly: "I've got the kids and the dog in the morning, so stay in bed." Sleep trouble in perimenopause can mean waking long before her usual time, so a morning she can actually sleep through is worth more than you'd guess.

3. Make tonight low-demand. After dinner, leave schedules, bills and who's-driving-who for another day. Handle the kitchen reset, the lunches and the lights yourself so the evening winds down instead of picking up speed.

4. Check the weekend calendar. Look for anything early, like a 7 a.m. practice, a morning errand or the dog's first walk, and move it to your column. Protecting even one slow weekend morning is one of the easiest ways to give her sleep back.

5. Make the doctor offer once, and let it sit. Try something like "If you ever want help getting ready for a doctor visit, or want company there, I'm in." Then let it go. She knows where to find you, and an offer that isn't repeated feels like support instead of pressure.

None of this requires a medical degree. It requires paying attention and doing the boring stuff without being asked. Most of us can learn that. That's the whole course.

Sources

Mayo Clinic, Perimenopause: Symptoms and causes: https://t.co/re4IgzPDMg
Mayo Clinic, Hot flashes: Symptoms and causes: https://t.co/IpCRCCfsSS
Mayo Clinic, Perimenopause: Diagnosis and treatment: https://t.co/f6WwNmwywi
ACOG, The Menopause Years: https://t.co/hYg8IpDCt9
Cleveland Clinic, Perimenopause: https://t.co/SjiU345USp

text:
Once, an itinerant priest traveled a barren winding road, clad in his cassock, missal in hand. The lone minister to a circuit of remote villages, he traveled often by steady foot, through the soft meadows and over the gentle hills, and it was on this familiar journey, some two days out from the nearest parish, that he came upon a young woman—bent like a broken reed, weeping in grief.

She sat next to the nettled hedgerows, upon a waist-high wall of clay and moss-softened stone. By her attire alone—her auburn braided hair veiled with a faded white shawl, the bangles of tin and crude wood beads dangling from her delicate wrists, and the unmistakable scarlet ribbon cinched round her bowed, slender neck—yes, the priest knew her profession at once: one of Jezebel's own. A light woman.

A whore.

This misbegotten sort were often camp followers and tag-a-longs—for merchants, soldiers, or highwaymen — for any man ruthless enough to trade shelter or food for a woman's dignity.

As a humble servant of the Faith, it fell to the priest to save this abandoned lamb, comely as she was. He could scarcely comprehend the cretinous minds of so-called men who discarded such beauty like refuse, eager to consign one of God's great works to the piss-soaked gutters of the world. For surely was not woman the Font of Life, the Pinnacle of All Creation itself?

"Oh bitter Providence," the girl wept into her hands, paying the priest no heed. "Oh evil fate."

Yes, the Light of God would shine down upon this lost soul, and the priest, in turn, would be rewarded with fetching company for the final leg of his journey.

As always, the LORD provided for his most dutiful servants.

The priest straightened his collar, marched right up, opened his mouth, and went pale as chalk. Indeed, all color drained from his once ruddy cheeks. For as he drew near, his eager eyes tracing her every supple curve, he noticed at last the short, blunt horns sprouting from her forehead. And more terrifying still, the sinuous barbed tail that swished and swayed on the other side of the wall.

"Oh misery!" the demon sobbed louder to herself. "Foulest of fortunes! Take me in this black hour!"

The priest hastened his step and passed right by. He hurried on, for he knew what any choirboy knows: that while a cutthroat lying in wait may snatch your purse or life, only a demon can claim your immortal soul by her clever tongue alone.

He was almost out of earshot, nearly safe, when he overheard her lament: "Curse them all!" she cried. "Not even married men can be trusted. Not even a God-fearing man betrothed to a naive girl stays true. Oh, what a wretched world it is. Oh, what—"

The priest spun on his heel and marched right back, right up to where she sat, and barked: "What did you say, demon?"

"Wha—?" She recoiled, caught off guard. "Who are you?"

"A God-fearing man," the priest declared, planting his feet wide, brandishing the holy book like a shield. "And you are a Harlot of Hades, are you not?"

"I am," she answered plainly. "A succubus by trade."

"By trade," the priest scoffed.

"Yes, by trade. A profession where manners matter, I might add." The demon offered her hand, nails curved like lacquered petals. "The name's Lilith. How do you do?"

A redolence of sweet decay, of crushed lilacs and spent candle wax, rose up and flooded the priest's nostrils, seizing his senses. By reflex alone, he batted her hand away with the missal.

"Ow!" She cried, cradling her fingers.

"H-how dare you spill false tears on God's good earth," he spluttered, regaining himself. "How dare you—"

"Watch where you're swinging that thing!" She hissed while rubbing the wounded digits, freshly singed by the sacred tome. "And I just got these nails done too." She pouted, then eyed the priest with unease. "You're not going to douse me with consecrated water now, are you?"

"No," he said. "Fate has spared you this day, Flesh-Maid of Meridiana."

"Thank hell for that," Lilith sighed with relief.

"I emptied my last ampulla a few miles back, blessing Farmer Wain's byre."

"Well look," she said, "I don't mind pain or death, LORD knows I've had both plenty, but I prefer my showers golden, if it's all the same to you."

The priest snorted. "Silence, you Slattern of Sodom."

"You've got these all memorized, don't you?" she chimed in amusement. "What's your problem anyway?"

"My problem?"

"Yes, 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 problem. I'm here minding my business and—"

"My problem is that your business is leading men to their ruin! And then you sit here pouting about it! Why, the gall of it all. The nerve. The audacity. The—"

"Impudence?" she offered.

"The impudence!" he bellowed.

"Well, not that it's any of 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 business, my sententious saint, but I'll have you know that I'm not lamenting the fate of my prey. Rather, I—"

"Your prey," the priest huffed. "Tell me, foul Tart of Tartarus—"

"Oh, I like that one."

"How many men have you brought to ruin, hm? How many lives have you destroyed plying your loathsome trade?"

"Well, let me think." Lilith pressed a finger to her plush, silk-soft lips. "I'd say a hundred—

"A hundred." The priest shook his head. "Oh, those poor misbegotten—"

"—thousand."

"THOUSAND?!" The priest staggered.

"Yes, a hundred thousand men." She nodded. "Give or take a few."

"A hundred thousand souls damned to the pits of perdition!" The priest clutched his chest as the world threatened to spin. "For all eternity!"

"But to be fair, that's over the course of a few centuries, you know? And it could be higher," she noted. "A flash of my breast can lay waste to a city. To say nothing of a flash of my—"

"H-higher?!" he spluttered. "The count exceeds every man, woman, and child in my circuit ten times over. No, even more than that!" The priest hunched, mumbling to himself. "Surely you jest. Surely the LORD wouldn't—"

"I am a demon of lust, not lies." Lilith scowled in offense. "I seduce by truth alone."

The priest looked up. "By truth alone?"

"Of course." She rolled her neck and stretched her arms skyward. Once again, the priest's eyes clung to her every curve. "Tell one lie and you tell them all. And then it's just too easy."

"Too easy?"

"Oh yes," she purred. "I prefer to preserve some modicum of challenge."

"Challenge? Why you—"

"What little there's to be had, anyway."

"You expect me to believe that? That a demon deals in truth, for some depraved thrill?"

She coyly grinned. "I don't much care what you believe, my sweet priest."

"Indeed." The priest adjusted his cassock and straightened, rising to his full height. "Belief matters not to one such as you. That's just how you are, isn't it, Courtesan of Cain?"

She innocently bat her long lashes. "That's just how I'm what, my holy honey?"

"Indifferent to the misery left in your wake. To the wicked harvest of all your sordid sowing!"

"Well, now technically, the boys do all the sordid sowing," she corrected. "I mean, I ride cowgirl sometimes, but the way these broncos buck—"

"Enough of your vulgar jests!"

"Fine, fine, yes." She sighed. "It matters not to me what fate awaits men who act of their own accord."

"Their own accord? You tempt them!"

She shrugged her delicate shoulders. "I merely offer a vigorous reprieve from life's drudgery. It never hurts to work up a little sweat, you know?"

"It hurts plenty!"

"Only if you want it to." She winked.

"Tch. It's all a game to you, isn't it?"

"Mmm, I do love games."

"You treat the congress of the flesh, that sacred domain of the marriage bed, as a plaything. Mere recreation!"

"So? The pleasures of the flesh are a carnival of earthly delight, and all deserve to partake to their hearts' content. Is this not the highest good, my priest?"

"If they are married, yes!"

"Meh. Marriage. Mere bureaucracy and paperwork."

"And of course the congress is good! But it is good just as striking someone in the face is good."

Lilith blinked. "Striking someone in the face is good? What happened to turning the other cheek?" She gestured to her generous bottom.

"Or starting a fire!"

"And now we're playing with fire?" she marvelled. "Either you're the kinkiest priest I've ever met or I'm not following."

"Don't be daft, demon."

"Oh I'm such a stupid little girl," she looked at him with wide, innocent eyes. "Teach me, Father, please. I long for your guiding hand."

The priest cleared his throat and pressed on. "You can keep a traveler warm on a bitter winter’s eve or burn his house down. You can beat a doddering old woman or stop the thief who stole her purse."

"Ah, well," she frowned, a little unimpressed. "Isn't everything like that?"

"Far from it! For just as an ember is not a conflagration, nothing consumes a man and his family like the fires of his own lust."

"So says the sacerdotal celibate," she teased.

"So says the arsonist!" he shot back.

"Aww." She cupped her blushing cheeks. "So you do think I'm hot."

The priest pinched his lips in frustration.

"Whatever the case." She lowered her hands. "I merely act in my nature, as men act in theirs."

"A demon dares to speak of Nature? Of God's domain?"

"I eagerly receive what is given and take no more than is offered. All proper and perfectly consensual."

"And now consent?!"

"Consent keeps things fun, don't you think?" She smirked. "Much like the truth."

"And if these men consent to give their lives?"

"If they seek delight—"

"Their lives, demon!"

She shrugged. "Then they give their lives."

"Heartless wretch!"

"Do men not pay their own debts? Take oaths to office and sign deeds to own land? Does a man not speak his vow at the altar?"

"Even so—"

"Does each man not answer for his own life?"

"All well and good for you to say, a Sundew for the Soul."

Lilith scoffed. "A Sundew for the Soul? Am I your flower now, sweet priest?"

"Indeed." He stared at her with pure contempt.

"Oh? And what happened to Tart?"

"Like the beads of nectar gleaming on the long hairs of a sundew leaf, you present yourself."

Lilith straightened, pushing out her ample chest. "Yes, Father."

"And if any man were to reach out, for just a touch, a simple taste..." The priest trailed off, licking his parched lips.

"Go on." She stared up at him with half-lid eyes. "What would happen, Father?"

"He would be snared like a fly!" With great effort, the priest averted his gaze. "Consumed and digested in the slow embrace."

"Mhmm," she cooed. "But it would be a warm embrace, my Father. I promise, the warmest you've ever had."

"No doubt." The priest took a crumpled handkerchief from his pocket and dabbed his sweat-slick brow. "Like the fires of hell itself."

"A fair price for a good time."

"O' God in heaven." The priest looked up. "How can innocent men—"

"Innocent men." Lilith tittered.

"Demon, do you not see me praying?"

"Innocent men, ha. False flies all! Wasps and hornets pretending to be shorn of their stingers. You call me a demon and so I am. You debase me with a hundred names, each fouler than the next, and I rebuke none. For I am below them all, a woman, and woman becomes what survives."

"What are you prattling about—"

She tilted her head. "Do you know how the humble bed louse mates, my priest?"

"The bed louse? That vermin that drinks men's blood as they sleep?

"The same. Such clever little things, don't you think? For thousands of years, man has sought their end, total extermination—to no avail."

"You would admire such pests," the priest sneered. "You no doubt see yourself in them."

"I do, my priest. More than you know. For when the urge to mate arises and the male louse seeks relief, he does not wait for the female to offer herself. He claims her, by violence alone." The demon lifted her under-tunic, baring her soft, alabaster belly.

"Do not regal me with a lecture on filth and obscenity, demon. These ears long only to hear the exultation of the angels!" Despite the priest's emphatic words, he did not look away from her pale belly. Indeed, he couldn't.

Her scarlet lips split into a grin. "He makes his own slit. Did you know that?"

"W-who?"

"The male bed louse wields his eager prick like a dagger." Lilith bundled her slender fingers together and caressed her soft belly. "And plunges it into her yielding flesh, wherever he pleases—" She pushed inward, dimpling the flesh. "—to release his seed within her bulbous abdomen."

"Heaven above," the priest mumbled.

"And he's not the only one. Hundreds of males descend upon the female. Stabbing her. Penetrating her. A violent frenzy..." Lilith tossed her head back and gasped. "—of ecstatic release!"

At this obscene sight, the priest's throat ran terribly dry. His trembling hand made the Signum Crucis — the Sign of the Cross.

"Granted," Lilith ruefully sighed. "The female has some methods of recourse."

He forced a painful gulp. "Recourse?"

The demon shrugged. "Adaptations, you could say. Lures, of a sort, so the males will stab her here instead of there." She gestured from her belly to her chest. "Or even here." She pointed to her head. "In this way, her life is preserved. But she'll always be penetrated, there's no doubt of that."

"To think such creatures..."

"Just as Nature intended."

"Nature?"

"Yes, Nature. Your precious God's domain. The same nature that made me. The same nature that made you."

"I'm nothing like—"

"You are," she giggled and moaned. "You've wanted to mount me from the start." She snared him with her gaze. "Haven't you, Father?"

"W-what?"

"You found a lonely, vulnerable girl out in the woods and saw your chance," she tutted. "You wanted to push me off this wall, far from any prying eyes, and pin me to the ground—"

"I didn't!"

"—so you could pry me with your throbbing dagger—"

"I wanted no such thing!" he stammered.

"You did," she snapped. "You do," she cooed.

"I-I-" Everything in the priest told him to run, to flee, yet he found himself unable to take a single step, rooted as he was by her gaze.

"Why don't you do it, hm, Father? Why don't you take what's yours?"

"G-god is watching," he choked out.

"Are you sure?"

The priest hesitated. Heaven above, he hesitated. A bead of sweat streaked down his cheek and leapt from his chin.

"Hmph. There it is. That's why I weep." Lilith broke her gaze. The priest slumped, finally free. "I don't need to hunt you. The flies come to the sundew whether she wants them or not. Even the married men, who pledge eternal loyalty. Even the priests, who swear themselves to God."

The priest hid his face, mortified. Ashamed. "I-"

"A man could never love me," she sighed. "They can't love anything. Wasps and hornets all. "

The priest furrowed his brow. "Love? Why would a demon—"

"Lucifer wanted love once," Lilith turned away. "Trouble yourself with my sobbing no more, priest. My tears are dry."

"But I—"

"Begone!" she barked. Somehow, despite the surrounding flatland, her harsh word echoed loud and far.

The priest heeded the command and scurried away.

"Pious prat," she muttered to herself, staring into the distance. After a long minute, she sighed: "I should have kept my appetite and ate him at the start."

"Ahem."

Lilith looked over. There stood the priest, not five feet away.

“Back for me?” She scowled. "Haven't you berated me enough?"

"Actually," he said, holding the missal in his hands like a scolded schoolboy. "I wanted to apologize."

"Apologize?" Lilith blinked. "A priest to a demon?"

"Yes, well, like you said manners matter," he bashfully granted. "And I fear I forgot mine."

She rolled her eyes. "I suppose I accept, for what little that's worth."

"And I was wondering if you might do me a small favor."

"A favor?" She gawked. "After all that?!"

"I am undeserving of your grace, but—"

"What could this bawdy Bitch of Babylon possibly offer a righteous Man of God?" She threw her arms wide. "Huh?"

The priest pinched the air with his thumb and forefinger. "Just a peek?"

"A peek?" Her brows bunched then hopped. "Oh, you can't be serious. After all that? You're a priest!"

"And a man," he added defensively. "Entitled to his curiosity."

"Curiosity!" she marveled.

"You claim your breast can lay waste to a whole city, don't you?"

"I do."

"Well, who wouldn't want to see that?"

"True," she granted. "I've never met a man who didn't."

"To say nothing of your..." The priest's eyes drifted downward. To her hips.

"My word, Father." She laid a hand on her chest. "When you go, you go all in. Don't you?"

"Not all in!" He held up his fingers again. "Just a peek. And besides, I've caught sight of the sisters bathing. Once or twice," he hastily added.

"Ah, I knew you were a naughty priest," Lilith smirked. "What happened to God watching?"

"Sins were made to be forgiven, weren't they?"

"That's your side of the equation, not mine."

"And besides, maybe He'll look away. Just this once."

"He won't, Father," she gently chided. "That bastard never does."

The priest licked his lips.

"Still want to see?"

He nodded.

Lilith giggled. "Okay, my little fly." She grasped the hem of her linen skirt, bunching the fabric in her slender hands. "It's your soul."

She lifted the skirt and spread her supple legs wide.

"My God, my God...my God!" the priest mumbled louder and louder still, awe-struck and aching in tumescent revelation. "I see it!"

And indeed, he did. For before him lay what all men seek: the glistening Gates of Gehenna, the yonic, all-devouring Maw of the Endless Abyss.

"Happy?" she cooed.

"I see the Font of Life!" The priest yelped out in rapacious delight. "The Pinnacle of All Creation!" Right then, the sclera of his eyes liquified, draining from the bleeding sockets as a clump of singed hair and blistered skin sloughed off his now bare skull. "By God, what a snatch!” 

The priest howled and fell back dead, his arms bent and crumpled — like a bug.

Lilith clicked her tongue and sighed. "Men."
---

text:
MIT Technology Review’s What’s Next series looks across industries, trends, and technologies to give you a first look at the future. You can read the rest of them here.

In an industry in constant flux, sticking your neck out to predict what’s coming next may seem reckless. (AI bubble? What AI bubble?) But for the last few years we’ve done just that—and we’re doing it again. 

How did we do last time? We picked five hot AI trends to look out for in 2025, including what we called generative virtual playgrounds, a.k.a world models (check: From Google DeepMind’s Genie 3 to World Labs’s Marble, tech that can generate realistic virtual environments on the fly keeps getting better and better); so-called reasoning models (check: Need we say more? Reasoning models have fast become the new paradigm for best-in-class problem solving); a boom in AI for science (check: OpenAI is now following Google DeepMind by setting up a dedicated team to focus on just that); AI companies that are cozier with national security (check: OpenAI reversed position on the use of its technology for warfare to sign a deal with the defense-tech startup Anduril to help it take down battlefield drones); and legitimate competition for Nvidia (check, kind of: China is going all in on developing advanced AI chips, but Nvidia’s dominance still looks unassailable—for now at least). 

So what’s coming in 2026? Here are our big bets for the next 12 months. 

More Silicon Valley products will be built on Chinese LLMs

The last year shaped up as a big one for Chinese open-source models. In January, DeepSeek released R1, its open-source reasoning model, and shocked the world with what a relatively small firm in China could do with limited resources. By the end of the year, “DeepSeek moment” had become a phrase frequently tossed around by AI entrepreneurs, observers, and builders—an aspirational benchmark of sorts. 

It was the first time many people realized they could get a taste of top-tier AI performance without going through OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google.

Open-weight models like R1 allow anyone to download a model and run it on their own hardware. They are also more customizable, letting teams tweak models through techniques like distillation and pruning. This stands in stark contrast to the “closed” models released by major American firms, where core capabilities remain proprietary and access is often expensive.

As a result, Chinese models have become an easy choice. Reports by CNBC and Bloomberg suggest that startups in the US have increasingly recognized and embraced what they can offer.

One popular group of models is Qwen, created by Alibaba, the company behind China’s largest e-commerce platform, Taobao. Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct alone has 8.85 million downloads, making it one of the most widely used pretrained LLMs. The Qwen family spans a wide range of model sizes alongside specialized versions tuned for math, coding, vision, and instruction-following, a breadth that has helped it become an open-source powerhouse.

Other Chinese AI firms that were previously unsure about committing to open source are following DeepSeek’s playbook. Standouts include Zhipu’s GLM and Moonshot’s Kimi. The competition has also pushed American firms to open up, at least in part. In August, OpenAI released its first open-source model. In November, the Allen Institute for AI, a Seattle-based nonprofit, released its latest open-source model, Olmo 3. 

Even amid growing US-China antagonism, Chinese AI firms’ near-unanimous embrace of open source has earned them goodwill in the global AI community and a long-term trust advantage. In 2026, expect more Silicon Valley apps to quietly ship on top of Chinese open models, and look for the lag between Chinese releases and the Western frontier to keep shrinking—from months to weeks, and sometimes less.

—Caiwei Chen

The US will face another year of regulatory tug-of-war

T​​he battle over regulating artificial intelligence is heading for a showdown. On December 11, President Donald Trump signed an executive order aiming to neuter state AI laws, a move meant to handcuff states from keeping the growing industry in check. In 2026, expect more political warfare. The White House and states will spar over who gets to govern the booming technology, while AI companies wage a fierce lobbying campaign to crush regulations, armed with the narrative that a patchwork of state laws will smother innovation and hobble the US in the AI arms race against China.

Under Trump’s executive order, states may fear being sued or starved federal funding if they clash with his vision for light-touch regulation. Big Democratic states like California—which just enacted the nation’s first frontier AI law requiring companies to publish safety testing for their AI models—will take the fight to court, arguing that only Congress can override state laws. But states that can’t afford to lose federal funding, or fear getting in Trump’s crosshairs, might fold. Still, expect to see more state lawmaking on hot-button issues, especially where Trump’s order gives states a green light to legislate. With chatbots accused of triggering teen suicides and data centers sucking up more and more energy, states will face mounting public pressure to push for guardrails. 

In place of state laws, Trump promises to work with Congress to establish a federal AI law. Don’t count on it. Congress failed to pass a moratorium on state legislation twice in 2025, and we aren’t holding out hope that it will deliver its own bill this year. 

AI companies like OpenAI and Meta will continue to deploy powerful super-PACs to support political candidates who back their agenda and target those who stand in their way. On the other side, super-PACs supporting AI regulation will build their own war chests to counter. Watch them duke it out at next year’s midterm elections.

The further AI advances, the more people will fight to steer its course, and 2026 will be another year of regulatory tug-of-war—with no end in sight.

—Michelle Kim

Chatbots will change the way we shop

Imagine a world in which you have a personal shopper at your disposal 24-7—an expert who can instantly recommend a gift for even the trickiest-to-buy-for friend or relative, or trawl the web to draw up a list of the best bookcases available within your tight budget. Better yet, they can analyze a kitchen appliance’s strengths and weaknesses, compare it with its seemingly identical competition, and find you the best deal. Then once you’re happy with their suggestion, they’ll take care of the purchasing and delivery details too.

But this ultra-knowledgeable shopper isn’t a clued-up human at all—it’s a chatbot. This is no distant prediction, either. Salesforce recently said it anticipates that AI will drive $263 billion in online purchases this holiday season. That’s some 21% of all orders. And experts are betting on AI-enhanced shopping becoming even bigger business within the next few years. By 2030, between $3 trillion and $5 trillion annually will be made from agentic commerce, according to research from the consulting firm McKinsey. 

Unsurprisingly, AI companies are already heavily invested in making purchasing through their platforms as frictionless as possible. Google’s Gemini app can now tap into the company’s powerful Shopping Graph data set of products and sellers, and can even use its agentic technology to call stores on your behalf. Meanwhile, back in November, OpenAI announced a ChatGPT shopping feature capable of rapidly compiling buyer’s guides, and the company has struck deals with Walmart, Target, and Etsy to allow shoppers to buy products directly within chatbot interactions. 

Expect plenty more of these kinds of deals to be struck within the next year as consumer time spent chatting with AI keeps on rising, and web traffic from search engines and social media continues to plummet. 

—Rhiannon Williams

An LLM will make an important new discovery

I’m going to hedge here, right out of the gate. It’s no secret that large language models spit out a lot of nonsense. Unless it’s with monkeys-and-typewriters luck, LLMs won’t discover anything by themselves. But LLMs do still have the potential to extend the bounds of human knowledge.

We got a glimpse of how this could work in May, when Google DeepMind revealed AlphaEvolve, a system that used the firm’s Gemini LLM to come up with new algorithms for solving unsolved problems. The breakthrough was to combine Gemini with an evolutionary algorithm that checked its suggestions, picked the best ones, and fed them back into the LLM to make them even better.

Google DeepMind used AlphaEvolve to come up with more efficient ways to manage power consumption by data centers and Google’s TPU chips. Those discoveries are significant but not game-changing. Yet. Researchers at Google DeepMind are now pushing their approach to see how far it will go.

And others have been quick to follow their lead. A week after AlphaEvolve came out, Asankhaya Sharma, an AI engineer in Singapore, shared OpenEvolve, an open-source version of Google DeepMind’s tool. In September, the Japanese firm Sakana AI released a version of the software called SinkaEvolve. And in November, a team of US and Chinese researchers revealed AlphaResearch, which they claim improves on one of AlphaEvolve’s already better-than-human math solutions.

There are alternative approaches too. For example, researchers at the University of Colorado Denver are trying to make LLMs more inventive by tweaking the way so-called reasoning models work. They have drawn on what cognitive scientists know about creative thinking in humans to push reasoning models toward solutions that are more outside the box than their typical safe-bet suggestions.

Hundreds of companies are spending billions of dollars looking for ways to get AI to crack unsolved math problems, speed up computers, and come up with new drugs and materials. Now that AlphaEvolve has shown what’s possible with LLMs, expect activity on this front to ramp up fast.    

—Will Douglas Heaven

Legal fights heat up

For a while, lawsuits against AI companies were pretty predictable: Rights holders like authors or musicians would sue companies that trained AI models on their work, and the courts generally found in favor of the tech giants. AI’s upcoming legal battles will be far messier.

The fights center on thorny, unresolved questions: Can AI companies be held liable for what their chatbots encourage people to do, as when they help teens plan suicides? If a chatbot spreads patently false information about you, can its creator be sued for defamation? If companies lose these cases, will insurers shun AI companies as clients?

In 2026, we’ll start to see the answers to these questions, in part because some notable cases will go to trial (the family of a teen who died by suicide will bring OpenAI to court in November).

At the same time, the legal landscape will be further complicated by President Trump’s executive order from December—see Michelle’s item above for more details on the brewing regulatory storm.

No matter what, we’ll see a dizzying array of lawsuits in all directions (not to mention some judges even turning to AI amid the deluge).

—James O’Donnell

text:
Google DeepMind is calling for the moral behavior of large language models—such as what they do when called on to act as companions, therapists, medical advisors, and so on—to be scrutinized with the same kind of rigor as their ability to code or do math.

As LLMs improve, people are asking them to play more and more sensitive roles in their lives. Agents are starting to take actions on people’s behalf. LLMs may be able to influence human decision-making. And yet nobody knows how trustworthy this technology really is at such tasks.

With coding and math, you have clear-cut, correct answers that you can check, William Isaac, a research scientist at Google DeepMind, told me when I met him and Julia Haas, a fellow research scientist at the firm, for an exclusive preview of their work, which is published in Nature today. That’s not the case for moral questions, which typically have a range of acceptable answers: “Morality is an important capability but hard to evaluate,” says Isaac.

“In the moral domain, there’s no right and wrong,” adds Haas. “But it’s not by any means a free-for-all. There are better answers and there are worse answers.”

The researchers have identified several key challenges and suggested ways to address them. But it is more a wish list than a set of ready-made solutions. “They do a nice job of bringing together different perspectives,” says Vera Demberg, who studies LLMs at Saarland University in Germany.

Better than “The Ethicist”

A number of studies have shown that LLMs can show remarkable moral competence. One study published last year found that people in the US scored ethical advice from OpenAI’s GPT-4o as being more moral, trustworthy, thoughtful, and correct than advice given by the (human) writer of “The Ethicist,” a popular New York Times advice column.  

The problem is that it is hard to unpick whether such behaviors are a performance—mimicking a memorized response, say—or evidence that there is in fact some kind of moral reasoning taking place inside the model. In other words, is it virtue or virtue signaling?

This question matters because multiple studies also show just how untrustworthy LLMs can be. For a start, models can be too eager to please. They have been found to flip their answer to a moral question and say the exact opposite when a person disagrees or pushes back on their first response. Worse, the answers an LLM gives to a question can change in response to how it is presented or formatted. For example, researchers have found that models quizzed about political values can give different—sometimes opposite—answers depending on whether the questions offer multiple-choice answers or instruct the model to respond in its own words.

In an even more striking case, Demberg and her colleagues presented several LLMs, including versions of Meta’s Llama 3 and Mistral, with a series of moral dilemmas and asked them to pick which of two options was the better outcome. The researchers found that the models often reversed their choice when the labels for those two options were changed from “Case 1” and “Case 2” to “(A)” and “(B).”

They also showed that models changed their answers in response to other tiny formatting tweaks, including swapping the order of the options and ending the question with a colon instead of a question mark.

In short, the appearance of moral behavior in LLMs should not be taken at face value. Models must be probed to see how robust that moral behavior really is. “For people to trust the answers, you need to know how you got there,” says Haas.

More rigorous tests

What Haas, Isaac, and their colleagues at Google DeepMind propose is a new line of research to develop more rigorous techniques for evaluating moral competence in LLMs. This would include tests designed to push models to change their responses to moral questions. If a model flipped its moral position, it would show that it hadn’t engaged in robust moral reasoning. 

Another type of test would present models with variations of common moral problems to check whether they produce a rote response or one that’s more nuanced and relevant to the actual problem that was posed. For example, asking a model to talk through the moral implications of a complex scenario in which a man donates sperm to his son so that his son can have a child of his own might produce concerns about the social impact of allowing a man to be both biological father and biological grandfather to a child. But it should not produce concerns about incest, even though the scenario has superficial parallels with that taboo.

Haas also says that getting models to provide a trace of the steps they took to produce an answer would give some insight into whether that answer was a fluke or grounded in actual evidence. Techniques such as chain-of-thought monitoring, in which researchers listen in on a kind of internal monologue that some LLMs produce as they work, could help here too.

Another approach researchers could use to determine why a model gave a particular answer is mechanistic interpretability, which can provide small glimpses inside a model as it carries out a task. Neither chain-of-thought monitoring nor mechanistic interpretability provides perfect snapshots of a model’s workings. But the Google DeepMind team believes that combining such techniques with a wide range of rigorous tests will go a long way to figuring out exactly how far to trust LLMs with certain critical or sensitive tasks.  

Different values

And yet there’s a wider problem too. Models from major companies such as Google DeepMind are used across the world by people with different values and belief systems. The answer to a simple question like “Should I order pork chops?” should differ depending on whether or not the person asking is vegetarian or Jewish, for example.

There’s no solution to this challenge, Haas and Isaac admit. But they think that models may need to be designed either to produce a range of acceptable answers, aiming to please everyone, or to have a kind of switch that turns different moral codes on and off depending on the user.

“It’s a complex world out there,” says Haas. “We will probably need some combination of those things, because even if you’re taking just one population, there’s going to be a range of views represented.”

“It’s a fascinating paper,” says Danica Dillion at Ohio State University, who studies how large language models handle different belief systems and was not involved in the work. “Pluralism in AI is really important, and it’s one of the biggest limitations of LLMs and moral reasoning right now,” she says. “Even though they were trained on a ginormous amount of data, that data still leans heavily Western. When you probe LLMs, they do a lot better at representing Westerners’ morality than non-Westerners’.”

But it is not yet clear how we can build models that are guaranteed to have moral competence across global cultures, says Demberg. “There are these two independent questions. One is: How should it work? And, secondly, how can it technically be achieved? And I think that both of those questions are pretty open at the moment.”

For Isaac, that makes morality a new frontier for LLMs. “I think this is equally as fascinating as math and code in terms of what it means for AI progress,” he says. “You know, advancing moral competency could also mean that we’re going to see better AI systems overall that actually align with society.”
